\caption{\label{fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-table-pair}Plot of 10
pairs of values, each pair simulated from a Normal(30, 10) model,
recorded in Table~\ref{tbl-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-table-pair}. Each
dot represents a pair. The components of each pair are marked on the
horizontal and vertical axes.}

\end{figure}%

Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-pair} displays 1000 pairs of
(Regina, Cady) arrival times, resulting from 1000 pairs of spins of the
Normal(30, 10) spinner. Compared with the simulated pairs from the
Uniform(0, 60) spinner (in
Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-uniform-sim-pair}), we see many more
simulated pairs in the center of the plot (when both arrive near 12:30)
than in the corners of the plot (where either arrives near 12:00 or
1:00). If we simulated more values and summarized them in an appropriate
plot, we would expect to see something like
Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-independent-normal}.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-pair-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-pair}Plot of 1000 pairs
of values, each pair simulated from a Normal(30, 10) model. Each dot
represents a pair. The components of each pair are marked on the
horizontal and vertical axes.}

\end{figure}%

Example~\ref{exm-meeting-box-sim} and
Example~\ref{exm-meeting-tactile-sim-normal} assumed that Regina's and
Cady's arrival times individually followed the same model, both
Uniform(0, 60) or both Normal(30, 10), so we just spun the same spinner
twice to simulate a pair of arrival times. However, we could easily
simulate from different models. Suppose Regina's arrival time follows a
Uniform(0, 60) model while Cady's follows a Normal(30, 10) model,
independently of each other. Then we could simulate a pair of arrival
times by spinning the Uniform(0, 60) spinner for Regina and the
Normal(30, 10) spinner for Cady.

So far we have assumed that Regina and Cady arrive independently, but
what if they coordinate and their arrival times are related? Recall that
Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-dependent-normal} reflects a model where Regina
and Cady each are more likely to arrive around 12:30 than noon or 1:00,
and also more likely to arrive around the same time. In such a
situation, we could still use spinners to simulate pairs of arrival
times, but it's more involved than just spinning a single spinner twice
(or having just one spinner for each person). We'll revisit using
spinners to simulate dependent pairs later.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-17}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-tactile-dartboard}{}\label{exr-tactile-dartboard}

Katniss throws a dart at a circular dartboard with radius 12 inches.
Suppose that the dart lands uniformly at random anywhere on the
dartboard, and assume that Katniss's dart never misses the dartboard.
Suppose that the dartboard is on a coordinate plane, with the center of
the dartboard at (0, 0) and the north, south, east, and west edges,
respectively, at coordinates (0, 12), (0,-12), (12, 0), (-12, 0). When
the dart hits the board its \((X, Y)\) coordinates are recorded. Let
\(R\) be the distance (inches) from the location of the dart to the
center of the dartboard.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Sketch a Uniform(0, 12) spinner.
\item
  Describe how you could use a fair coin and the Uniform(0, 12) spinner
  to simulate the \((X, Y)\) coordinates of a single throw of the dart
  and the value of \(R\). Hint: you might need to flip the coin and spin
  the spinner multiple times. What will you do if your simulated
  coordinates correspond to ``off the board''?
\item
  Suppose you want to simulate \(R\) directly. Could you just spin the
  Uniform(0, 12) spinner and record the value? Explain. Hint: see
  Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-dartboard-b}.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-tactile-dartboard-b}{}\label{exr-tactile-dartboard-b}

Continuing Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-dartboard}. Computing like we did
in Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-dartboard-b}, we can show

\begin{table}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{lr}
\toprule
Range & Probability that \$R\$ is in range\\
\midrule
0 to 1 & 0.0069\\
1 to 2 & 0.0208\\
2 to 3 & 0.0347\\
3 to 4 & 0.0486\\
4 to 5 & 0.0625\\
\addlinespace
5 to 6 & 0.0764\\
6 to 7 & 0.0903\\
7 to 8 & 0.1042\\
8 to 9 & 0.1181\\
9 to 10 & 0.1319\\
\addlinespace
10 to 11 & 0.1458\\
11 to 12 & 0.1597\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sketch a spinner that could be used to simulate values of \(R\). You
should label 12 sectors on the spinner. Hint: the sectors won't be the
same size and the values on the outside axis of the spinner won't be
evenly spaced.

\end{exercise}

\section{Computer simulation: Dice rolling}\label{sec-technology-intro}

We will perform computer simulations using the Python package Symbulate.
The syntax of Symbulate mirrors the language of probability in that the
primary objects in Symbulate are the same as the primary components of a
probability model: probability spaces, random variables, events. Once
these components are specified, Symbulate allows users to simulate many
times from the probability model and summarize the results.

This section contains a brief introduction to Symbulate; more examples
can be found throughout the text. Symbulate can be installed with
\texttt{pip}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pip install git}\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{https:}\OperatorTok{//}\NormalTok{github.com}\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{kevindavisross}\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{symbulate}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Import Symbulate during a Python session using the following command.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ symbulate }\ImportTok{import} \OperatorTok{*}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We'll start with a dice rolling example. Unless indicated otherwise, in
this section \(X\) represents the sum of two rolls of a \emph{fair}
four-sided die, and \(Y\) represents the larger of the two rolls (or the
common value if a tie). We have already discussed a tactile simulation;
now we'll carry out the process on a computer.

There aren't many examples for you to work in this section. Instead, we
encourage you to open a Python session and copy and run the code as you
read. In particular, you can run Python code using this
\href{https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1YU0BaezMxInwCT5IP1TdSVJd9w2uYwim?usp=sharing}{template
Colab notebook} which includes the code needed to get started with
Symbulate.

\subsection{Simulating outcomes}\label{simulating-outcomes}

The following Symbulate code defines a probability space\footnote{We
  primarily view a Symbulate probability space as a description of the
  probability model rather than an explicit specification of the sample
  space \(\Omega\). For example, we define a \texttt{BoxModel} instead
  of creating a set with all possible outcomes. We tend to represent a
  probability space with \texttt{P}, even though this is a slight abuse
  of notation (since \(\textrm{P}\) typically refers to a probability
  measure).} \texttt{P} for simulating the 16 equally likely ordered
pairs of rolls via a box model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The above code tells Symbulate to draw 2 tickets (\texttt{size\ =\ 2}),
with replacement\footnote{The default argument for \texttt{replace} is
  \texttt{True}, so we could have just written
  \texttt{BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]},\ size\ =\ 2)}.}, from a box with
tickets labeled 1, 2, 3, and 4 (entered as the Python list
\texttt{{[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]}}). Each simulated outcome consists of an
ordered\footnote{There is an additional argument \texttt{order\_matters}
  which defaults to \texttt{True}, but we could set it to \texttt{False}
  for unordered pairs.} pair of rolls .

The \texttt{sim(r)} command simulates \texttt{r} realizations of
probability space outcomes (or events or random variables). Here is the
result of one repetition.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 3)
\end{verbatim}

And here are the results of 10 repetitions. (We will typically run
thousands of repetitions, or more, but in this section we just run a few
repetitions for illustration.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (1, 2)
1     (2, 1)
2     (4, 3)
3     (3, 2)
4     (4, 4)
5     (4, 3)
6     (4, 1)
7     (1, 4)
8     (4, 3)
9     (3, 2)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Warning}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

Every time \texttt{.sim()} is called, a new simulation is run.
\textbf{When running a simulation, the ``simulate'' step should be
performed with a \emph{single} call to \texttt{sim}} so that all
analysis of results corresponds to the same simulated values. We'll show
how to do this below.

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Simulating random
variables}\label{simulating-random-variables}

A Symbulate \texttt{RV} is specified by the probability space on which
it is defined and the mapping function which defines it. Recall that
\(X\) is the sum of the two dice rolls and \(Y\) is the larger (max).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The above code simply defines the random variables. Again, we can
simulate values with \texttt{.sim()}. Since every call to \texttt{sim}
runs a new simulation, we typically store the simulation results as an
object. The following commands simulate 100 values of the random
variable \texttt{X} and store the results as \texttt{x}. For consistency
with standard probability notation\footnote{We generally use names in
  our code that mirror and reinforce standard probability notation,
  e.g., uppercase letters near the end of the alphabet for random
  variables, with corresponding lowercase letters for their realized
  values. Of course, these naming conventions are not necessary and you
  are welcome to use more descriptive names in your code. For example,
  we could have named the probability space \texttt{DiceRolls} and the
  random variables \texttt{DiceSum} and \texttt{DiceMax} rather than
  \texttt{P,\ X,\ Y}. Whatever you do, we encourage you to use names
  that distinguish the objects themselves from their simulated values,
  e.g.~\texttt{Dice\_Sum} for the random variable and
  \texttt{dice\_sum\_sim} for the simulated values.}, the random
variable itself is denoted with an uppercase letter \texttt{X}, while
the realized values of it are denoted with a lowercase letter
\texttt{x}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x }\CommentTok{\# this just displays x; only the first few and last values will print}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     5
1     4
2     5
3     2
4     5
5     8
6     7
7     5
8     2
..    .
99    4
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Simulating multiple random
variables}\label{simulating-multiple-random-variables}

If we call \texttt{X.sim(10000)} and \texttt{Y.sim(10000)} we get two
separate simulations of 10000 pairs of rolls, one which returns the sum
of the rolls for each repetition, and the other the max. If we want to
study relationships between \(X\) and \(Y\) we need to compute both
\(X\) and \(Y\) for each pair of rolls in the same simulation.

We can simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs using\footnote{Technically \texttt{\&}
  joins two \texttt{RV}s together to form a random \emph{vector}. While
  we often interpret Symbulate \texttt{RV} as ``random variable'', it
  really functions as ``random vector''.} \texttt{\&}. We store the
simulation output as \texttt{x\_and\_y} to emphasize that
\texttt{x\_and\_y} contains pairs of values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\CommentTok{\# this just displays x\_and\_y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (5, 3)
1     (6, 4)
2     (5, 4)
3     (7, 4)
4     (4, 3)
5     (2, 1)
6     (2, 1)
7     (8, 4)
8     (6, 4)
9     (6, 4)
\end{verbatim}

Think of \texttt{x\_and\_y} as a table with two columns. We can select
columns using brackets \texttt{{[}{]}}. Remember that Python uses
zero-based indexing, so 0 corresponds to the first column, 1 to the
second, etc.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     5
1     6
2     5
3     7
4     4
5     2
6     2
7     8
8     6
9     6
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     3
1     4
2     4
3     4
4     3
5     1
6     1
7     4
8     4
9     4
\end{verbatim}

We can also select multiple columns.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (5, 3)
1     (6, 4)
2     (5, 4)
3     (7, 4)
4     (4, 3)
5     (2, 1)
6     (2, 1)
7     (8, 4)
8     (6, 4)
9     (6, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Simulating outcomes and random
variables}\label{simulating-outcomes-and-random-variables}

When calling \texttt{X.sim(10)} or \texttt{(X\ \&\ Y).sim(10)} the
outcomes of the rolls are generated in the background but not saved. We
can create a \texttt{RV} which returns the outcomes of the probability
space\footnote{You might try \texttt{(P\ \&\ X).sim(10)}. But \texttt{P}
  is a probability space object, and \texttt{X} is an \texttt{RV}
  object, and \texttt{\&} can only be used to join like objects
  together. Much like in probability theory in general, in Symbulate the
  probability space plays a background role, and it is usually random
  variables we are interested in.}. The default mapping function for
\texttt{RV} is the identity function, \(g(u) = u\), so simulating values
of \texttt{U\ =\ RV(P)} below returns the outcomes of the BoxModel
\texttt{P} representing the outcome of the two rolls.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{U.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (3, 3)
1     (1, 1)
2     (3, 2)
3     (2, 2)
4     (4, 3)
5     (2, 3)
6     (2, 3)
7     (2, 3)
8     (1, 2)
9     (3, 2)
\end{verbatim}

Now we can simulate and display the outcomes along with the values of
\(X\) and \(Y\) using \texttt{\&}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(U }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     ((3, 1), 4, 3)
1     ((3, 3), 6, 3)
2     ((4, 3), 7, 4)
3     ((2, 3), 5, 3)
4     ((4, 3), 7, 4)
5     ((2, 2), 4, 2)
6     ((4, 4), 8, 4)
7     ((2, 1), 3, 2)
8     ((4, 4), 8, 4)
9     ((4, 4), 8, 4)
\end{verbatim}

Because the probability space \texttt{P} returns pairs of values,
\texttt{U\ =\ RV(P)} above defines a random vector. The individual
components\footnote{The components of an \texttt{RV} can also be
  accessed using brackets. \texttt{U1,\ U2\ =\ RV(P)} is shorthand for\\
  \texttt{U\ =\ RV(P);\ U1\ =\ U{[}0{]};\ U2\ =\ U{[}1{]}}.} of
\texttt{U} can be ``unpacked'' as \texttt{U1,\ U2} in the following.
Here \texttt{U1} is an \texttt{RV} representing the result of the first
roll and \texttt{U2} the second.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U1, U2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}
\NormalTok{(U1 }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ U2 }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 4, 6, 4)
1     (1, 2, 3, 2)
2     (1, 1, 2, 1)
3     (2, 1, 3, 2)
4     (4, 2, 6, 4)
5     (2, 2, 4, 2)
6     (3, 2, 5, 3)
7     (4, 2, 6, 4)
8     (1, 3, 4, 3)
9     (4, 3, 7, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Simulating events}\label{simulating-events}

Events involving random variables can also be defined and simulated. For
programming reasons, events are enclosed in parentheses \texttt{()}
rather than braces \(\{\}\). For example, we can define the event that
the larger of the two rolls is less than 3, \(A=\{Y<3\}\), as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\# an event}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We can use \texttt{sim} to simulate events. A realization of an event is
\texttt{True} if the event occurs for the simulated outcome, or
\texttt{False} if not.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     False
1     False
2     False
3     True
4     False
5     True
6     False
7     False
8     True
9     False
\end{verbatim}

For logical equality use a double equal sign \texttt{==}. For example,
\texttt{(Y\ ==\ 3)} represents the event \(\{Y=3\}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     True
1     True
2     False
3     False
4     False
5     True
6     False
7     False
8     False
9     False
\end{verbatim}

In most situations, events of interest involve random variables. It is
much more common to simulate random variables directly, rather than
events; see Section~\ref{sec-symbulate-two-worlds} for further
discussion. Events are primarily used in Symbulate for conditioning.

\subsection{Simulating transformations of random
variables}\label{simulating-transformations-of-random-variables}

Transformations of random variables (defined on the same probability
space) are random variables. If \texttt{X} is a Symbulate \texttt{RV}
and \texttt{g} is a function, then \texttt{g(X)} is also a Symbulate
\texttt{RV}.

For example, we can simulate values of \(X^2\). (In Python,
exponentiation is represented by \texttt{**}; e.g.,
\texttt{2\ **\ 5\ =\ 32}.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     64
1     9
2     9
3     25
4     9
5     36
6     36
7     25
8     25
9     9
\end{verbatim}

For many common functions (e.g., \texttt{sqrt}, \texttt{log},
\texttt{cos}), the syntax \texttt{g(X)} is sufficient. Here
\texttt{sqrt(u)} is the square root function \(g(u) = \sqrt{u}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ sqrt(X)).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 1.4142135623730951)
1     (2, 1.4142135623730951)
2     (5, 2.23606797749979)
3     (7, 2.6457513110645907)
4     (6, 2.449489742783178)
5     (4, 2.0)
6     (4, 2.0)
7     (6, 2.449489742783178)
8     (5, 2.23606797749979)
9     (4, 2.0)
\end{verbatim}

For general functions, including user defined functions, the syntax for
defining \(g(X)\) is \texttt{X.apply(g)}. Here we define the function
\(g(u) = (u-5)^2\) and then define\footnote{We could have actually
  defined \texttt{Z\ =\ (X\ -\ 5)\ **\ 2} here. We'll see examples where
  the \texttt{apply} syntax is necessary later.} the random variable
\(g(X) = (X - 5)^2\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# define a function g; u represents a generic input}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ g(u):}
  \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ (u }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}

\CommentTok{\# define the RV g(X)  }
\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(g)}

\CommentTok{\# simulate X and Z pairs}
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Z).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (5, 0)
1     (5, 0)
2     (3, 4)
3     (6, 1)
4     (5, 0)
5     (7, 4)
6     (7, 4)
7     (4, 1)
8     (5, 0)
9     (4, 1)
\end{verbatim}

We can also apply transformations of multiple \texttt{RV}s \emph{defined
on the same probability space}. (We will look more closely at how
Symbulate treats this ``same probability space'' issue later.)

For example, we can simulate values of \(XY\), the product of \(X\) and
\(Y\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     2
1     18
2     8
3     12
4     6
5     18
6     24
7     24
8     8
9     28
\end{verbatim}

Recall that we defined \(X\) via \texttt{X\ =\ RV(P,\ sum)}. Defining
random variables \(U_1, U_2\) to represent the individual rolls, we can
define \(X=U_1 + U_2\). Recall that we previously defined\footnote{We
  can also define \texttt{U\ =\ RV(P)} and then
  \texttt{X\ =\ U.apply(sum)}.} \texttt{U1,\ U2\ =\ RV(P)}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U1 }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U2}

\NormalTok{X.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     8
1     3
2     4
3     2
4     4
5     5
6     8
7     2
8     5
9     4
\end{verbatim}

Unfortunately \texttt{max(U1,\ U2)} does not work, but we can use the
\texttt{apply} syntax. Since we want to apply \texttt{max} to
\((U_1, U_2)\) pairs, we must\footnote{We can also define
  \texttt{U\ =\ RV(P)} and then \texttt{X\ =\ U.apply(max)}.} first join
them together with \texttt{\&}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y  }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (U1 }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ U2).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{Y.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     4
1     1
2     4
3     2
4     4
5     3
6     4
7     4
8     3
9     2
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Other probability spaces}\label{other-probability-spaces}

So far we have assumed a \emph{fair} four-sided die. Now consider the
weighted die in Example~\ref{exm-die-weighted}: a single roll results in
1 with probability 0.1, 2 with probability 0.2, 3 with probability 0.3,
and 4 with probability 0.4. \texttt{BoxModel} assumes equally likely
tickets by default, but we can specify non-equally likely tickets using
the \texttt{probs} option. The probability space \texttt{WeightedRoll}
in the following code corresponds to a single roll of the weighted die;
the default \texttt{size} option is 1.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{WeightedRoll }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{WeightedRoll.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     4
1     4
2     2
3     3
4     1
5     1
6     4
7     2
8     4
9     4
\end{verbatim}

We could add \texttt{size\ =\ 2} to the \texttt{BoxModel} to create a
probability space corresponding to two rolls of the weighted die.
Alternatively, we can think of
\texttt{BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]},\ probs\ =\ {[}0.1,\ 0.2,\ 0.3,\ 0.4{]})}
as defining the middle spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-die-three-spinners}
that we want to spin two times, which we can do with \texttt{**\ 2}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{]) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{Q.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (4, 4)
1     (2, 1)
2     (4, 2)
3     (2, 3)
4     (3, 4)
5     (4, 1)
6     (4, 4)
7     (4, 4)
8     (2, 3)
9     (4, 1)
\end{verbatim}

You can interpret
\texttt{BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]},\ probs\ =\ {[}0.1,\ 0.2,\ 0.3,\ 0.4{]})}
as defining the middle spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-die-three-spinners}
and \texttt{**\ 2} as ``spin the spinner two times''. In Python,
\texttt{**} represents exponentiation; e.g., \texttt{2\ **\ 5\ =\ 32}.
So \texttt{BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]})\ **\ 2} is equivalent to
\texttt{BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]})\ *\ BoxModel({[}1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4{]})}.
In light of our discussion in Section~\ref{sec-independence}, the
product \texttt{*} notation should seem natural for \emph{independent}
spins.

We could use the product notation to define a probability space
corresponding to a pair of rolls, one from a fair die and one from a
weighted-die.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{MixedRolls }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{]) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{MixedRolls.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 3)
1     (3, 3)
2     (3, 3)
3     (3, 2)
4     (3, 1)
5     (2, 4)
6     (3, 3)
7     (1, 3)
8     (4, 4)
9     (4, 2)
\end{verbatim}

Now consider the weighted die from Example~\ref{exm-dice-normalize},
represented by the spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-die-three-spinners-3}. We
could use the \texttt{probs} option, but we can also imagine a box model
with 15 tickets---four tickets labeled 1, six tickets labeled 2, three
tickets labeled 3, and two tickets labeled 4---from which a single
ticket is drawn. A \texttt{BoxModel} can be specified in this way using
the following \texttt{\{label:\ number\ of\ tickets\ with\ the\ label\}}
formulation\footnote{Braces \texttt{\{\}} are used here because this
  defines a Python \emph{dictionary}. But don't confuse this code with
  set notation.}. This formulation is especially useful when multiple
tickets are drawn from the box \emph{without replacement}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(\{}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{Q.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     4
1     1
2     1
3     4
4     2
5     2
6     1
7     2
8     3
9     3
\end{verbatim}

While many scenarios can be represented by box models, there are also
many Symbulate probability spaces other than \texttt{BoxModel}. When
tickets are equally likely and sampled with replacement, a
\emph{Discrete Uniform} model can also be used. Think of a
\texttt{DiscreteUniform(a,\ b)} probability space corresponding to a
spinner with sectors of \emph{equal area} labeled with integer values
from \texttt{a} to \texttt{b} (inclusive). For example, the spinner in
Figure~\ref{fig-die-three-spinners-1} corresponds to the
\texttt{DiscreteUniform(1,\ 4)} model. This gives us another way to
represent the probability space corresponding to two rolls of a
fair-four sided die.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ DiscreteUniform(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 2)
1     (3, 2)
2     (1, 2)
3     (1, 1)
4     (1, 2)
5     (1, 2)
6     (4, 3)
7     (3, 2)
8     (4, 3)
9     (1, 2)
\end{verbatim}

Note that \texttt{BoxModel} is the only probability space with the
\texttt{size} argument. For other probability spaces, the product
\texttt{*} or exponentiation \texttt{**} notation must be used to
simulate multiple spins.

This section has only introduced how to set up a probability model and
simulate realizations. We'll see how to summarize and use simulation
output soon.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-18}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-collector}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-collector}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Let \(X\) be the number of
distinct prizes obtained in these 3 packages. Let \(Y\) be the number of
these 3 packages that contain prize 1.

Write Symbulate code to define an appropriate probability space and
random variables, and simulate a few repetitions. Hint: you'll need to
define a function to define \(X\); try \texttt{len(unique(...))}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-collector-b}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-collector-b}

Continuing Exercise~\ref{exr-computer-simulation-collector}. Now suppose
that 10\% of boxes contain prize 1, 30\% contain prize 2, and 60\%
contain prize 3. Write Symbulate code to define an appropriate
probability space and random variables, and simulate a few repetitions.

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-birthday}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-birthday}

Recall the birthday problem of Example~\ref{exm-birthday}. Let \(B\) be
the event that at least two people in a group of \(n\) share a birthday.

Write Symbulate code to define an appropriate probability space, and
simulate a few realizations of \(B\) (that is, simulate whether or not
\(B\) occurs).

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-geometric}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-geometric}

Maya is a basketball player who makes 40\% of her three point field goal
attempts. Suppose that at the end of every practice session, she
attempts three pointers until she makes one and then stops. Let \(X\) be
the total number of shots she attempts in a practice session. Assume
shot attempts are independent, each with probability of 0.4 of being
successful.

Write Symbulate code to define an appropriate probability space and
random variable, and simulate a few repetitions.

\end{exercise}

\section{Computer simulation: Meeting problem}\label{sec-meeting-sim}

Now we'll introduce computer simulation of the continuous models in
Section~\ref{sec-language-simulation-tactile-meeting}. Throughout this
section we'll consider the two-person meeting problem. Let \(R\) be the
random variable representing Regina's arrival time (minutes after noon,
including fractions of a minute), and \(Y\) for Cady. Also let
\(T=\min(R, Y)\) be the time (minutes after noon) at which the first
person arrives, and \(W=|R-Y|\) be the time (minutes) the first person
to arrive waits for the second person to arrive.

\subsection{Independent Uniform
model}\label{sec-meeting-sim-independent-uniform}

First consider the situation of Example~\ref{exm-meeting-box-sim} where
Regina and Cady each arrive at a time uniformly at random in {[}0,
60{]}, independently of each other. The following code defines a
Uniform(0, 60) spinner\footnote{Careful: don't confuse
  \texttt{Uniform(a,\ b)} with \texttt{DiscreteUniform(a,\ b)}.
  \texttt{Uniform(a,\ b)} corresponds to the continuous interval
  \([a, b]\).}, like in Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-uniform-spinner}, which
we spin twice to get the (Regina, Cady) pair of outcomes.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (41.0408474659083, 10.17025206410582)
1     (28.402967065678567, 58.370188024349325)
2     (50.75552925389327, 35.53957395707245)
3     (2.7103831183762916, 21.50153116569667)
4     (17.207109128157786, 46.80709630064162)
5     (42.009467735444275, 5.899104305598861)
6     (8.673286178395072, 45.67180608113506)
7     (6.665943790441357, 5.217117199002487)
8     (25.82312961284174, 11.27594536596983)
9     (17.663489614504833, 51.672194540717214)
\end{verbatim}

Notice (again) the number of decimal places; any value in the continuous
interval between 0 and 60 is a distinct possible value

A probability space outcome is a (Regina, Cady) pair of arrival times.
We can define the random variables \(R\) and \(Y\), representing the
individual arrival times, by ``unpacking'' the outcomes.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (42.95040460772375, 15.9669449685697)
1     (7.010279437036058, 15.37203437204491)
2     (55.044215666662325, 26.44005535982256)
3     (24.938774161786906, 5.309818737507612)
4     (11.928698876007285, 7.7653258022320575)
5     (18.310676455254786, 51.32200081659493)
6     (14.0171085190848, 53.164133742353634)
7     (36.92429573949422, 19.753345225866177)
8     (13.068737071524495, 33.464784345809335)
9     (50.460859518371215, 27.25854442919644)
\end{verbatim}

We can define \(W = |R-Y|\) using the \texttt{abs} function. In order to
define \(T = \min(R, Y)\) we need to use the \texttt{apply} syntax with
\texttt{R\ \&\ Y}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now we can simulate values of \(R\), \(Y\), \(T\), and \(W\) with a
single call to \texttt{sim}. Each row in the resulting
Table~\ref{tbl-meeting-independent-uniform-sim} corresponds to a single
simulated outcome (pair of arrival times).

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tbl-meeting-independent-uniform-sim}}

\centering{

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ T }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ W).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (7.495036063322543, 5.574234241002727, 5.574234241002727, 1.9208018223198158)
1     (2.8219493977826926, 21.47341851248353, 2.8219493977826926, 18.651469114700838)
2     (17.70575208755269, 5.754334000198645, 5.754334000198645, 11.951418087354044)
3     (50.5207362499285, 2.39901457998295, 2.39901457998295, 48.12172166994554)
4     (1.207713652454525, 49.734759107693634, 1.207713652454525, 48.52704545523911)
5     (48.681819530823276, 31.058705291996024, 31.058705291996024, 17.623114238827252)
6     (9.659069959635326, 9.98909939419406, 9.659069959635326, 0.33002943455873357)
7     (25.672774747372486, 24.255552785778043, 24.255552785778043, 1.4172219615944428)
8     (3.358464477004095, 38.542831662472985, 3.358464477004095, 35.184367185468886)
9     (29.285408096792658, 38.09381082018246, 29.285408096792658, 8.808402723389804)
\end{verbatim}

}

\end{table}%

We can simulate values of \(R\) and plot them along a number line in a
``rug'' plot; compare to
Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-uniform-sim-table}. Notice how we have
chained together the \texttt{sim} and \texttt{plot} commands. (We'll see
some more interesting and useful plots later.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{R.sim(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{).plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}rug\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png}

Calling \texttt{.plot()} (without
\texttt{\textquotesingle{}rug\textquotesingle{}}) for simulated values
of a \emph{continuous} random variable produces a \emph{histogram},
which we will discuss in much more detail in
\textbf{?@sec-simulation-marginal-continuous}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{R.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-41-3.png}

We can simulate and plot many \((R, Y)\) pairs of arrival times; compare
to Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-uniform-sim-pair} (without the rug).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-43-5.png}

When plotting simulated pairs, the first component is plotted on the
horizontal axis and the second component on the vertical axis. In the
following plots, we'll \texttt{import\ matplotlib.pyplot\ as\ plt} and
use \texttt{plt.xlabel("x-axis\ text")} and
\texttt{plt.ylabel("y-axis\ text")}to label axes.

We can also simulate and plot many \((T, W)\) pairs. For purposes of
illustration, first we simulate all four random variables, then we'll
select the columns corresponding to \((T, W)\) and plot the simulated
pairs.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ T }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ W).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{].plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"T"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"W"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-45-7.png}

\subsection{Independent Normal
model}\label{sec-meeting-sim-independent-normal}

Now consider a \texttt{Normal(30,\ 10)} model, represented by the
spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-normal-spinner}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Normal(mean }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     28.500800573510723
1     15.527637022927358
2     21.45898904357567
3     39.47722387370127
4     36.169698798352286
5     36.48161000765437
6     35.29031468526315
7     15.456752477070701
8     24.633921639575505
9     34.68174478955214
\end{verbatim}

We define a probability space corresponding to (Regina, Cady) pairs of
arrival times, by assuming that their arrival times individually follow
a Normal(30, 10) model, independently of each other. That is, we spin
the Normal(30, 10) spinner twice to simulate a pair of arrival times.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (25.117825303927393, 28.86934873876588)
1     (20.461858362670544, 26.770064157704013)
2     (54.214691596683835, 43.14925862504083)
3     (23.141159076921255, 26.15955334247312)
4     (28.043246677448955, 42.30537143758215)
5     (31.559207633062996, 20.984893995089497)
6     (19.26549745184642, 24.61045705064965)
7     (14.990904654869553, 25.535565233441744)
8     (39.0007179183176, 15.45554427126763)
9     (26.68327322427153, 28.96683694977026)
\end{verbatim}

We can unpack the individual \(R\), \(Y\) random variables and define
\(W\), \(T\) as before.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We can simulate values of \(R\) and plot them along a number line in a
rug plot; compare to Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-table}.
(Technically, the Normal(30, 10) assigns small but positive probability
to values outside of {[}0, 60{]}, so we might see some values outside of
{[}0, 60{]}.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{R.sim(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{).plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}rug\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-49-9.png}

We can simulate many values and summarize them in a histogram. We'll
discuss histograms in more detail later, but notice that the histogram
conveys that for a Normal(30, 10) distribution values near 30 are more
likely than values near 0 or 60.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{R.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-50-11.png}

We can simulate and plot many \((R, Y)\) pairs of arrival times; compare
to Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-tactile-normal-sim-pair} (without the rug).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"R"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"Y"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-52-13.png}

We can also simulate and plot many \((T, W)\) pairs. Notice that the
plot looks quite different from the one for the independent Uniform(0,
60) model for arrival times.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{meeting\_sim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ T }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ W).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{].plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"T"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"W"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-54-15.png}

\subsection{Bivariate Normal
model}\label{sec-language-simulation-computer-meeting-bvn}

Now assume that Regina and Cady tend to arrive around the same time. We
haven't yet seen how to construct spinners to reflect dependence, but
we'll briefly introduce a particular model and some code. One way to
model pairs of values that have a relationship or \emph{correlation} is
with a \texttt{BivariateNormal} model, like in the following.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (13.625585214842278, 16.11533255242663)
1     (21.918077029787767, 20.8274384461305)
2     (9.75470313259028, 26.36186268160224)
3     (32.28135941246177, 37.34429480434329)
4     (28.50483456592004, 34.479247333260325)
5     (31.217841530129288, 37.89963838784024)
6     (18.544608760432336, 17.339166420192612)
7     (28.009637223727392, 22.58833219148691)
8     (34.81457264824674, 34.36536797435535)
9     (27.721220747499956, 41.05080570057361)
\end{verbatim}

Note that a \texttt{BivariateNormal} probability space returns pairs
directly. We can unpack the pairs as before, and plot some simulated
values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"R"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"Y"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-57-17.png}

Now we see that Regina and Cady tend to arrive near the same time,
similar to Figure~\ref{fig-meeting-dependent-normal}.

If we plot \((T, W)\) pairs, we expect values of the waiting time \(W\)
to tend to be closer to 0 than in the independent arrivals models.
Compare the scale on the vertical axis, corresponding to \(W\), in each
of the three plots of \((T, W)\) pairs in this section.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ T }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ W).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{].plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"T"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"W"}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-59-19.png}

A call to \texttt{sim} always simulates independent repetitions from the
model, but be careful about what this means. In the Bivariate Normal
model, the \(R\) and \(Y\) values are dependent \emph{within a
repetition}. However, the \((R, Y)\) pairs are independent \emph{between
repetitions}. Thinking in terms of a table, the \(R, Y\) columns are
dependent, but the rows are independent.

We will study specific probability models like \texttt{Normal} and
\texttt{BivariateNormal} in much more detail as we go.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-19}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-dartboard}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-dartboard}

Write Symbulate code to conduct the simulation in
Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-dartboard}. Caveat: don't worry about the code
to discard repetitions where the dart lands off the board. (We'll return
to this later.)

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-computer-simulation-continuous-dice}{}\label{exr-computer-simulation-continuous-dice}

Consider a continuous version of the dice rolling problem where instead
of rolling two fair four-sided dice (which return values 1, 2, 3, 4) we
spin twice a Uniform(1, 4) spinner (which returns any value in the
continuous range between 1 and 4). Let \(X\) be the sum of the two spins
and let \(Y\) be the larger of the two spins. Write Symbulate code to
define an appropriate probability space and random variables, and
simulate a few repetitions.

\end{exercise}

\section{Approximating probabilities: Relative
frequencies}\label{sec-language-simulation-relative-frequency}

We can use simulation-based relative frequencies to approximate
probabilities. That is, the probability of event \(A\) can be
approximated by simulating---according to the assumptions encoded in the
probability measure \(\textrm{P}\)---the random phenomenon a large
number of times and computing the relative frequency of \(A\).

\[
{\small
\textrm{P}(A) \approx \frac{\text{number of repetitions on which $A$ occurs}}{\text{number of repetitions}}, \quad \text{for a large number of repetitions simulated according to $\textrm{P}$}
}
\]

In practice, many repetitions of a simulation are performed on a
computer to approximate what happens in the ``long run''. However, we
often start by carrying out a few repetitions by hand to help make the
process more concrete.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-dice-sim-tactile}{}\label{exm-dice-sim-tactile}

Recall your simulation results from Example~\ref{exm-dice-sim}; ours are
in Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sim-tactile-results}. Based only on your 10
repetitions, how would you approximate the following? (Don't worry if
the approximations are any good yet.)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(A)\), where \(A\) is the event that the first roll is 3.
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X=6)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 6)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(Y = 3)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(Y \ge 3)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X=6, Y=3)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X\ge6, Y \ge 3)\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
See Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sim-tactile-results} for the results of our
simulation.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(A)\) by 4/10 = 0.4, the relative frequency of
  event \(A\) in the simulation; that is, the proportion of repetitions
  where the first roll is 3.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(X=6)\) by 2/10 = 0.2, the proportion of
  repetitions where the sum is 6.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(X\ge 6)\) by 5/10 = 0.5, the proportion of
  repetitions where the sum is at least 6.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(Y=3)\) by 3/10 = 0.3, the proportion of
  repetitions where the max is 3.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(Y\ge 3)\) by 7/10 = 0.7, the proportion of
  repetitions where the max is at least 3.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(X=6, Y = 3)\) by 1/10 = 0.1, the proportion
  of repetitions where both the sum is 6 and the max is 3.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(X\ge 6, Y \ge 3)\) by 5/10 = 0.5, the
  proportion of repetitions where both the sum is at least 6 and the max
  is at least 3. (Since \(X\ge 6\) implies \(Y\ge 3\),
  \(\textrm{P}(X\ge 6, Y\ge 3) = \textrm{P}(X\ge 6)\).)
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-dice-sim-tactile}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-dice-sim-tactile-dist}{}\label{exm-dice-sim-tactile-dist}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-dice-sim-tactile}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Construct a table of the simulated relative frequencies of each
  possible value \(x\) of \(X\).
\item
  Construct a table of the simulated relative frequencies of each
  possible value \((x, y)\) pair of \((X, Y)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
For discrete random variables like these we can make tables or plots
summarizing the observed values of the random variables and their
corresponding relative frequencies.

Summarizing our simulation results from
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sim-tactile-results}, the observed values of \(X\)
and corresponding relative frequencies are

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\(x\) & Relative frequency \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
2 & 1/10 \\
3 & 2/10 \\
4 & 0 \\
5 & 2/10 \\
6 & 2/10 \\
7 & 3/10 \\
8 & 0 \\
\end{longtable}

The above table\footnotemark{} represents an approximation of the
distribution of \(X\), albeit a bad approximation; compare with
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sum-dist-table}.

We can summarize simulated \((X, Y)\) \emph{pairs} and their relative
frequencies, as in the following two-way table; compare with
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-joint-dist-twoway}.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\(x, y\) & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
2 & 1/10 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
3 & 0 & 2/10 & 0 & 0 \\
4 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
5 & 0 & 0 & 2/10 & 0 \\
6 & 0 & 0 & 1/10 & 1/10 \\
7 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3/10 \\
8 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\end{longtable}

\label{sol-dice-sim-tactile-dist}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\footnotetext{We would typically only include the values observed in the
simulation in the summary. However, we include 4 and 8 here because if
we had performed more repetitions we would have observed these values.}

You might have noticed that many of the simulated relative frequencies
in Example~\ref{exm-dice-sim-tactile} provide terrible estimates of the
corresponding probabilities. For example, the true probability that the
first roll is a 3 is \(\textrm{P}(A) = 0.25\) while the simulated
relative frequency is 0.4. The problem is that the simulation only
consisted of 10 repetitions. Probabilities can be approximated by
\emph{long run} relatively frequencies, but 10 repetitions certainly
doesn't qualify as the long run! The more repetitions we perform the
better our estimates should be. But how many repetitions is sufficient?
And how accurate are the estimates? We will address these issues in
Section~\ref{sec-moe}.

\subsection{A few Symbulate commands for summarizing simulation
output}\label{a-few-symbulate-commands-for-summarizing-simulation-output}

We'll continue with the dice rolling example. Recall the setup.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ DiscreteUniform(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

First we'll simulate and store 10 values of \(X\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{x }\CommentTok{\# displays the simulated values}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     5
1     6
2     3
3     3
4     3
5     4
6     6
7     7
8     6
9     4
\end{verbatim}

Suppose we want to find the relative frequency of 6. We can count the
number of simulated values equal to 6 with \texttt{count\_eq()}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
3
\end{verbatim}

The count is the frequency. To find the relative frequency we simply
divide by the number of simulated values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{10}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.3
\end{verbatim}

We can find frequencies of other events using the ``count'' functions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{count\_eq(u)}: count \emph{equal to} (\(=\)) \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count\_neq(u)}: count \emph{not equal to} (\(\neq\))
  \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count\_leq(u)}: count \emph{less than or equal to} (\(\le\))
  \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count\_lt(u)}: count \emph{less than} (\(<\)) \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count\_geq(u)}: count \emph{greater than or equal to}
  (\(\ge\)) \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count\_gt(u)}: count \emph{greater than} (\(>\)) \texttt{u}
\item
  \texttt{count}: count according to a custom True/False criteria (see
  examples below)
\end{itemize}

Using \texttt{count()} with no inputs to defaults to ``count all'',
which provides a way to count the total number of simulated values.
(This is especially useful when conditioning.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.3
\end{verbatim}

The \texttt{tabulate} method provides a quick summary of the individual
simulated values and their frequencies.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Frequency
3     3
4     2
5     1
6     3
7     1
Total 10
\end{verbatim}

By default, \texttt{tabulate} returns frequencies (counts). Adding the
argument\footnote{``Normalize'' is used in the sense of
  Section~\ref{sec-consistency} and refers to rescaling the values so
  that they add up to 1 but the ratios are preserved.}
\texttt{normalize\ =\ True} returns relative frequencies (proportions).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
3     0.3
4     0.2
5     0.1
6     0.3
7     0.1
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

We often initially simulate a small number of repetitions to see what
the simulation is doing and check that it is working properly. However,
in order to accurately approximate probabilities or distribution we
simulate a large number of repetitions (usually thousands for our
purposes). Now let's simulate many \(X\) values and summarize the
results.

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tbl-dice-sum-marginal-sim}Table representing
simulation-based approximate distribution of \(X\), the sum of two rolls
of a fair four-sided die.}

\centering{

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
2     0.064
3     0.1229
4     0.1913
5     0.2448
6     0.1893
7     0.1254
8     0.0623
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

}

\end{table}%

Compare to Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sum-dist-table}; with 10000 repetitions
the simulation based approximations are pretty close to the theoretical
probabilities.

Graphical summaries play an important role in analyzing simulation
output. We have previously seen rug plots of individual simulated
values. Rug plot emphasize that realizations of a random variable are
numbers along a number line. However, a rug plot does not adequately
summarize relative frequencies. Instead, calling \texttt{.plot()} for
simulated values of a \emph{discrete} random variable
produces\footnote{For discrete random variables
  \texttt{\textquotesingle{}impulse\textquotesingle{}} is the default
  plot type. Like \texttt{.tabulate()}, the \texttt{.plot()} method also
  has a \texttt{normalize} argument; the default is
  \texttt{normalize=True}.} an \emph{impulse plot} which displays the
simulated values and their relative frequencies; see
Figure~\ref{fig-dice-sum-marginal-sim} and compare to
Figure~\ref{fig-dice-sum-dist-plot22}. Since we stored the simulated
values as \texttt{x}, the same simulated values are used to produce
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-sum-marginal-sim} and
Figure~\ref{fig-dice-sum-marginal-sim}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.plot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-dice-sum-marginal-sim-21.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-dice-sum-marginal-sim}Impulse plot representing
simulation-based approximate distribution of \(X\), the sum of two rolls
of a fair four-sided die.}

\end{figure}%

Now we simulate and summarize a few \((X, Y)\) pairs.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (5, 4)
1     (4, 3)
2     (5, 4)
3     (7, 4)
4     (7, 4)
5     (6, 3)
6     (3, 2)
7     (4, 3)
8     (6, 4)
9     (8, 4)
\end{verbatim}

Pairs of values can also be tabulated.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value  Frequency
(3, 2) 1
(4, 3) 2
(5, 4) 2
(6, 3) 1
(6, 4) 1
(7, 4) 2
(8, 4) 1
 Total 10
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value  Relative Frequency
(3, 2) 0.1
(4, 3) 0.2
(5, 4) 0.2
(6, 3) 0.1
(6, 4) 0.1
(7, 4) 0.2
(8, 4) 0.1
 Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

Individual pairs can be plotted in a scatter plot, which is a
two-dimensional analog of a rug plot.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.plot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-72-23.png}

The values can be ``jittered'' slightly, as below, so that points do not
coincide.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.plot(jitter }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-74-25.png}

The two-dimensional analog of an impulse plot is a \emph{tile plot}. For
two discrete variables, the
\texttt{\textquotesingle{}tile\textquotesingle{}} plot type produces a
tile plot (a.k.a. heat map) where rectangles represent the simulated
pairs with their relative frequencies visualized on a color scale.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}tile\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-76-27.png}

Custom functions can be used with \texttt{count} to compute relative
frequencies of events involving multiple random variables. Suppose we
want to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X<6, Y \ge 2)\). We first define a
Python function which takes as an input a pair
\texttt{u\ =\ (u{[}0{]},\ u{[}1{]})} and returns \texttt{True} if
\texttt{u{[}0{]}\ \textless{}\ 6} and
\texttt{u{[}1{]}\ \textgreater{}=\ 2}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ is\_x\_lt\_6\_and\_y\_ge\_2(u):}
  \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ u[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{6} \KeywordTok{and}\NormalTok{ u[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{:}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{True}
  \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \VariableTok{False}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now we can use this function along with \texttt{count} to find the
simulated relative frequency of the event \(\{X <6, Y \ge 2\}\).
Remember that \texttt{x\_and\_y} stores \((X, Y)\) pairs of values, so
the first coordinate \texttt{x\_and\_y{[}0{]}} represents values of
\(X\) and the second coordinate \texttt{x\_and\_y{[}1{]}} represents
values of \(Y\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.count(is\_x\_lt\_6\_and\_y\_ge\_2) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.5
\end{verbatim}

We could also count use Boolean logic; basically using indicators and
the property
\(\textrm{I}_{\{X<6,Y\ge 2\}}=\textrm{I}_{\{X<6\}}\textrm{I}_{\{Y\ge 2\}}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{((x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)).count\_eq(}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.5
\end{verbatim}

Now we simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs and summarize their frequencies.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value  Frequency
(2, 1) 628
(3, 2) 1254
(4, 2) 606
(4, 3) 1298
(5, 3) 1232
(5, 4) 1253
(6, 3) 642
(6, 4) 1219
(7, 4) 1279
(8, 4) 589
 Total 10000
\end{verbatim}

Here are the relative frequencies; compare with
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-joint-dist-flat}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value  Relative Frequency
(2, 1) 0.0628
(3, 2) 0.1254
(4, 2) 0.0606
(4, 3) 0.1298
(5, 3) 0.1232
(5, 4) 0.1253
(6, 3) 0.0642
(6, 4) 0.1219
(7, 4) 0.1279
(8, 4) 0.0589
 Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

When there are thousands of simulated pairs, a scatter plot does not
adequately display relative frequencies, even with jittering.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.plot(jitter }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-83-29.png}

The tile plot provides a better summary. Notice how the colors represent
the relative frequencies in the previous table.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}tile\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-85-31.png}

Finally, we find the simulated relative frequency of the event
\(\{X <6, Y \ge 2\}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.count(is\_x\_lt\_6\_and\_y\_ge\_2) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y.count()}
\end{Highlighting}

\begin{verbatim}
0.5643
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Approximating probabilities in the meeting
problem}\label{approximating-probabilities-in-the-meeting-problem}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-meeting-sim-independent-uniform-rel-freq}{}\label{exm-meeting-sim-independent-uniform-rel-freq}

Recall the independent Uniform(0, 60) model for arrival times of
Example~\ref{exm-meeting-box-sim}. Use the simulation results in
Table~\ref{tbl-meeting-tactile-uniform-sim-table-pair} to approximate
the following. (Don't worry if the approximations are any good yet.)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(T < 15)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(W < 15)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(T < 15, W < 15)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(R = 20)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(19.5 < R < 20.5)\)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(T < 15)\) by 3/10 = 0.3, the proportion of
  repetitions where the first arrival time is less than 15 minutes.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(W < 15)\) by 6/10 = 0.6, the proportion of
  repetitions where the waiting time is less than 15 minutes.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(T < 15, W < 15)\) by 2/10 = 0.2, the
  proportion of repetitions where both the first arrival time and the
  waiting time are less than 15 minutes.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(R=20)\) by 0, the proportion of repetitions
  where \(R\) is equal to 20.
\item
  Approximate \(\textrm{P}(19.5 < R < 20.5)\) by 1/10 = 0.1, the
  proportion of repetitions where \(R\), rounded to the nearest minute,
  is equal to 20.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-meeting-sim-independent-uniform-rel-freq}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

An event either happens or not. Regardless of whether an event involves
a discrete or continuous random variable, the probability of the event
is approximated in the same way. However, the kinds of events we're
interested in differ between those involving discrete and those
involving continuous random variables. The probability that a continuous
random variable is equal to any particular value is 0, so we're not
interested in approximating ``equals to'' probabilities for continuous
random variables. When dealing with continuous random variables in
practice, ``equals to'' is really ``close to'', and we compute
approximate ``close to'' probabilities with relative frequencies are
usual. (Later, we'll see what it means to \emph{condition} on a
continuous random variable being equal to some value.)

To get better approximations for the probabilities in
Example~\ref{exm-meeting-box-sim} we would need to simulate many more
repetitions. But the process of approximating probabilities with
simulated relative frequencies is the same as in
Example~\ref{exm-meeting-box-sim}.

Simulation can also be used to investigate how sensitive (approximate)
probabilities are to changes in assumptions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-meeting-sim-intro}{}\label{exm-meeting-sim-intro}

Write Symbulate code to run simulations and use the results to
approximate the probability that Regina and Cady arrive with 15 minutes
of each other for each of the three models in
Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Independent Uniform model
\item
  Independent Normal model
\item
  Bivariate Normal model
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
There are a few ways to code this, but one way is to define the waiting
time random variable \(W=|R-Y|\) and find simulated relative frequencies
of the event \(\{W<15\}\).

First the independent Uniform model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{w }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{w.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ w.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.4381
\end{verbatim}

Next the independent Normal model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{w }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{w.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ w.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.708
\end{verbatim}

Finally, the Bivariate Normal model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{w }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{w.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ w.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.9502
\end{verbatim}

We see that these changes in assumptions have substantial influence on
this probability. The simulations shows that they are roughly 1.7 times
more likely to arrive within 15 minutes of each other under the
independent Normal model than under the independent Uniform model, and
roughly 1.3 times more likely under the Bivariate Normal model than
under the independent Normal model.

\label{sol-meeting-sim-intro}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

We have previously seen rug plots of individual simulated values. Rug
plot emphasize that realizations of a random variable are numbers along
a number line. However, a rug plot does not adequately summarize the
distribution of values. Instead, calling \texttt{.plot()} for simulated
values of a \emph{continuous} random variable produces a
\emph{histogram}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{w.plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-90-33.png}

We will cover histograms and marginal distributions of continuous random
variables in much more detail in
\textbf{?@sec-simulation-marginal-continuous}.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-20}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-approximate-probability-collector}{}\label{exr-approximate-probability-collector}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Let \(X\) be the number of
distinct prizes obtained in these 3 packages. Let \(Y\) be the number of
these 3 packages that contain prize 1.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain how you could, in principle, conduct a simulation by hand and
  use the results to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 2)\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(Y = 1)\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 2, Y = 1)\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate the
  values in part 1.
\item
  Write Sybulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Marginal distribution of \(X\)
  \item
    Marginal distribution of \(Y\)
  \item
    Joint distribution of \(X\) and \(Y\)
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-approximate-probability-collector-b}{}\label{exr-approximate-probability-collector-b}

Repeat Exercise~\ref{exr-approximate-probability-collector}, but now
assuming that 10\% of boxes contain prize 1, 30\% contain prize 2, and
60\% contain prize 3.

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-approximate-probability-geometric}{}\label{exr-approximate-probability-geometric}

Maya is a basketball player who makes 40\% of her three point field goal
attempts. Suppose that at the end of every practice session, she
attempts three pointers until she makes one and then stops. Let \(X\) be
the total number of shots she attempts in a practice session. Assume
shot attempts are independent, each with probability of 0.4 of being
successful.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain in words you could use simulation to approximate the
  distribution of \(X\) and \(\textrm{P}(X > 3)\).
\item
  Write Symbulate code to approximate the distribution of \(X\) and
  \(\textrm{P}(X > 3)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-approximate-probability-continuous-dice}{}\label{exr-approximate-probability-continuous-dice}

Consider a continuous version of the dice rolling problem where instead
of rolling two fair four-sided dice (which return values 1, 2, 3, 4) we
spin twice a Uniform(1, 4) spinner (which returns any value in the
continuous range between 1 and 4). Let \(X\) be the sum of the two spins
and let \(Y\) be the larger of the two spins.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
