\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sd-matching}{}\label{exm-sd-matching}

The plots below summarize hypothetical distributions of quiz scores in
six classes. Each quiz score is a whole number between 0 and 10
inclusive. All plots are on the same scale with quiz scores on the
horizontal axis, and probability on the vertical axis.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Donny Dont says that of these six plots, C represents the smallest SD,
  since there is ``no variability in the heights of the bars''. Do you
  agree that C represents ``no variability''? Explain.
\item
  What is the smallest \emph{possible} value the SD of quiz scores could
  be? What would need to be true about the distribution for this to
  happen? (This scenario might not be represented by one of these six
  plots.)
\item
  Without doing any calculations, identify which of these six classes
  exhibits the smallest standard deviation of quiz scores.
\item
  Without doing any calculations, arrange the classes in order based on
  their standard deviations from smallest to largest.\\
\item
  In one of the classes, the standard deviation of quiz scores is 5.
  Which one? Why?
\item
  Is the standard deviation in F greater than, less than, or equal to 1?
  Why?
\item
  Provide a ballpark estimate of standard deviation in each case.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  We disagree with Donny. Standard deviation measures variability of the
  \emph{values of the variable}, not their probabilities. If we were to
  simulate values according to the distribution in C, we would observe
  some 0s, some 1s, some 2s, all the way through some 10s (with roughly
  equal frequency). So there would certainly be variability in the
  values of the variable. Remember that values of the variable are along
  the horizontal axis, so standard deviation measures average distance
  from the mean horizontally.
\item
  The smallest possible value of standard deviation is 0, which occurs
  only if the random variable is a constant (with probability 1). In
  this context, if every student had the same quiz score, e.g., if 100\%
  of students scored an 8, then the standard deviation would be 0. The
  distribution plot would have a single spike at a single value.
\item
  Remember that values of the variable are along the horizontal axis, so
  standard deviation measures average distance from the mean
  horizontally. The distribution in F represents the smallest standard
  deviation. The mean is 7, most of the scores are 7, and some of the
  scores are only 1 unit away from the mean. In all other situations,
  the probability that the random variable is equal to its mean is
  smaller, and the probability that the random variables takes a value
  more than 1 unit away from its mean is larger than in F.
\item
  In all plots other than F the mean is 5, so the smallest standard
  deviation occurs where the values tend to be close to 5, and the
  largest occurs where the values tend to be far from 5. In order from
  smallest to largest standard deviation: F, E, A, C, B, D.
\item
  In D, the score takes values 0 and 10 with probability 0.5. The mean
  is 5, and all deviations are 5 units away from the mean, so the
  average squared deviation will be \(5^2\) and the standard deviation
  will be 5.
\item
  Less than 1. Don't forget that there is a high probability of a
  deviation of 0 in this case. So the average deviation will be
  somewhere between 0 and 1.
\item
  Some of these are harder than others. In E, many values are 0 units
  away from mean, many values are 1 unit away, and some values are 2. So
  the standard deviation in E is maybe around 1. In C, there are values
  that are 0 units away, and about as many values that are each 1, 2, 3,
  4, and 5 units away; we might expect standard deviation to be around
  2.5. But remember, while considering the average absolute deviation
  helps intuition, standard deviation is actually the square root of the
  average squared deviation so the exact value can be difficult to
  ascertain without computation. The actual values are: F = 0.45, E =
  1.15, A = 2.4, C = 3.1, B = 3.7, D = 5.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-sd-matching}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Variance and standard deviation are both based on average squared
deviations from the mean. Variance has some nice mathematical properties
(which we'll see later), but standard deviation is the more
``practical'' number since it has the same measurement units as the
variable. In computations we often work with variances then take the
square root at the end to report and interpret standard deviations.

Standard deviation is the most commonly used single-number measure of
variability, but it's not the only one. Average absolute deviation also
measures variability; why not use that? It turns out that squaring
deviations, rather than taking absolute values, leads to nicer
mathematical properties\footnote{Think Pythagorean theorem: it's
  \(a^2+b^2=c^2\). On the other hand, for absolute values we only have
  the triangle inequality \(|a+b| \le |a| + |b|\).}. Also, standard
deviation is the natural measure of variability for Normal distributions
(we'll investigate why later). While standard deviation is commonly
used, there are other, sometimes better, ways to summarize variability.
For example, we will see later how percentiles can be used to summarize
the pattern of variability.

The following definiton states our notion of variance in expected value
terms.

\begin{definition}[Variance and standard deviation of a random
varible]\protect\hypertarget{def-variance}{}\label{def-variance}

The \textbf{variance} of a random variable \(X\) is \[
\textrm{Var}(X) = \textrm{E}((X-\textrm{E}(X))^2)
\] The \textbf{standard deviation} of a random variable \(X\) is
\(\textrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}(X)}\).

\end{definition}

Recall that an expected value is a long run average. Thefore we can
interpret \(\textrm{E}(\cdot)\) as ``simulate many values of what's
inside \((\cdot)\) and average''. In this way \[
\textrm{E}((X-\textrm{E}(X))^2) = \text{Long Run Average of } [(X - \text{Long Run Average of } X)^2]
\]

Recall that for discrete random variables we can compute expected values
as probability-weighted average values. We can compute variances for
discrete random variables in a similar way.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sd-compute-dice}{}\label{exm-sd-compute-dice}

In the dice rolling problem, let \(Y\) be the larger of the two rolls.
The marginal distribution of \(Y\) is represented by
Table~\ref{tbl-dice-max-dist-table}. In Example~\ref{exm-dice-ev-intro}
we computed \(\textrm{E}(Y) = 3.125\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Var}(Y)\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{SD}(Y)\).
\item
  Describe in detail how \(\textrm{Var}(Y)\) can be simulated via
  approximation
\item
  Write Symbulate code to approximate \(\textrm{Var}(Y)\) and
  \(\textrm{SD}(Y)\) and compare to the values from parts 1 and 2.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(Y\) takes values 1, 2, 3, 4, and \(\textrm{E}(Y)=3.125\), so
  \((Y-\textrm{E}(Y))^2\) takes values \((1-3.125)^2\), \((2-3.125)^2\),
  \((3-3.125)^2\), \((4-3.125)^2\), with respective probability 1/16,
  3/16, 5/16, 7/16. To compute \(\textrm{E}((Y-\textrm{E}(Y))^2)\) as a
  probability-weighted average value, multiply each possible of
  \((Y-\textrm{E}(Y))^2\) by its probability and sum. \[
  (1-3.125)^2\times 0.0625 + (2-3.125)^2 \times 0.1875 + (3-3.125)^2 \times 0.3125 + (4-3.125)^2 \times 0.4375  = 0.8594
  \] See Table~\ref{tbl-sd-compute-dice} for more detail.
  \(\textrm{Var}(Y) = 0.8594\).
\item
  \(\textrm{SD}(Y)=\sqrt{\textrm{Var}(Y)} = \sqrt{0.8594} = 0.9270\).
\item
  We have already discussed how to simulate a value of \(Y\) in this
  content. To approximate the variance

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Simulate many values of \(Y\)
  \item
    Compute the average of the simulated values of \(Y\) (to approximate
    \(\textrm{E}(Y)\))
  \item
    From each simulated value of \(Y\) subtract the average, and then
    square
  \item
    Compute the average of the squared deviations from the previous part
    to approximate the variance
  \end{itemize}
\item
  See below for the code, both the long way and using the \texttt{var}
  and \texttt{sd} shortcuts. The simulation-based approximations are
  close to the values from parts 1 and 2.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-sd-compute-dice}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sd-compute-dice2}{}\label{exm-sd-compute-dice2}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-sd-compute-dice}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(Y^2)\).
\item
  Describe in detail how \(\textrm{E}(Y^2)\) can be approximated via
  simulation.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(Y^2) - (\textrm{E}(Y))^2\). What do you notice?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(Y\) takes values 1, 2, 3, 4, so \(Y^2\) takes values
  \(1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2\), with respective probability 1/16, 3/16, 5/16,
  7/16. To compute \(\textrm{E}(Y^2)\) as a probability-weighted average
  value, multiply each possible of \(Y^2\) by its probability and sum.
  \[
  1^2\times 0.0625 + 2^2 \times 0.1875 + 3^2 \times 0.3125 + 4^2 \times 0.4375  = 10.625
  \] \(\textrm{E}(Y^2) = 10.625\). Notice this is \emph{not} the same as
  \(\textrm{E}(Y)^2=3.125^2.\)
\item
  We have already discussed how to simulate a value of \(Y\) in this
  content. To approximate \(\textrm{E}(Y^2)\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Simulate many values of \(Y\)
  \item
    Square each simulated value of \(Y\)
  \item
    Compute the average of the squared values from from the previous
    part to approximate \(\textrm{E}(Y^2)\). See the Symbulate code
    below.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(Y^2) - (\textrm{E}(Y))^2 = 10.625 - 3.125^2 = 0.8594\),
  which is \(\textrm{Var}(Y)\).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-sd-compute-dice2}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Example~\ref{exm-sd-compute-dice2} illustrates an alternative formula
for computing variance. Definition~\ref{def-variance} represents the
concept of variance. However, variance is usually computed using the
following equivalent but slightly simpler formula.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-variance-shortcut}{}\label{lem-variance-shortcut}

\[
\textrm{Var}(X) = \textrm{E}(X^2) - (\textrm{E}(X))^2
\]

\end{lemma}

That is, the variance of \(X\) is the expected value of the square of
\(X\) minus the square of the expected value of \(X\).

We will see that variance has many nice theoretical properties. Whenever
you need to compute a standard deviation, first find the variance and
then take the square root at the end.

We will see how to compute variance for continuous random variables
later. But Definition~\ref{def-variance} and
Lemma~\ref{lem-variance-shortcut} apply for both discrete and continuous
random variables. Furthermore, variance can be approximated via
simulation in the same way for discrete or continuous random variables:
simulate many values of the random variable and compute the average of
the squared deviations from the mean.

\subsection{Standardization}\label{standardization}

Standard deviation provides a ``ruler'' by which we can judge a
particular value of a random variable relative to the distribution of
values. This idea is particularly useful when comparing random variables
with different measurement units but whose distributions have similar
shapes.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-sat-z-score}{}\label{exm-sat-z-score}

SAT scores have, approximately, a Normal distribution with a mean of
1050 and a standard deviation of 200. ACT scores have, approximately, a
Normal distribution with a mean of 21 and a standard deviation of 5.5.
Darius's score on the SAT is 1500. Alfred's score on the ACT is 31.
We'll investigate who scored relatively better on their test.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute the deviation from the mean for Darius's SAT score. How large
  is this value relative to the standard deviation for SAT scores (which
  measures, roughly, the average deviation from the mean)?
\item
  Compute the deviation from the mean for Alfred's ACT score. How large
  is this value relative to the standard deviation for ACT scores?
\item
  Who scored relatively better on their test? Explain.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Darius's score is \(1500-1050 = 450\) points above the mean SAT score.
  The standard deviation of SAT scores is 200 points. Roughly, the
  deviation of Darius's score from the mean is \(450/200 = 2.25\) times
  larger the average deviation.\\
  That is, Darius's SAT score of 1500 is \emph{2.25 standard deviations}
  above the mean SAT score.
\item
  Alfred's score is \(31-21 = 10\) points above the mean ACT score. The
  standard deviation of ACT scores is 5.5 points. Roughly, the deviation
  of Alfred's score from the mean is \(10/5.5 = 1.82\) times larger than
  the average deviation. That is, Alfred's ACT score of 31 is \emph{1.82
  standard deviations} above the mean ACT score.
\item
  Both scores are above average, but relative to other test scores,
  Darius's is farther above average than Alfred's. Both distributions
  are Normal, so the probability that an SAT score is greater than
  Darius's is smaller than the probability that an ACT score is greater
  than Alfred's. That is, Darius scored relatively better. See
  Figure~\ref{fig-sat-z-score-plot}.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-sat-z-score}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-sat-z-score-plot-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-sat-z-score-plot}Comparison of the Normal
distributions in Example~\ref{exm-sat-z-score}.}

\end{figure}%

Standard deviation provides a ``ruler'' by which we can judge a
particular value of a random variable relative to the distribution of
values. Consider the plot for SAT scores in
Figure~\ref{fig-sat-z-score-plot}. For now, pay attention to the two
horizontal axis scales on each plot; we'll discuss the Normal ``bell
shape'' in more detail later. There are two scales on the variable axis:
one representing the actual measurement units, and one representing
``standardized units''. In the standardized scale, values are measured
in terms of standard deviations away from the mean:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The mean corresponds to a value of 0.
\item
  A one unit increment on the standardized scale corresponds to an
  increment equal to the standard deviation in the measurement unit
  scale.
\end{itemize}

For example, each one unit increment in the standardized scale
corresponds to a 200 point increment in the measurement unit scale for
SAT scores, and a 5.5 point increment in the measurement unit scale for
ACT scores. An SAT score of 1250 is ``1 standard deviation above the
mean''; an ACT score of 10 is ``2 standard deviations below the mean''.
Given a specific distribution, the more standard deviations a particular
value is away from its mean, the more extreme or ``unusual'' it is.

Given a value of a variable, its \textbf{standardized value} marks where
the value lies on the standardized scale (e.g., 1500 on the SAT scale
corresponds to 2.25 on the standardized scale).

\[
\text{Standardized value} = \frac{\text{Value - Mean}}{\text{Standard deviation}}
\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Warning}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

Standardization is useful when comparing random variables with different
measurement units but whose distributions have similar shapes (like the
two Normal distributions in Figure~\ref{fig-sat-z-score-plot}). However,
standardized values are only based on two features of a
distribution---mean and standard deviation---rather than the complete
pattern of variability. Distributions with different shapes have
different patterns of variability. We will see later than when comparing
distributions with different shapes, it is better to compare percentiles
rather than standardized values to determine what is ``extreme'' or
``unusual''.

\end{tcolorbox}

Any random variable can be standardized, but keep in mind that just how
extreme any particular standardized value is depends on the shape of the
distribution. We will see that standardization is most natural for
random variables that follow a Normal distribution.

\subsection{Normal distributions
(briefly)}\label{normal-distributions-briefly}

Standardization is most natural for random variables that follow a
Normal distribution. The Normal(30, 10) model that we assumed for
arrival times in the meeting problem is an example of a \emph{Normal
distribution}. The pattern of variability for any Normal distribution
follows a particular bell shape, like in
Figure~\ref{fig-sat-z-score-plot}. A Normal distribution has two
parameters: its mean (typically denoted \(\mu\)) and its standard
deviation (typically denoted \(\sigma\)). For Normal distributions the
probability that a value is within (or beyond) a given number of
standard deviations from the mean follows a specific pattern called the
``empirical rule''. For example, the empirical rule for Normal
distributions specifies that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  68\% of values are within 1 standard deviation of the mean
\item
  95\% of values are within 2 standard deviations of the mean
\item
  99.7\% of values are within 3 standard deviations of the mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=8.97in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{_graphics/normal_empirical.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-normal-empirical-rule}Illustration of the empirical
rule for Normal distributions}

\end{figure}%

Therefore the key to working with Normal distributions is to work in
terms of standardized values. The ``standard'' Normal distribution is a
Normal(0, 1) distribution, with a mean 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
Notice how the empirical rule corresponds to the spinner in
Figure~\ref{fig-standard-normal-spinner}.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-standard-normal-spinner-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-standard-normal-spinner}A standard \emph{Normal(0,
1)} spinner. Only selected rounded values are displayed, but in the
idealized model the spinner is infinitely precise so that any real
number is a possible outcome. Notice that the values on the axis are
\emph{not} evenly spaced.}

\end{figure}%

If a random variable follows a Normal distribution, a value of it can be
simulated by spinning the standard Normal spinner in
Figure~\ref{fig-standard-normal-spinner} to determine how many standard
deviations the value is away from the mean (above or below) and then
converting to the measurement units of the variable.

We have only introduced a small part of the empirical rule in this
section, corresponding to 1, 2, or 3 standard deviations away from the
mean. We will cover Normal distributions and the empirical rule in much
more detail later.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-23}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-variance-collector}{}\label{exr-simulation-variance-collector}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Let \(X\) be the number of
distinct prizes obtained in these 3 packages. Let \(Y\) be the number of
these 3 packages that contain prize 1.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain how you could, in principle, conduct a simulation by hand and
  use the results to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{Var}(X)\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{SD}(X)\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate the
  values in part 1.
\item
  Compute the theoretical values of \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) and
  \(\textrm{SD}(X)\) and compare to the simulation results.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-variance-continuous-dice}{}\label{exr-simulation-variance-continuous-dice}

Consider a continuous version of the dice rolling problem where instead
of rolling two fair four-sided dice (which return values 1, 2, 3, 4) we
spin twice a Uniform(1, 4) spinner (which returns any value in the
continuous range between 1 and 4). Let \(X\) be the sum of the two spins
and let \(Y\) be the larger of the two spins.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the marginal distributions of \(X\) and
  \(Y\).
\item
  Which will have the larger standard deviation, \(X\) or \(Y\)? Make a
  ballpark estimate the of the standard deviation of each.
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) and \(\textrm{SD}(X)\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{E}(Y)\) and \(\textrm{SD}(Y)\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation to approximate the
  quantities in the previous part.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\section{Measuring relationships: Covariance and
correlation}\label{sec-sim-corr}

Quantities like expected value, variance, and standard deviation
summarize characteristics of the \emph{marginal} distribution of a
single random variable. When there are multiple random variables their
\emph{joint} distribution is of interest. Covariance and correlation
each summarize in a single number a characteristic of the joint
distribution of two random variables, namely, the degree to which they
``co-deviate from the their respective means''.

\subsection{Covariance}\label{covariance}

Consider the independent Uniform(0, 60) model of arrival times in the
meeting problem from Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim-independent-uniform}.
Let \(R\) and \(Y\) be the two arrival times, and let \(T=\min(R, Y)\)
and \(W=|R-Y|\) be the first arrival time and waiting time random
variables, respectively. Our goal is to compute the covariance between
\(T\) and \(W\).

We'll illustrate the calculation using the simulation results from
Table~\ref{tbl-meeting-tactile-uniform-sim-table-pair}. The simulated
\((T, W)\) pairs are displayed in Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc}. The mean
of the 10 simulated values of \(T\) is 22.6, and the mean of the 10
simulated values of \(W\) is 20.7. We want to measure the degree to
which \(T\) and \(W\) ``co-deviate from the their respective means''.
For each value of \(T\) we find its deviation from the mean, and
likewise for \(W\); see the ``T\_deviation'' and ``W\_deviation''
columns of Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc}. Notice that we do care about
the sign since we are interested in the \emph{relationship} between
\(T\) and \(W\), which involves questions like: if \(T\) is above the
mean, does \(W\) tend to be above or below the mean? For each simulated
\((T, W)\) pair, we now have a pair of deviations from the respective
mean.

We want to measure the degree of co-deviation between \(X\) and \(Y\);
one way to do this is to measure the interaction between the paired
deviations by taking their \emph{product}. See the
``product\_of\_deviations'' column of Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc}.
Within each row, the value in the product column is the product of the
values in the ``T\_devation'' and ``W\_deviation'' columns. The
\emph{covariance} is the \emph{average of the product of the
deviations}: sum the 10 values of the product and divide by 10 to get a
covariance of -134.1. \[
\text{Covariance($X$, $Y$)} = \text{Average of} ((X - \text{Average of }X)(Y - \text{Average of }Y))
\]

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tbl-sim-cov-calc}Calculation of covariance based on 10
simulated values}

\centering{

\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{l|r|r|r|r|r}
\hline
repetition & T & W & T\_deviation & W\_deviation & product\_of\_deviations\\
\hline
1 & 49.505 & 3.244 & 26.917 & -17.458 & -469.925\\
\hline
2 & 22.041 & 33.344 & -0.547 & 12.643 & -6.912\\
\hline
3 & 7.524 & 2.433 & -15.064 & -18.269 & 275.198\\
\hline
4 & 39.636 & 11.695 & 17.049 & -9.007 & -153.555\\
\hline
5 & 26.338 & 17.435 & 3.751 & -3.267 & -12.254\\
\hline
6 & 28.619 & 13.894 & 6.032 & -6.808 & -41.063\\
\hline
7 & 31.155 & 9.963 & 8.567 & -10.739 & -91.999\\
\hline
8 & 4.406 & 39.610 & -18.181 & 18.908 & -343.770\\
\hline
9 & 8.867 & 26.600 & -13.721 & 5.898 & -80.928\\
\hline
10 & 7.784 & 48.801 & -14.803 & 28.099 & -415.960\\
\hline
Sum & 225.877 & 207.018 & 0.000 & 0.000 & -1341.168\\
\hline
Average & 22.588 & 20.702 & 0.000 & 0.000 & -134.117\\
\hline
\end{tabular}

}

\end{table}%

Why take the product of the deviations? For two random variables \(X\)
and \(Y\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If both \(X\) and \(Y\) values are far above the mean, the product of
  the deviations will be positive and large in magnitude
\item
  If both \(X\) and \(Y\) values are far below the mean, the product of
  the devations will be positive and large in magnitude
\item
  If the \(X\) value is far above the mean but the \(Y\) value is far
  below the mean, the product of the deviations will be negative and
  large in magnitude
\item
  If the \(X\) value is far below the mean but the \(Y\) value is far
  above the mean, the product of the deviations will be negative and
  large in magnitude
\item
  If the \(X\) value is close to its mean, the product of the deviations
  will be close to 0 regardless of the \(Y\) value
\item
  If the \(Y\) value is close to its mean, the product of the deviations
  will be close to 0 regardless of the \(X\) value
\end{itemize}

So the average of the products of the deviations gives insight to the
overall relationship between \(T\) and \(W\); is the association:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{positive}: above average values of \(X\) tend to be associated
  with above average values of \(Y\), and below average values of \(X\)
  tend to be associated with below average values of \(Y\)
\item
  \emph{negative}: above average values of \(X\) tend to be associated
  with below average values of \(Y\), and below average values of \(X\)
  tend to be associated with above average values of \(Y\)
\item
  \emph{zero}: no overall positive or negative association between \(X\)
  and \(Y\).
\end{itemize}

Figure~\ref{fig-cov-calc-rectangles} visualizes the covariance
calculation. The ten \((T, W)\) pairs from Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc}
are displayed in each plot. The green ``+'' represents the two means.
Figure~\ref{fig-cov-calc-rectangles-1} highlights the first row of
Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc}. The horizontal orange segment represents
the deviation of the \(T\) value from the mean of the \(T\) values, and
the vertical blue segment represents the deviation of the \(W\) value
from the mean of the \(W\) values. If we think of these deviations as
the sides of the shaded rectangle, the area of the rectangle represents
the magnitude of the product of the deviations. For this pair the
product would be negative since the value of \(T\) is above the mean but
the value of \(W\) is below the mean.
Figure~\ref{fig-cov-calc-rectangles-2} displays ten rectangles, one for
each \((T, W)\) pair. The rectangles are shaded grey if the product of
the deviations is negative, and yellow if positive. The covariance is
the average of the ten areas, keeping in mind that the areas can
represent either positive (yellow) or negative (gray) values. There is
more gray area than yellow area, so the covariance is negative.

\begin{figure}

\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}

}

\subcaption{\label{fig-cov-calc-rectangles-1}A single point with its
paired deviations and product rectangle}

\end{minipage}%

\end{minipage}%

Table~\ref{tbl-sim-cov-calc} and Figure~\ref{fig-cov-calc-rectangles}
motivate the idea and calculation of covariance, but we're really
interested in what happens in the long run. We'll start by simulating
many \((T, W)\) pairs.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y)}

\NormalTok{meeting\_sim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ T }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ W).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{t\_and\_w }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ meeting\_sim[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{t\_and\_w}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\end{Shaded}

(19.665661915617488, 20.103022180388443)

Now within each simulated \((t, w)\) pair, we subtract the mean of the
\(T\) values from \(t\) and the mean of the \(W\) values from \(w\), We
can do this subtraction in a ``vectorized'' way: the following code
subtracts the first component of \texttt{t\_and\_w.mean()} (the average
of the \(T\)) from the first component of each of the \texttt{t\_and\_w}
values (the individual \(t\) value), and similarly for the second.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ t\_and\_w.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (20.769045373555503, -19.029811133280397)
1     (-18.893753869823914, 34.694011488168115)
2     (15.490609195243092, -2.638374517071867)
3     (-11.119138265200128, 27.91141167255902)
4     (27.935656601120936, -17.335284104597463)
5     (-17.7201910335478, 27.10990120467185)

....  .......................................

For each simulated pair, we now have a pair of deviations from the
respective mean. To measure the interaction between these deviations, we
take the product of the deviations within each pair. First, we split the
paired deviations into two separate columns and then take the product
within each row.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_deviations }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (t\_and\_w }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ t\_and\_w.mean())[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\CommentTok{\# first column (Python 0)}
\NormalTok{w\_deviations }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (t\_and\_w }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ t\_and\_w.mean())[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\CommentTok{\# second column (Python 1)}

\NormalTok{t\_deviations }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ w\_deviations}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     -395.23101087729225
1     -655.5001138142917
2     -40.87002855464851
3     -310.3508455641045
4     -484.27254382890493
5     -480.3926282473928
6     9.989545805752678
7     -227.98423576108553
8     -430.3857205708229
....  .................
9999  -25.0388766789837
\end{verbatim}

Now we take the average of the products of the paired deviations.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(t\_deviations }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ w\_deviations).mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
-99.55382175149128
\end{verbatim}

This value is the \emph{covariance}, which we could have arrived at more
quickly by calling \texttt{cov} on the simulated \((T, W)\) pairs.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-99.55382175149128)
\end{verbatim}

The covariance between \(T\) and \(W\) is negative because the two
variables have an overall negative association. The largest values of
\(T\) (near 60) are associated with the smallest values of \(W\) (near
0) and vice versa. Since both people need to arrive in the 0 to 60 time
interval, if the first person arrives very late then they won't have to
wait very long. Note that the association isn't perfect; the smallest
values of \(T\) (near 0) are associated with the whole range of waiting
times (from 0 to 60). But the \emph{overall tendency} is a negative
association.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-covariance-arrivals-meeting}{}\label{exm-covariance-arrivals-meeting}

Now consider the arrival times \(R\) and \(Y\) of the two people in the
meeting problem.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain in words in full detail how you could simulation to
  approximate the covariance between \(R\) and \(Y\). Assume that \(R\)
  and \(Y\) following the independent Uniform(0, 60) model of
  Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim-independent-uniform}
\item
  For each of the following, explain if the covariance between \(R\) and
  \(Y\) will be positive, negative, or close to 0. Then use Symbulate to
  approximate the covariance.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    the independent Uniform(0, 60) model of
    Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim-independent-uniform}
  \item
    the independent Normal(30, 10) model of
    Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim-independent-normal}
  \item
    the Bivariate Normal model of
    Section~\ref{sec-language-simulation-computer-meeting-bvn}
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Spin the Uniform(0, 60) spinner twice to simulate an \((R, Y)\) pair.
  Repeat to simulate many \((R, Y)\) pairs. Compute the average of the
  simulated \(R\) values and the deviations of the \(R\) values from
  their average; likewise for \(Y\). Now you have a pair of deviations
  for each repetition; compute the product of the paired deviations and
  then average the products to approximate the covariance between \(R\)
  and \(Y\). (The only difference for the other models in the next part
  would be how you simulate and \((R, Y)\) pair; once you have the pairs
  you would approximate the covariance using the same method.)
\item
  We basically assumed the covariance in definining the model for \(R\)
  and \(Y\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(R\) and \(Y\) are independent, so there will be no overall
    association and we expect the covariance to be near 0
  \item
    \(R\) and \(Y\) are independent, so there will be no overall
    association and we expect the covariance to be near 0. The pattern
    of variability of \((R, Y)\) would be different than in the previous
    part but there is still no relationship between \(R\) and \(Y\).
  \item
    We expect the covariance to be positive because we assumed that
    there was a positive association---they tend to arrive around the
    same time---when definiing the model.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-covariance-arrivals-meeting}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# independent Uniform(0, 60)}
\NormalTok{meeting\_sim[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{].cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-2.2742151730458056)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# independent Normal(30, 10)}

\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-1.0043556230372825)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Bivariate Normal model}

\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(71.69663064347587)
\end{verbatim}

The following definiton states our notion of covariance in expected
value terms.

\begin{definition}[Covariance between two random
variables]\protect\hypertarget{def-covariance}{}\label{def-covariance}

The \textbf{covariance} between two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) is
\[
\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{E}((X-\textrm{E}(X))(Y-\textrm{E}(Y)))
\]

\end{definition}

Recall that an expected value is a long run average. Thefore we can
interpret \(\textrm{E}(\cdot)\) as ``simulate many values of what's
inside \((\cdot)\) and average''. In this way \[
\textrm{E}((X-\textrm{E}(X))(Y-\textrm{E}(Y))) = \text{Long Run Average of} ((X - \text{Long Run Average of }X)(Y - \text{Long Run Average of }Y))
\] where the average is over many \((X, Y)\) \emph{pairs}.

Unfortunately, the actual \emph{value} of covariance is hard to
interpret as it depends heavily on the measurement unit scale of the
random variables. In the meeting problem, if \(T\) and \(W\) are both
measured in minutes then the covariance is measured in minutes
\(\times\) minutes, e.g., -100 \(\text{minutes}^2\). If we converted the
\(T\) values from minutes to seconds, then the value of covariance would
change accordingly and would be measured in minutes \(\times\) seconds,
e.g., -6000 minutes \(\times\) seconds. In another context, if the
covariance between height (m) and weight (kg) is 0.3
\(\text{m}\times\text{kg}\), then the covariance between height (cm) and
weight (g) is 300,000 \(\text{cm}\times\text{g}\).

But the \emph{sign} of the covariance does have an intuitive meaning.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A positive covariance indicate an overall \emph{positive association}:
  above average values of \(X\) tend to be associated with above average
  values of \(Y\)
\item
  A negative covariance indicates am overall \emph{negative
  association}: above average values of \(X\) tend to be associated with
  below average values of \(Y\)
\item
  A covariance of zero indicates that the random variables are
  \textbf{uncorrelated}: there is no overall positive or negative
  association. But be careful: if \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated there
  can still be a relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\). We will see
  examples later that demonstrate that being uncorrelated does not
  necessarily imply that random variables are independent.
\end{itemize}

We discussed how variance has many nice theoretical properties, but
standard deviation is easier to interpret. Similarly, covariance has
many nice theoretical properties, but \emph{correlation} is easier to
interpret. We will introduce correlation in the next subsection.

Recall that for discrete random variables we can compute expected values
as probability-weighted average values. We can compute covariances for
discrete random variables in a similar way.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-cov-compute-dice}{}\label{exm-cov-compute-dice}

In the dice rolling problem, let \(X\) be the sum and \(Y\) be the
larger of the two rolls. The joint distribution of \(X\) and \(Y\) is
represented\footnotemark{} by Table~\ref{tbl-dice-joint-dist-flat}. In
Example~\ref{exm-dice-ev-intro} we computed \(\textrm{E}(X) = 5\) and
\(\textrm{E}(Y) = 3.125\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Will \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\) be positive, negative, or close to 0?
  Explain without computing.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Describe in detail how \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\) can be simulated via
  approximation
\item
  Write Symbulate code to approximate \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\) and compare
  to the values from part 2.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\footnotetext{We usually represent joint distributions as two-way
tables, but for this problem it helps to think of a table with one row
for each pair.}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The covariance will be positive. The smallest value of \(Y\) only
  occurs with the smallest value of \(X\), and when \(Y\) is its largest
  value \(X\) is above average.
\item
  For the pair (2, 1), which occurs with probability (1/16) the paired
  deviations are \((2-5, 1 - 3.125)\), the product is
  \((2-5)(1-3.125)\), and so the contribution to the
  probability-weighted average is \((2-5)(1-3.125)(1/16) = 0.3984\); see
  the first row of Table~\ref{tbl-sd-compute-dice}. We repeat for each
  possible \((X, Y)\) pair; see Table~\ref{tbl-sd-compute-dice} for more
  detail. The covariance is the sum of the values in the last column,
  \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 1.25\).
\item
  We have already discussed how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs in this
  content. To approximate the covariance

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs
  \item
    Compute the average of the simulated values of \(X\) (to approximate
    \(\textrm{E}(X)\)), and likewise for \(Y\)
  \item
    From each simulated value of \(X\) subtract the average, and
    likewise for \(Y\)
  \item
    Compute the product of the two deviations from the previous part for
    each simulated pair
  \item
    Average the products from the previous part to approximate the
    covariance
  \end{itemize}
\item
  See below for the code, both the long way and using the \texttt{cov}
  shortcut. The simulation-based approximation is close to 1.25.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-cov-compute-dice}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-cov-compute-dice2}{}\label{exm-cov-compute-dice2}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-cov-compute-dice}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(XY)\). (We'll see why very soon.) Is it equal to
  \(\textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y)\)?
\item
  Describe in detail how \(\textrm{E}(XY)\) can be approximated via
  simulation.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y)\). What do you
  notice?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(X\) is 5 and \(Y\) is 3, which occurs with probability 2/16, then
  the product \(XY\) is (5)(3) = 15. To compute \(\textrm{E}(XY)\) as a
  probability-weighted average value, multiply each possible of \(XY\)
  by its probability and sum. \[
  {\scriptsize
  (2)(1)(1/16)+(3)(2)(2/16)+(4)(2)(1/16)+(4)(3)(2/16)+(5)(3)(2/16)+(5)(4)(2/16)+(6)(3)(1/16)+(6)(4)(2/16)+(7)(4)(2/16)+(8)(4)(1/16)
  }
  \] \(\textrm{E}(XY) = 16.875\). Notice this is \emph{not} the same as
  \(\textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y)=(5)(3.125) = 15.625\)
\item
  We have already discussed how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs in this
  content. To approximate \(\textrm{E}(XY)\)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs
  \item
    For each simulated \((X, Y)\) pair compute the product \(XY\). For
    example, if \(X\) is 5 and \(Y\) is 3 then the product \(XY\) is
    (5)(3)=15.
  \item
    Average the products from the previous part to approximate
    \(\textrm{E}(XY)\) See the Symbulate code below.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y) = 16.875-(5)(3.125) = 1.25\),
  which is \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-cov-compute-dice2}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Example~\ref{exm-cov-compute-dice2} illustrates an alternative formula
for computing covariance. Definition~\ref{def-covariance} represents the
concept of covariance. However, covariance is usually computed using the
following equivalent but slightly simpler formula.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-covariance-shortcut}{}\label{lem-covariance-shortcut}

\[
\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y)
\]

\end{lemma}

That is, the covariance of \(X\) and \(Y\) is the expected value of the
product minus the product of the expected values.

We will see how to compute covariance for continuous random variables
later. But Definition~\ref{def-covariance} and
Lemma~\ref{lem-covariance-shortcut} apply for both discrete and
continuous random variables. Furthermore, covariance can be approximated
via simulation in the same way for discrete or continuous random
variables: simulate many pairs of the random variables and compute the
average of the products of the paired deviations from the respective
means.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-dice-covariance}{}\label{exm-dice-covariance}

Consider the probability space corresponding to two rolls of a fair
four-sided die. Let \(X\) be the sum of the two rolls, \(Y\) the larger
of the two rolls, \(W\) the number of rolls equal to 4, and \(Z\) the
number of rolls equal to 1. Without doing any calculations, determine if
the covariance between each of the following pairs of variables is
positive, negative, or zero. Explain your reasoning conceptually.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) and \(W\)
\item
  \(X\) and \(Z\)
\item
  \(X\) and \(V\), where \(V = W + Z\).
\item
  \(W\) and \(Z\). Hint: remember that there are two rolls.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Positive. If \(W\) is large (roll many 4s) then \(X\) (sum) tends to
  be large.
\item
  Negative. If \(Z\) is large (roll many 1s) then \(X\) (sum) tends to
  be small.
\item
  Zero. Basically, the positive association between \(X\) and \(W\)
  cancels out with the negative association of \(X\) and \(Z\). \(V\) is
  large when there are many 1s or many 4s, or some mixture of 1s and 4s.
  So knowing that W is large doesn't really tell you anything about the
  sum.
\item
  Negative.\\
  There is a fixed number of rolls. If you roll lots of 4s (\(W\) is
  large) then there must be few rolls of 1s (\(Z\) is small).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-dice-covariance}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Correlation}\label{correlation}

The numerical value of the covariance depends on the measurement units
of both variables, so interpreting it can be difficult. Covariance is a
measure of joint association between two random variables that has many
nice theoretical properties, but the correlation (coefficient) is often
a more practical measure.

Recall that we can standardize a random variable to put in on a standard
measurement scale in which values are measured in terms of standard
deviations above or below the mean. It is useful to standardize random
variables when measuring their co-deviation, measuring the deviations in
standard deviation terms rather than measurement units. The correlation
between two random variables is the covariance between the corresponding
standardized random variables. Therefore, correlation is a
\emph{standardized} measure of the association between two random
variables.

\begin{definition}[Correlation between two random
variables]\protect\hypertarget{def-correlation}{}\label{def-correlation}

The \textbf{correlation} (a.k.a. correlation coefficient) between two
random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[
\textrm{Corr}(X, Y) = \textrm{Cov}\left(\frac{X-\textrm{E}(X)}{\textrm{SD}(X)}\frac{Y-\textrm{E}(Y)}{\textrm{SD}(Y)}\right)
\]

\end{definition}

Returning to the \((T, W)\) example, we carry out the same process of
computing the covariance, but first standardize each of the simulated
values of \(T\) by subtracting their mean and dividing by their
standardization, and similarly for \(W\). Then we compute the product
for each pair of standardized values and average the products to get the
correlation -0.619.
