\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(19.665661915617488, 20.103022180388443)
\end{verbatim}

Compute the standard deviations

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(14.08210820502724, 14.229580156949096)
\end{verbatim}

We'll use the \texttt{standardize} method to standardize the simulated
values. Note that values are standardized using the respective means and
standard deviations.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.standardize()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (1.4748534147849441, -1.337341715172607)
1     (-1.3416850371224205, 2.438161288351512)
2     (1.1000206055591182, -0.18541478300632797)
3     (-0.7895932983408446, 1.9615063385358087)
4     (1.9837694892266238, -1.2182568925711894)
5     (-1.2583478819756393, 1.9051792748384482)
6     (0.38610046996243713, 0.1291176606414834)
7     (-0.762935596888709, 1.4912730730428325)
8     (2.024645159776047, -1.0608382506897733)
....  ..........................................
9999  (0.3963737014401267, -0.31524647960363644)
\end{verbatim}

Now we compute the covariance of the standardized values to get the
correlation.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.standardize().cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-0.4968189735657518)
\end{verbatim}

We can also just call \texttt{corr} on the simulated \((T, W)\) pairs.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.corr()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-0.4968189735657507)
\end{verbatim}

When standardizing, subtracting the means doesn't change the scale of
the possible pairs of values or how far away they are from their means;
it merely shifts the center of the joint distribution. Dividing by the
standard deviations does change the scale. It can be shown that
correlation is the covariance divided by the product of the standard
deviations.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-correlation-shortcut}{}\label{lem-correlation-shortcut}

\[
\textrm{Corr}(X, Y) = \frac{\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\textrm{SD}(X)\textrm{SD}(Y)}
\]

\end{lemma}

The simulated values provide an example of this property.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_and\_w.cov() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (t\_and\_w.sd()[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (t\_and\_w.sd()[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(-0.4968189735657516)
\end{verbatim}

Definition~\ref{def-correlation} reflects the concept of correlation,
but Lemma~\ref{lem-correlation-shortcut} is usually how we compute
correlation. The hard work is in computing the covariance and the
standard deviations; once we have those it's just a matter of dividing
to get the correlation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-corr-compute-dice}{}\label{exm-corr-compute-dice}

In the dice rolling problem, let \(X\) be the sum and \(Y\) be the
larger of the two rolls.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Write Symbulate code to approximate \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\) and
  compare to the values from part 2.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In Example~\ref{exm-cov-compute-dice} we computed
  \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 1.25\), and in
  Example~\ref{exm-sd-compute-dice} we computed
  \(\textrm{SD}(Y) = 0.927\). We just need to compute
  \(\textrm{SD}(X)\). \(\textrm{E}(X)=5\), \(\textrm{E}(X^2) = 27.5\),
  \(\textrm{Var}(X) = 2.5\), and \(\textrm{SD}(X) = 1.581\). Therefore
  \[
  \textrm{Corr}(X, Y) = \frac{\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\textrm{SD}(X)\textrm{SD}(Y)} = \frac{1.25}{(1.581)(0.927)} = 0.853
  \]
\item
  See the code below (we simulated \texttt{x\_and\_y} pairs previously).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-corr-compute-dice}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(1.5778022404597718, 0.9242606504660418)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.cov()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(1.2426980500000007)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_and\_y.corr()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.8521549767231541)
\end{verbatim}

A correlation coefficient has no units and is measured on a universal
scale. Regardless of the original measurement units of the random
variables \(X\) and \(Y\) \[
-1\le \textrm{Correlation}(X,Y)\le 1
\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{Correlation}(X,Y) = 1\) if and only if \(Y=mX+b\) for some
  \(m>0\)
\item
  \(\textrm{Correlation}(X,Y) = -1\) if and only if \(Y=mX+b\) for some
  \(m<0\)
\end{itemize}

Therefore, correlation is a standardized measure of the strength of the
\emph{linear} association between two random variables. The closer the
correlation is to 1 or \(-1\), the closer the joint distribution of
\((X, Y)\) pairs hugs a straight line, with positive or negative slope.

Because correlation is computed between standardized random variables,
correlation is not affected by a linear rescaling of either variable. A
value that is ``one standard deviation above the mean'' is ``one
standard deviation above the mean'', whether the variable measured in
feet or inches or meters.

In some problems we are given the correlation and the standard
deviations and we need to compute the covariance

\[
\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\textrm{SD}(X)\textrm{SD}(Y)
\]

\subsection{Bivariate Normal distributions (briefly)}\label{sec-sim-bvn}

Just as Normal distributions are commonly assumed for marginal
distributions of individual random variables, joint Normal distributions
are often assumed for joint distributions of several random variables.
We'll focus ``Bivariate Normal'' distributions which describe a specific
pattern of joint variability for \emph{two} random variables.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-dd-bvn-spinner}{}\label{exm-dd-bvn-spinner}

Donny Don't has just completed a problem where it was assumed that SAT
Math scores follow a Normal(500, 100) distribution. Now a follow up
problem asks Donny how he could simulate a single (Math, Reading) pair
of scores. Donny says: ``That's easy; just spin the Normal(500, 100)
twice, once for Math and once for Reading.'' Do you agree? Explain your
reasoning.

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
You should not agree with Donny, for two reasons.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  It's possible that the distribution of SAT Math scores follow a
  different pattern than SAT Reading scores. So we might need one
  spinner to simulate a Math score, and a second spinner to simulate the
  Reading score. (In reality, SAT Math and Reading scores do follow
  pretty similar distributions. But it's possible that they could follow
  different distributions.)
\item
  Furthermore, there is probably some relationship between scores. It is
  plausible that students who do well on one test tend to do well on the
  other. For example, students who score over 700 on Math are probably
  more likely to score above than below average on Reading. If we
  simulate a pair of scores by spinning one spinner for Math and a
  separate spinner for Reading, then there will be no relationship
  between the scores because the spins are physically independent.
\end{itemize}

\label{sol-dd-bvn-spinner}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

In the previous problem, what we really need is a spinner that generates
a pair of scores simultaneously to reflect their association. This is a
little harder to visualize, but we could imagine spinning a ``globe''
with lines of latitude corresponding to SAT Math score and lines of
longitutde to SAT Reading score. But this would not be a typical globe:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The lines of latitude would not be equally spaced, since SAT Math
  scores are not equally likely. (We have seen similar issues for
  one-dimensional Normal spinners.) Similarly for lines of longitude.
\item
  The scale of the lines of latitude would not necessarily match the
  scale of the lines of longitude, since Math and Reading scores could
  follow difference distributions. For example, the equator (average
  Math) might be 500 while the prime meridian (average Reading) might be
  520.
\item
  The ``lines'' would be tilted or squiggled to reflect the relationship
  between the scores. For example, the region corresponding to Math
  scores near 700 and Reading scores near 700 would be larger than the
  region corresponding to Math scores near 700 but Reading scores near
  200.
\end{itemize}

So we would like a model that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulates Math scores that follow a Normal distribution pattern, with
  some mean and some standard deviation.
\item
  Simulates Reading scores that follow a Normal distribution pattern,
  with possibly a different mean and standard deviation.
\item
  Reflects how strongly the scores are associated.
\end{itemize}

Such a model is called a ``Bivariate Normal'' distribution. There are
five parameters: the two means, the two standard deviations, and the
\emph{correlation} which reflects the strength of the association
between the two scores.

Recall that in
Section~\ref{sec-language-simulation-computer-meeting-bvn} we assumed
that Regina and Cady tend to arrive around the same time. One way to
model pairs of values that have correlation is with a Bivariate Normal
distribution, like in the following. We assumed a Bivariate Normal
distribution for the \((R, Y)\) pairs, with mean (30, 30), standard
deviation (10, 10) and correlation 0.7. (We could have assumed different
means and standard deviations.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-172-1.png}

Now we see that the points tend to follow the \(R = Y\) line, so that
Regina and Cady tend to arrive near the same time.

Simulated values of a random variable with a Normal distribution follow
a ``bell-shaped'' curve. Similarly, simulated pairs of values of two
random variables with a Bivariate Normal distribution follow a
``mound-shaped'' or ``fin-shaped'' surface.

Figure~\ref{fig-bivariate-normal-densities} display a few Bivariate
Normal distributions with different correlations. Notice how the
correlation changes the shape of the distribution.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-bivariate-normal-densities-3.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-bivariate-normal-densities}Bivariate Normal
distributions}

\end{figure}%

We will cover Bivariate Normal distributions in much more detail later.

\subsection{Independent versus
uncorrelated}\label{independent-versus-uncorrelated}

The condition for independence of random variables is fairly strict.
Random variables are independent only if the joint distribution is
determined by the product of the marginal distributions for all values
of the random variables. Otherwise, the random variables are not
independent. However, you can imagine that there are different degrees
of dependence.

We wish to measure degree of dependence in a single number.
Unfortunately, there are many different ways two random variables can be
related, and there is no single measure that works well in all cases.

The most commonly used measure of the degree of an association between
two random variables is covariance, or its standardized counterpart,
correlation.\\
While covariance does have many uses and nice properties, it does NOT
measure whether two random variables are independent.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-zero-covariance}{}\label{exm-zero-covariance}

Find \(\textrm{Cov}(X,Y)\) in each of the following situations. Notice
that the marginal distribution of \(X\) is the same for each part, and
similarly for \(Y\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  & \(p_{X, Y}(x, y)\) & & & & \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  \(x\) \textbackslash{} \(y\) & & -1 & 0 & 1 & \(p_X(x)\) \\
  0 & & 1/6 & 1/6 & 1/6 & 1/2 \\
  1 & & 1/6 & 1/6 & 1/6 & 1/2 \\
  \(p_Y(y)\) & & 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 & \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  & \(p_{X, Y}(x, y)\) & & & & \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  \(x\) \textbackslash{} \(y\) & & -1 & 0 & 1 & \(p_X(x)\) \\
  0 & & 5/24 & 2/24 & 5/24 & 1/2 \\
  1 & & 3/24 & 6/24 & 3/24 & 1/2 \\
  \(p_Y(y)\) & & 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 & \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  In which of the previous parts are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent? Why?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y) = \textrm{E}(XY)\)
  since \(\textrm{E}(Y)=0\).
  \(\textrm{E}(XY) = 0 + (1)(1)(1/6) + (1)(-1)(1/6) = 0\). So the
  covariance is 0.
\item
  Again, \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{E}(XY)\) since
  \(\textrm{E}(Y)=0\).
  \(\textrm{E}(XY) = 0 + (1)(1)(3/24) + (1)(-1)(3/24) = 0\). So the
  covariance is 0.
\item
  \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent in part 1 because the joint
  distribution is the product of the marginal distributions. However,
  \(X\) and \(Y\) in part 2 are not independent even though the
  covariance is 0.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-zero-covarance-}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent then \(X\) and \(Y\) are
uncorrelated, that is, \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0\). However, the converse
is not true in general: there are many situations in which
\(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0\) but \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent.
Independence means there is no probabilistic relationship between two
random variables. Covariance only measures a particular kind of
probabilistic relationship, namely: how closely do the \((X, Y)\) pairs
tend to follow a single straight line with non-zero slope?

Correlation is most natural as a measure of association for Bivariate
Normal distributions. If \(X\) and \(Y\) have a Bivariate Normal
distribution and are uncorrelated, then \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-24}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-covariance-collector}{}\label{exr-simulation-covariance-collector}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Let \(X\) be the number of
distinct prizes obtained in these 3 packages. Let \(Y\) be the number of
these 3 packages that contain prize 1.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain how you could, in principle, conduct a simulation by hand and
  use the results to approximate \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate the
  covariance and correlation.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\) and \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent? Explain your reasoning.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-covariance-1}{}\label{exr-simulation-covariance-1}

Xavier and Yolanda are playing roulette. They both place bets on red on
the same 3 spins of the roulette wheel before Xavier has to leave.
(Remember, the probability that any bet on red on a single spin wins is
18/38.) After Xavier leaves, Yolanda places bets on red on 2 more spins
of the wheel. Let \(X\) be the number of bets that Xavier wins and let
\(Y\) be the number that Yolanda wins.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Find the marginal distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Compute \(\text{E}(X)\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Var}(X)\).
\item
  The joint distribution of \(X\) and \(Y\) is represented in the table
  below. Explain why \(\textrm{P}(X=1, Y = 4) = 0\) and
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 2, Y = 1) = 0\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 2, Y = 3)\). (Yes, the table tells you it's
  0.1766, but show how this number can be computed based on the
  assumptions of the problem.)
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent? Justify your answer with an
  appropriate calculation.
\item
  Compute and interpret \(\text{P}(X + Y = 4)\).
\item
  Make a table representing the marginal distribution of \(X+Y\).
\item
  Use the table from the previous part to compute \(\text{E}(X+Y)\), and
  verify that it is equal to \(\text{E}(X)+\text{E}(Y)\). (It can be
  shown that \(\textrm{E}(Y) = 5(18/38) = 2.37\))
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\). Interpret the sign of the covariance
  in context.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\). (It can be shown that
  \(\textrm{Var}(Y) = 5(18/38)(20/38) = 1.25\))
\end{enumerate}

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\(x\), \(y\) & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 0.0404 & 0.0727 & 0.0327 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0.109 & 0.1963 & 0.0883 & 0 & 0 \\
2 & 0 & 0 & 0.0981 & 0.1766 & 0.0795 & 0 \\
3 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.0294 & 0.053 & 0.0238 \\
\end{longtable}

\end{exercise}

\section{Conditioning}\label{sec-simulation-conditioning}

We can implement conditioning in simulations by only considering
repetitions that satisfy the condition. Conditioning can be thought of
as taking a subset of, or ``filtering'', the simulation results.

\subsection{Using simulation to approximate conditional
probabilities}\label{sec-simulation-conditioning-probabilities}

Conditional probabilities can be approximated using simulated relative
frequencies in a similar way to unconditional probabilities, but the
presence of conditioning requires more care.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-impeach-sim}{}\label{exm-impeach-sim}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-conditional-probability-def}. Consider
simulating a randomly selected U.S. adult and determining whether or not
the person is age 18-29 and whether or not they use Snapchat. Let \(A\)
be the event that the selected adult is age 18-29, \(C\) be the event
that the selected adult uses Snapchat, and \(\textrm{P}\) correspond to
randomly selecting an American adult. Suppose that
\(\textrm{P}(A) = 0.20\), \(\textrm{P}(C) = 0.24\), and
\(\textrm{P}(A\cap C) = 0.13\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Donny Don't says, ``we need two spinners to simulate this situation:
  One spinner with areas of 0.20 and 0.80 for age 18-29 or not, and
  another spinner with areas of 0.24 and 0.76 to represent uses Snapchat
  or not. Then spin each spinner once to simulate one repetition.'' Do
  you agree? Explain.
\item
  How could you perform one repetition of the simulation using just a
  single spinner? (Hint: it needs 4 sectors.)
\item
  How could you perform a simulation, using the spinner in the previous
  part, to estimate \(\textrm{P}(C | A)\)?
\item
  What determines the order of magnitude of the the margin of error for
  your estimate in the previous part?
\item
  What is another method for performing the simulation and estimating
  \(\textrm{P}(C |A)\) that has a smaller margin of error? What is the
  disadvantage of this method?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Donny's simulation assumes that age and Snapchat use are independent,
  but we know that younger people will be more likely to use Snapchat
  than older people. In general, you can not simulate pairs of events
  simply from the marginal probabilities of each.
\item
  You can construct a spinner for the possible occurrences of the
  \emph{pairs} of events---both occur, \(A\) occurs and \(C\) does not,
  \(C\) occurs and \(A\) does not, neither occurs---and their
  \emph{joint} probabilities. From the three given probabilities we can
  determine (see the interior cells in the two-way table in the solution
  to Example~\ref{exm-conditional-probability-def}):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    age 18-29 and uses Snapchat: \(\textrm{P}(A\cap C)= 0.13\)
  \item
    age 18-29 and does not use Snapchat: \(\textrm{P}(A\cap C^c)= 0.07\)
  \item
    not age 18-29, and uses Snapchat: \(\textrm{P}(A^c\cap C)= 0.11\)
  \item
    not age 18-29, and does not use Snapchat:
    \(\textrm{P}(A^c\cap C^c)= 0.69\) See the spinner in
    Figure~\ref{fig-impeach-sim-spinner}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The following method fixes the number of total spins, say 10000.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Spin the joint spinner from the previous part once to simulate a
    (age, Snapchat) pair.
  \item
    Repeat a fixed number of times, say 10000.
  \item
    Discard the repetitions on which the person was not age 18-29, that
    is, the repetitions on which \(A\) did not occur. You would expect
    to have around 2000 repetitions left.
  \item
    Among the remaining repetitions (on which \(A\) occurred), count the
    number of repetitions on which \(C\) also occurred. So for the
    roughly 2000 repetitions for which the person is age 18-29, count
    the repetitions on which the person also uses Snapchat; you would
    expect a count of around 1300.
  \item
    Estimate \(\textrm{P}(C|A)\) by dividing the two previous counts to
    obtain a conditional relative frequency. \[
    \textrm{P}(C | A)\approx \frac{\text{Number of repetitions on which both $A$ and $C$ occurred}}{\text{Number of repetitions on which $C$ occurred}}
    \]
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Only those repetitions in which \(A\) occurred are used to estimate
  \(\textrm{P}(C|A)\). So the order of magnitude of the margin of error
  is determined by the number of repetitions on which \(A\) occurs. This
  would be around 2000 repetitions for a margin of error of roughly
  \(1/\sqrt{2000} = 0.022\), rather than 0.01 based on the original
  10000 repetitions.
\item
  The previous method simulated a fixed number of repetitions first, and
  then discarded the ones that did not meet the condition \(A\). We
  could instead discard repetitions that do not meet the condition as we
  go, and keep performing repetitions until we get a fixed number, say
  10000, that do satisfy the condition \(A\). In this way, the estimate
  \(\textrm{P}(C |A)\) will be based on the fixed number of repetitions,
  say 10000, that satisfy event \(A\). The disadvantage is increased
  computational burden; we will need to simulate and discard many
  repetitions in order to achieve the desired number that satisfy the
  condition. Roughly, we would need to simulate about 50000 repetitions
  in total to obtain 10000 repetitions that satisfy event \(A\). The
  advantage is a more precise estimate of \(\textrm{P}(C|A)\) than in
  the previous part.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-impeach-sim}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-impeach-sim-spinner-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-impeach-sim-spinner}Spinner corresponding to
Example~\ref{exm-impeach-sim}.}

\end{figure}%

The conditional probability of event \(A\) given event \(B\) can be
approximated by simulating---according to the assumptions encoded in the
probability measure \(\textrm{P}\)---the random phenomenon a large
number of times and computing the relative frequency of \(A\)
\emph{among repetitions on which \(B\) occurs}.

\[
{\small
\textrm{P}(A|B) \approx \frac{\text{number of repetitions on which $A$ and $B$ occur}}{\text{number of repetitions on which $B$ occurs}}, \quad \text{for a large number of repetitions simulated according to $\textrm{P}$}
}
\] When using simulation to approximate \(\textrm{P}(A|B)\), we first
use \(B\) to determine which repetitions to \emph{keep}, then we find
the relative frequency of \(A\).

Remember that the margin of error when approximating a probability based
on a simulated relative frequency depends on the number of independently
simulated repetitions used to calculate the relative frequency. When
approximating \(\textrm{P}(A|B)\) as above, the margin of error is
determined by the number of independently simulated repetitions \emph{on
which \(B\) occurs}.

There are two basic ways to use simulation\footnote{All of our
  simulations are based on \emph{independently} simulated repetitions.
  More sophisticated methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
  methods, allow dependent repetitions and can approximate conditional
  probabilities much more efficiently.} to approximate a conditional
probability \(\textrm{P}(A|B)\).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulate the random phenomenon for a set number of repetitions (say
  10000), \emph{discard those repetitions on which \(B\) does not
  occur}, and compute the relative frequency of \(A\) among the
  remaining repetitions (on which \(B\) does occur).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Disadvantage: the margin of error is based on only the number of
    repetitions used to compute the relative frequency. So if you
    perform 10000 repetitions but \(B\) occurs only on 1000, then the
    margin of error for estimating \(\textrm{P}(A|B)\) is roughly on the
    order of \(1/\sqrt{1000} = 0.032\) (rather than
    \(1/\sqrt{10000} = 0.01\)). Especially if \(\textrm{P}(B)\) is
    small, the margin of error could be large resulting in an imprecise
    estimate of \(\textrm{P}(A|B)\).
  \item
    Advantage: not computationally intensive.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Simulate the random phenomenon \emph{until obtaining a certain number
  of repetitions (say 10000) on which \(B\) occurs}, discarding those
  repetitions on which \(B\) does not occur as you go, and compute the
  relative frequency of \(A\) among the remaining repetitions (on which
  \(B\) does occur).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Advantage: the margin of error will be based on the set number of
    repetitions on which \(B\) occurs.
  \item
    Disadvantage: requires more time/computer power. Especially if
    \(\textrm{P}(B)\) is small, it will require a large number of
    repetitions of the simulation to achieve the desired number of
    repetitions on which \(B\) occurs. For example, if
    \(\textrm{P}(B)=0.1\), then it will require roughly 100,000
    repetitions in total to obtain 10,000 on which \(B\) occurs.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Conditioning in Symbulate}\label{conditioning-in-symbulate}

In Symulate, \texttt{filter} can be used to extract repetitions that
satisfy a condition. First we'll simulate age and Snapchat use for 10000
hypothetical adults. Each ticket in the \texttt{BoxModel} has a (age,
Snapchat) pair of labels, like the spinner in
Figure~\ref{fig-impeach-sim-spinner}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Snapchat user\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Not Snapchat user\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Not Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Snapchat user\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Not Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Not Snapchat user\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)],}
\NormalTok{             probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.13}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.07}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.11}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.69}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{sim\_all }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sim\_all}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
1     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
2     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
3     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
4     ('Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
5     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
6     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
7     ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
8     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
....  ......................................
9999  ('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sim\_all.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Outcome                                Frequency
('Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')     691
('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')         1332
('Not Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user') 6889
('Not Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')     1088
                                 Total 10000
\end{verbatim}

Now we'll apply \texttt{filter} to retain only those age 18-29. The
function \texttt{is\_Age18} takes as an input\footnote{\texttt{Age\_Snapchat}
  is a pair so \texttt{Age\_Snapchat{[}0{]}} is the first component
  (Age) and \texttt{Age\_Snapchat{[}1{]}} is the second component
  (Snapchat user).} a (age, Snapchat) pair and returns \texttt{True} if
age 18-29 (and \texttt{False} otherwise). Applying
\texttt{filter(is\_Age18)} will only return results for which
\texttt{is\_Age18} returns \texttt{True}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ is\_Age18(Age\_Snapchat):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Age\_Snapchat[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}
  
\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sim\_all.}\BuiltInTok{filter}\NormalTok{(is\_Age18)}

\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     ('Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user')
1     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
2     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
3     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
4     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
5     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
6     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
7     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
8     ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
....  ..............................
2022  ('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Outcome                            Frequency
('Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user') 691
('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')     1332
                             Total 2023
\end{verbatim}

Conditional relative frequencies are computed based only on repetitions
which satisfy the event being conditioned on.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Outcome                            Relative Frequency
('Age 18-29', 'Not Snapchat user') 0.34157192288680177
('Age 18-29', 'Snapchat user')     0.6584280771131982
                             Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

Based on these results, we would estimate \(\textrm{P}(C |A)\) to be
around the true value of 0.65 with a margin of error of roughly
\(1/\sqrt{2000} = 0.022\).

In Symbulate, the ``given'' symbol \texttt{\textbar{}} applies the
second method to simulate a fixed number of repetitions that satisfy the
event being conditioned on. Be careful when using \texttt{\textbar{}}
when conditioning on an event with small probability. In particular, be
careful when conditioning on the value of a continuous random variable
(which we'll discuss in more detail soon).

Below we use \texttt{RV} syntax to carry out the simulation and
conditioning\footnote{In Symbulate, events being conditioned on need to
  be based on \texttt{RV}s. But the code shows that Symbulate has a
  pretty broad interpretation of what can be an \texttt{RV}.}.
Technically, a random variable always returns a number, but \texttt{RV}
in Symbulate does allow for non-numerical outputs. In most situations,
we will usually deal with true random variables, and the code syntax
below will be more natural.

The following code simulates (Age, Snapchat) pairs until 10000 adults
age 18-29 are obtained.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Age, Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ( (Age }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Snapchat) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Age }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Age 18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
1     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
2     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
3     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
4     (Age 18-29, Not Snapchat user)
5     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
6     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
7     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
8     (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
....  ..........................
9999  (Age 18-29, Snapchat user)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18.tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value                          Frequency
(Age 18-29, Not Snapchat user) 3548
(Age 18-29, Snapchat user)     6452
                         Total 10000
\end{verbatim}

Since all 10000 simulated pairs satisfy the event being conditioned on
(age 18-29), they are all included in the computation of the conditional
relative frequencies.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Age18.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value                          Relative Frequency
(Age 18-29, Not Snapchat user) 0.3548
(Age 18-29, Snapchat user)     0.6452
                         Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

Based on these results, we would estimate \(\textrm{P}(C |A)\) to be
around the true value of 0.65 with a margin of error of roughly
\(1/\sqrt{10000} = 0.01\). We have obtained a more precise estimate, but
the simulation takes longer to run.

\subsection{Using conditional probabilities to
simulate}\label{using-conditional-probabilities-to-simulate}

In Example~\ref{exm-impeach-sim} we directly simulated pairs of events
using joint probabilities, and used the results to approximate
conditional probabilities. But in many problems conditional
probabilities are provided or can be determined directly.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-impeach2-sim}{}\label{exm-impeach2-sim}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-conditional-probability-def2}. Suppose that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  65\% of American adults age 18-29 use Snapchat
\item
  24\% of American adults age 30-49 use Snapchat
\item
  12\% of American adults age 50-64 use Snapchat
\item
  2\% of American adults age 65+ use Snapchat
\end{itemize}

Also suppose that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  20\% of American adults are age 18-29
\item
  33\% of American adults are age 30-49
\item
  25\% of American adults are age 50-64
\item
  22\% of American adults are age 65+
\end{itemize}

Consider simulating a randomly selected U.S. adult and determining the
person's age group and whether or not they use Snapchat. How could you
perform one repetition of the simulation using spinners based solely on
the percentages provided above, without first constructing a two-way
table or finding \(\textrm{P}(A_1\cap C)\), etc? (Hint: you'll need a
few spinners, but you might not spin them all in a single repetition.)

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
It's a two-stage simulation: first spin a spinner to determine age
group, then given the result spin an appropriate spinner to determine
Snapchat use. There will be 4 spinners for Snapchat use, but only 1 will
be spun---along with the age spinner---in any single repetition. See
Figure~\ref{fig-impeach-sim-spinner2}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  ``Age'' spinner: Areas of 0.20, 0.33, 0.25, 0.22 corresponding to,
  respectively, 18-29, 30-49, 50-64. 65+. Spin this to determine age
  group.
\item
  ``Snapchat'' spinners---only one of the following will be spun in a
  single repetition:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Snapchat given age 18-29: areas of 0.65 and 0.35 corresponding to,
    respectively, uses Snapchat and does not use Snapchat. If the result
    of the ``age'' spinner is 18-29, spin this spinner to determine
    whether or not the person uses Snapchat.
  \item
    Snapchat given age 30-49: areas of 0.24 and 0.76 corresponding to,
    respectively, uses Snapchat and does not use Snapchat. If the result
    of the ``age'' spinner is 30-49, spin this spinner to determine
    whether or not the person uses Snapchat.
  \item
    Snapchat given age 50-64: areas of 0.12 and 0.88 corresponding to,
    respectively, uses Snapchat and does not use Snapchat. If the result
    of the ``age'' spinner is 50-64, spin this spinner to determine
    whether or not the person uses Snapchat.
  \item
    Snapchat given age 65+: areas of 0.02 and 0.98 corresponding to,
    respectively, uses Snapchat and does not use Snapchat. If the result
    of the ``age'' spinner is 65+, spin this spinner to determine
    whether or not the person uses Snapchat.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\label{sol-impeach2-sim}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-impeach-sim-spinner2-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-impeach-sim-spinner2}Spinners corresponding to
Example~\ref{exm-impeach2-sim}. The spinner in the top row is spun first
to simulate age group, then the corresponding spinner in the bottom row
is spun to determine Snapchat use.}

\end{figure}%

A two-stage simulation like the one above basically implements the
multiplication rule, joint = conditional \(\times\) marginal. We first
simulate age based on marginal probabilities, then use conditional
probabilities to simulate Snapchat use, resulting in (age, Snapchat)
pairs with the appropriate joint relationship.

In Symbulate, we can code the scenario in Example~\ref{exm-impeach2-sim}
by defining a custom probability space. An outcome is a (Age, Snapchat)
pair. Each of the 5 spinners corresponds to a \texttt{BoxModel}. We
define a function that defines how to simulate one repetition in two
stages, using the \texttt{draw} method\footnote{\texttt{.draw()} is like
  \texttt{.sim(1)} but they have different properties. We will usually
  work with \texttt{.sim()} to actually run a simulation.
  \texttt{.draw()} is useful in situations like this where we have to
  build a custom probability space from scratch.}. Then we use that
function to define a custom \texttt{ProbabilitySpace}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ Age\_Snapchat\_sim():}
\NormalTok{    Age }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}30{-}49\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}50{-}64\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}65+\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.33}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.22}\NormalTok{]).draw()}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ Age }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}18{-}29\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Use\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NotUse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.65}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.35}\NormalTok{]).draw()}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ Age }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}30{-}49\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Use\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NotUse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.24}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.76}\NormalTok{]).draw()}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ Age }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}50{-}64\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Use\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NotUse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.12}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.88}\NormalTok{]).draw()}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ Age }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}65+\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Use\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}NotUse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.98}\NormalTok{]).draw()}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Age, Snapchat}
    
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ProbabilitySpace(Age\_Snapchat\_sim)}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     ('65+', 'NotUse')
1     ('50-64', 'NotUse')
2     ('30-49', 'NotUse')
3     ('30-49', 'NotUse')
4     ('65+', 'NotUse')
5     ('65+', 'NotUse')
6     ('18-29', 'Use')
7     ('50-64', 'NotUse')
8     ('50-64', 'NotUse')
9     ('50-64', 'NotUse')
\end{verbatim}

Once we have simulated pairs, we can proceed as in
Section~\ref{sec-simulation-conditioning-probabilities}. For example,
the following approximates conditional probabilities of age group given
that the adult uses Snapchat, based on 10000 repetitions which satisfy
the condition; compare to part 7 of
Example~\ref{exm-conditional-probability-def2}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Age, Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Snapchat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ( Age }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Snapchat }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Use\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sim\_given\_Snapchat.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
18-29 0.5268
30-49 0.3251
50-64 0.1258
65+   0.0223
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Conditioning on values of random
variables}\label{conditioning-on-values-of-random-variables}

If \(X\) is a discrete random variable, we can condition on it equalling
the value \(x\) by conditioning on the event \(\{X = x\}\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-dice-tactile-conditional-prob}{}\label{exm-dice-tactile-conditional-prob}

We'll continue with the dice rolling example: roll two fair four-sided
dice and let \(X\) be the sum and \(Y\) the larger of the rolls. For
each of the following, describe how to approximate the probability based
on 10000 repetitions of a tactile simulation (in principle).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 6 | Y = 4)\).
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(Y = 4 | X = 6)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
We have already seen how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulate an \((X, Y)\) pair. If \(Y=4\) keep the pair, otherwise
  discard it. Continue until 10000 \((X, Y)\) pairs with \(Y=4\) are
  obtained. Count the number of pairs for which \(X=6\) and divide by
  10000 to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X = 6 | Y = 4)\), with a margin of
  error of 0.01.
\item
  Simulate an \((X, Y)\) pair. If \(X=6\) keep the pair, otherwise
  discard it. Continue until 10000 \((X, Y)\) pairs with \(X=6\) are
  obtained. Count the number of pairs for which \(Y=4\) and divide by
  10000 to approximate \(\textrm{P}(Y = 4 | X = 6)\), with a margin of
  error of 0.01.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-dice-tactile-conditional-prob}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

To approximate a conditional probability of an event involving a random
variable \(X\) given the value of a random variable \(Y\), we first need
to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs. The variable being conditioned on (\(Y\)
here) determines which pairs to \emph{keep}, and the other variable
determines what to find the relative frequency of.

Here is some code for conditioning on \(\{Y = 4\}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ DiscreteUniform(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{( (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (7, 4)
1     (5, 4)
2     (6, 4)
3     (6, 4)
4     (5, 4)
5     (5, 4)
6     (7, 4)
7     (7, 4)
8     (7, 4)
9     (8, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Frequency
5     2838
6     2874
7     2879
8     1409
Total 10000
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
5     0.2939
6     0.2851

8     0.1383
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

Below we simulate values of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) for each of the values
\(y = 2, 3, 4\). (We omit conditioning on \(Y=1\) since then \(X = 2\)
with probability 1.) Each of the three simulations below approximates a
separate conditional distribution of \(X\) values.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq4 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq3 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We plot the three distributions on a single plot to compare how the
distribution of \(X\) changes depending on the given value of \(Y\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq4.plot()}
\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq3.plot(jitter }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\# shifts the spikes a little}
\NormalTok{x\_given\_Y\_eq2.plot(jitter }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\# so they don\textquotesingle{}t overlap}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-188-1.png}

Extra care is required when conditioning on the value of a continuous
random variable. We'll consider the Bivariate Normal model of the
meeting problem from Section~\ref{sec-meeting-sim}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-uniform-sum-max-conditional-sim-forever}{}\label{exm-uniform-sum-max-conditional-sim-forever}

Suppose we want to approximate the conditional probability that Cady
arrives first given that Regina arrives at 12:40.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Donny Don't writes the Symbulate code below to approximate this
  probability. What do you think will happen when Donny runs his code?
\item
  Can you think of how to fix Donny's code? (Hint: when we say ``Regina
  arrives at 12:40'', what do we really mean?)
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Donny\textquotesingle{}s code {-} don\textquotesingle{}t try to run this!}
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{y\_given\_Req40 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{y\_given\_Req40.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{10000}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Donny's code will run forever! Using \texttt{.sim(10000)} with
  conditioning via \texttt{\textbar{}} will continue the simulation
  until obtaining 10000 repetitions that satisfy the condition.
  Remember, \(R\) is a \emph{continuous} random variable, so
  \(\textrm{P}(R = 40)=\textrm{P}(R = 40.00000000000000000\ldots) = 0\).
  The simulation will never return a single \((R, Y)\) pair with \(Y\)
  equal to \(40.0000000000000\ldots\), let alone 10000 of them.
\item
  ``Regina arrives at 12:40'' doesn't really mean \(R\) ``is equal to
  40'' but rather \(R\) ``is close enough to 40'', where ``close
  enough'' depends on the context. Here, rounding to the nearest minute
  seems reasonable, in which case ``Regina arrives at 12:40'' really
  means ``Regina arrives within 0.5 minutes (30 seconds) of 12:40''. So
  we want to condition on the event
  \(\{40 - 0.5 < R < 40 + 0.5\}=\{|R - 40|<0.5\}\) rather than
  \(\{R = 40\}\). See the code below, where we condition on the event
  \texttt{(abs(R\ -\ 40)\ \textless{}\ 0.5)}. Aside from the
  conditioning event, Donny's code is fine, but note that we have
  changed the number of repetitions from 10000 to 1000; see the
  discussion below.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-uniform-sum-max-conditional-sim-forever}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{y\_given\_Req40 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{y\_given\_Req40.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{1000}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.654
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Warning}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

Be careful when conditioning on the value of a continuous random
variable. Remember that the probability that a continuous random
variable is equal to a particular value is 0. Mathematically, when we
condition on \(\{X=x\}\) we are really conditioning on
\(\{|X-x|<\epsilon\}\)---the event that the random variable \(X\) is
within \(\epsilon\) of the value \(x\)---and seeing what happens in the
idealized limit when \(\epsilon\) approaches 0. Practically,
\(\epsilon\) represents the degree of precision which determines ``close
enough'' in the problem context, e.g., \(\epsilon=0.01\) if ``within
0.01'' is close enough. When conditioning on a continuous random
variable \(X\) in a simulation, \emph{never} condition on \(\{X=x\}\);
rather, condition on \(\{|X-x|<\epsilon\}\) where \(\epsilon\)
represents a suitable degree of precision. What counts as ``suitable''
depends on the context and the scale of the \(X\) variable. For example,
if our variable is household income (U.S. dollars) and we're
conditioning on household income ``equal to'' 100,000 dollars, then
\(\epsilon\) of 1000 dollars might be reasonable.

\end{tcolorbox}

The event \(\{|X-x|<\epsilon\}\) will have non-zero probability, but the
probability might be small. Conditioning on low probability events
introduces some computational challenges. Remember that the margin of
error in using a relative frequency to approximate a probability is
based on the number of independently simulated repetitions used to
compute the relative frequency. When approximating a conditional
probability with a conditional relative frequency, the margin of error
is based only on the number of repetitions that satisfy the condition.
Naively discarding repetitions that do not satisfy the condition can be
horribly inefficient. For example, when conditioning on an event with
probability 0.01 we would need to run about 1,000,000 repetitions to
achieve 10,000 that satisfy the condition. There are more sophisticated
and efficient methods (e.g., ``Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)''
methods), but they are beyond the scope of this book. When conditioning
on the value of a continuous random variable with \texttt{\textbar{}} in
Symbulate, be aware that you might need to change either the number of
repetitions (but try not to go below 1000) or the degree of precision
\(\epsilon\) in order for the simulation to run in a reasonable amount
of time.

In the Bivariate Normal model of the meeting problem the event
\(\{|R - 40| < 0.5\}\) has probability 0.04. Running
\texttt{(Y\ \textbar{}\ (abs(R\ -\ 40)\ \textless{}\ 0.5)\ ).sim(1000)}
requires about 25000 repetitions in the background to achieve the 1000
the satisfy the condition. The margin of error for approximating
conditional probabilities is roughly \(1/\sqrt{1000} = 0.03\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BivariateNormal(mean1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, mean2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, sd2 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, corr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{( (R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (40.014148755019214, 30.911754280203805)
1     (40.019677586556014, 36.683379827298225)
2     (40.03600296500495, 28.33448993127884)
3     (40.3807516490601, 37.411398668645916)
4     (39.743846640397365, 49.47081907650252)
5     (40.05437065571705, 40.94088906907784)
6     (39.74059385376069, 52.941340418777855)
7     (40.315055661459176, 43.70771091779416)
8     (40.020907952051985, 34.70964243241205)
9     (40.10955885833382, 49.978921173433775)
\end{verbatim}
