\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-25}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-condition-collector}{}\label{exr-simulation-condition-collector}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Let \(X\) be the number of
distinct prizes obtained in these 3 packages. Let \(Y\) be the number of
these 3 packages that contain prize 1.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain how you could, in principle, conduct a simulation by hand and
  use the results to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(Y = 0 | X = 1)\)
  \item
    The conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=1\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 1 | Y = 0)\)
  \item
    The conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=0\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate the
  values in part 1. Each simulation should be based on 10000 repetitions
  that satisfy the conditioning event.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-condition-dartboard}{}\label{exr-simulation-condition-dartboard}

Write Symbulate code to conduct the simulation in
Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-dartboard}. Use conditioning to discard any
repetitions where the dart lands off the board. Use the simulation
results to approximate:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The marginal distribution of \(R\) (via plot)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(R < 1)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(R > 11)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(R)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{SD}(R)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-condition-continuous-dice}{}\label{exr-simulation-condition-continuous-dice}

Consider a continuous version of the dice rolling problem where instead
of rolling two fair four-sided dice (which return values 1, 2, 3, 4) we
spin twice a Uniform(1, 4) spinner (which returns any value in the
continuous range between 1 and 4). Let \(X\) be the sum of the two spins
and let \(Y\) be the larger of the two spins.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate

  \begin{enumerate}
  \def\labelenumii{\alph{enumii}.}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(Y < 2.7 | X = 3.5)\)
  \item
    The conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X = 3.5\)
  \end{enumerate}
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation to approximate the
  quantities from the previous part.
\end{enumerate}

Hint: be careful! What do we really mean by conditioning on \(X = 3.5\)?

\end{exercise}

\section{Independence}\label{sec-simulation-independence}

For independent events, the multiplication rule simplifies

\begin{align*}
\text{If $A$ and $B$ are independent then } && \textrm{P}(A \cap B) & = \textrm{P}(A)\textrm{P}(B)\\
\text{If independent then } && \text{Joint} & = \text{Product of Marginals}
\end{align*}

Similarly, the joint distribution of independent random variables is
this product of their marginal distributions. For this reason,
independence is represented by the product \texttt{*} syntax in
Symbulate.

For example, in the meeting problem, if Regina's arrival follows a
Uniform(0, 60) model, Cady's follows a Normal(30, 10) model, and they
arrive independently of each other, we can simulate pairs of arrivals as
follows; note the use of \texttt{*}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (16.044206462316154, 21.35589145095466)
1     (39.71431230106108, 29.1054439994742)
2     (19.93791822774121, 29.6577833519138)
3     (40.02486343885879, 18.58209626592855)
4     (12.359785751787932, 17.065231610343293)
\end{verbatim}

We can think of \texttt{*} as ``spin each spinner independently'', but
what \texttt{*} really does is create a joint probability space as the
product of two marginal probability spaces.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Warning}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

Be careful: \texttt{*} plays different roles for probability spaces and
named distributions (like \texttt{Uniform}, \texttt{Normal}) than it
does for random variables. Using \texttt{*} with probability spaces
indicates that the spaces are \emph{independent}. Likewise, using
\texttt{*} with \emph{distributions} of random variables, as in
\texttt{X,\ Y\ =\ RV(Distribution\_X\ *\ Distribution\_Y)}, indicates
that the random variables are \emph{independent} since their joint
distribution is the product of their marginal distributions. In
contrast, using \texttt{*} directly on random variables, as in
\texttt{X\ *\ Y}, literally means multiplication.
(Section~\ref{sec-rv-versus-distribution} has further discussion on the
difference between a random variable and its distribution.)

\end{tcolorbox}

Note the two uses of \texttt{*} in the code below. In the
\texttt{P\ =\ ...} line, \texttt{*} means that the two components of the
pair will be simulated independently (e.g., ``spin the Uniform(0, 60)
spinner then spin the Normal(30, 10) spinner''), resulting in random
variables \texttt{R} (first component) and \texttt{Y} (second component)
that are independent. In \texttt{(R\ *\ Y)}, \texttt{*} means multiply
the values of \texttt{R} and \texttt{Y}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Y) ).sim(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (26.635102169281673, 49.7396499240221, 1324.8206575906322)
1     (41.63652655516453, 31.43658402851235, 1308.9101657068156)
2     (24.007663694843504, 20.486788744774476, 491.8399343718507)
3     (31.341470144591522, 53.918662978739604, 1689.8901659844596)
4     (23.354497321679005, 17.805389909018437, 415.8359309416215)
\end{verbatim}

We could have also coded the following, which we interpret as defining
random variables \texttt{R} and \texttt{Y} whose joint distribution is
the product of their marginal distributions, \texttt{Uniform(0,\ 60)}
for \texttt{R} and \texttt{Normal(30,\ 10)} for \texttt{Y}, and thus
\texttt{R} and \texttt{Y} are independent.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Normal(}\DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{(R }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Y) ).sim(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (10.877226301316208, 17.465875734645003, 189.98028291640117)
1     (30.285010599125446, 46.553353421147115, 1409.8688017842733)
2     (46.17072173103157, 29.91520237245272, 1381.20648426601)
3     (4.324694352929031, 18.3379063790875, 79.30584016218096)
4     (23.634941124942085, 20.97000649190747, 495.6248688258863)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent}{}\label{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent}

Donny Don't writes the following code to simulate \(X\) and \(Y\) from
Example~\ref{exm-dice-joint-independent-conditional}, but it returns an
error. Can you explain why? Think about it first, but if you need a
hint, run the code to see the error. How could you fix the code so it
runs properly.

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]))}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]))}

\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
Donny's code defines the correct marginal distributions for \(X\) and
\(Y\), but to simulate \(X, Y\) pairs we need to know their joint
distribution. Recall the moral of
Example~\ref{exm-dice-joint-independent-conditional} and the discussion
following it: marginal distributions alone are not enough to determine
the joint distribution.

The error message is ``Events must be defined on same probability
space'', which in this case really should be ``random variables must be
defined on same probability space'', but even that is maybe not the most
informative message. The idea is that we have not provided enough
information to determine how to pair \(X\) and \(Y\) values when running
the simulation. If the random variables were defined on the same
probability space, the probaility space outcome would be simulated first
and then both \(X\) and \(Y\) would be computed for the same outcome, so
there would be no problem when simulating pairs. One way to define the
random variables on the same probability space is to specify their joint
distribution and then simulate pairs directly from the joint
distribution.

Recall from Example~\ref{exm-dice-joint-independent-conditional} that
\(X\) and \(Y\) here are independent, so their joint distribution is the
product of their marginal distribution. The code below achieves Donny's
goal, using the \texttt{*} syntax.

\label{sol-donny-sim-assume-independent}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]) }\OperatorTok{*} 
\NormalTok{          BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]))}

\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (2, 4)
1     (5, 4)
2     (8, 4)
3     (3, 4)
4     (5, 4)
5     (6, 3)
6     (5, 3)
7     (4, 2)
8     (7, 4)
9     (6, 3)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent2}{}\label{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent2}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent2}, Donny says:
``That error is annoying. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are \emph{independent} then
their marginal distributions determine their joint distribution, so my
code should be fine.'' How would you respond? (You might agree with
Donny here. If so, imagine you have been assigned to argue against
Donny.)

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
Donny is correct that if random variables are independent their marginal
distributions determine their joint distribution. The issue is that
independence is an \emph{assumption}---see
Section~\ref{sec-independence-is-an-assumption} ---and Symbulate
requires you to be explicit about all your assumptions. There are 3 main
assumptions in this example:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) is assumed to have a particular marginal distribution
\item
  \(Y\) is assumed to have a particular marginal distribution
\item
  \(X\) and \(Y\) are assumed to be independent
\end{itemize}

Donny's code has defined the first two assumptions, but not the third.

Suppose Donny had tried to run \texttt{(X\ \&\ Y).sim(10)} without first
defining \texttt{X}, hence not specifying the first assumption above.
That would also result in an error, because there would not be enough
information to run the simulation. If you don't specify the distribution
of a random variable---either directly or by defining it as a function
on a probability space---Symbulate will not assume a distribution by
default.

Likewise, Symbulate won't assume random variables are independent unless
you tell it to. You, like Donny, might want Symbulate to assume
independence by default, but that's just not the way it works. And it's
probably much safer that way because there are many real situations
where independence is not a reasonable assumption, and assuming
independence by default might lead to wildly inaccurate results.

\label{sol-donny-sim-assume-independent2}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Symbulate does offer a compromise, via the \texttt{AssumeIndependent}
command, which allows code like Donny's in
Example~\ref{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent} while also requiring
explicit specification of independence The following code would achieve
Donny's goal in Example~\ref{exm-donny-sim-assume-independent}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]))}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\OperatorTok{/}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{]))}

\NormalTok{X, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ AssumeIndependent(X, Y)}

\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (5, 3)
1     (6, 3)
2     (5, 2)
3     (5, 2)
4     (8, 3)
5     (7, 4)
6     (4, 4)
7     (3, 4)
8     (4, 4)
9     (5, 3)
\end{verbatim}

While \texttt{AssumeIndependent} works, we discourage its use for two
reasons. First, the code is clunky; in a sense the definition of
\texttt{X} and \texttt{Y} with \texttt{X\ =\ RV(...)} and
\texttt{Y\ =\ RV(...)} is incomplete until they are redefined with
\texttt{X,\ Y\ =\ AssumeIndependent(X,\ Y)}. More importantly, when
dealing with multiple random variables it is their joint distribution
that describes fully their probabilitistic behavior. Therefore we
encourage you to get in the habit of defining joint distributions
(possibly using the ``marginal then conditional'' construction). In many
situations random variables are not independent, so marginal
distributions alone are not enough. In the special case of independence,
define the joint distribution directly as the product of marginal
distributions using \texttt{*} rather than using
\texttt{AssumeIndependent}.

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-26}

\section{Working with Symbulate}\label{working-with-symbulate}

In this section we explore a little deeper some aspects of coding
simulations with Symbulate.

\subsection{Two ``worlds'' in Symbulate}\label{sec-symbulate-two-worlds}

Recall the dice rolling simulation in
Section~\ref{sec-technology-intro}. Suppose we want to simulate
realizations of the event \(A= \{Y < 3\}\). We saw previously that we
can define the event \texttt{(Y\ \textless{}\ 3)} in Symbulate and
simulate True/False realizations of it.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(DiscreteUniform(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Y }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{A.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     False
1     False
2     False
3     False
4     True
5     False
6     False
7     False
8     False
9     False
\end{verbatim}

Since event \(A\) is defined in terms of \(Y\), we can also first
simulate values of \texttt{Y}, store the results as \texttt{y}, and then
determine whether event \(A\) occurs for the simulated \texttt{y} values
using\footnote{Python automatically treats \texttt{True} as 1 and
  \texttt{False} as 0, so the code \texttt{(y\ \textless{}\ 3)}
  effectively returns both True/False realizations of the event itself
  and 1/0 realizations of the corresponding indicator random variable.}
\texttt{(y\ \textless{}\ 3)}. (The results won't match the above because
we are making a new call to \texttt{sim}.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     3
1     3
2     3
3     3
4     4
5     2
6     4
7     3
8     2
9     1
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(y }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     False
1     False
2     False
3     False
4     False
5     True
6     False
7     False
8     True
9     True
\end{verbatim}

These two methods illustrate the two ``worlds'' of Symbulate, which we
call ``random variable world'' and ``simulation world''. Operations like
transformations can be performed in either world. Think of random
variable world as the ``before'' world and simulation world as the
``after'' world, by which we mean before/after the \texttt{sim} step.

Most of the transformations we have seen so far happened in random
variable world. For example, we have seen how to define the sum of two
dice in \emph{random variable world} in a few ways, e.g., via

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{U }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U.}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The sum transformation is applied to define a new random variable
\texttt{X}, before the \texttt{sim} step. We could then call, e.g.,
\texttt{(U\ \&\ X).sim(10)}.

We could also compute simulated values of the sum in \emph{simulation
world} as follows.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{U }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{u }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{u}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (4, 1)
1     (2, 4)
2     (3, 2)
3     (4, 2)
4     (2, 2)
5     (1, 2)
6     (3, 3)
7     (1, 4)
8     (3, 4)
9     (1, 1)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u.}\BuiltInTok{apply}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     5
1     6
2     5
3     6
4     4
5     3
6     6
7     5
8     7
9     2
\end{verbatim}

The above code will simulate all the pairs of rolls first, store them as
\texttt{u} (which we can think of as a table), and then apply the sum to
the simulated values (which adds a column to the table). That is, the
sum transformation happens after the \texttt{sim} step.

While either world is ``correct'', we generally take the random variable
world approach. We do this mostly for consistency, but also to emphasize
some of the probability concepts we'll encounter. For example, the fact
that a sum of random variables (defined on the same probability space)
is also a random variable is a little more apparent in random variable
world. However, it is sometimes more convenient to code in simulation
world; for example, if complicated transformations are required.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-donny-rv-same-probspace}{}\label{exm-donny-rv-same-probspace}

Donny Don't writes the following code to simulate \(X\) and \(Y\) in the
dice problem, but it returns an error. Can you explain why? Think about
it first, but if you need a hint, run the code to see the error.

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
The problem is that there is one box model used to determine values of
\texttt{X} and a separate box model for \texttt{Y}; we can't simulate
\texttt{(X,\ Y)} \emph{pairs} of values if we're using different boxes.
The code above is basically saying to roll one fair four-sided die twice
and compute the sum, then roll another four-sided die twice and compute
the max, but we can only compute \(X\) \emph{and} \(Y\)
(\texttt{X\ \&\ Y}) for the same pair of rolls.

The error message is ``Events must be defined on same probability
space'', which in this case really should be ``random variables must be
defined on same probability space'', but the actual message at least
reflects the spirit of the error.

\label{sol-donny-rv-same-probspace}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-donny-sim-same-probspace}{}\label{exm-donny-sim-same-probspace}

Donny Don't tries again to simulate just \(X\) in the dice problem, this
time in simulation world, but Donny's code below still returns an error.
Can you explain why? Think about it first, but if you need a hint, run
the code to see the error.

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{U1, U2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{u1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U1.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{u2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U2.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ u1 }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ u2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
The error is basically the same as in
Example~\ref{exm-donny-rv-same-probspace}. Running \texttt{U1.sim(10)}
simulates one set of pairs of rolls to compute \texttt{u1}, but running
\texttt{u2\ =\ U2.sim(10)} simulates a separate set of pairs of rolls to
compute \texttt{u2}. The error occurs when running \texttt{u1+u2}
because it only makes sense to add the first roll and second roll for
the same pairs of rolls.

The error message is ``Results objects must come from the same
simulation'', which is maybe not the most informative message, but at
least reflects the spirit of the error.

\label{sol-donny-sim-same-probspace}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-donny-sim-world-assume-independent}{}\label{exm-donny-sim-world-assume-independent}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-donny-sim-same-probspace}, Donny says:
``That error is annoying. If \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) are independent then I
should be able to simulate then independently and then add them, so my
code should be fine.'' How would you respond? (You might agree with
Donny here. If so, imagine you have been assigned to argue against
Donny.)

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
This is essentially the same issue we discussed in
Solution~\ref{sol-donny-sim-assume-independent2}. Symbulate requires you
to be explicit about all your assumptions. Symbulate won't let you
operate on multiple random variables unless you have been explicit about
how they're related. In particular, Symbulate won't assume random
variables are independent unless you explicitly tell it to when you
define the \texttt{RV}s (e.g., by specifying their joint distribution as
the product of their marginal distributions using \texttt{*}). You, like
Donny, might want the ability to simulate individual independent random
variables separately and then combine the results of the simulations,
but that's just not the way Symbulate works. And it's probably much
safer that way because there are many real situations where independence
is not a reasonable assumption, and combining the results from
independent simulations might lead to wildly inaccurate results.

\label{sol-donny-sim-world-assume-independent}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

When working in random variable world, it only makes sense to transform
or simulate random variables defined on the same probability space.
Likewise, in simulation world, it only makes sense to apply
transformations to values generated in the same simulation, with all
assumptions---including indepedence, if appropriate---clearly defined,
via a single \texttt{sim} step.

The ``simulation'' step should be implemented in a single call to
\texttt{sim}, and in that single step you should simulate realizations
of all random variables of interest (e.g., with \texttt{\&}). Afterwards
you can select certain columns of the simulation results using brackets,
and manage these columns in simulation world. For example, if we wanted
to sum the rolls in simulation world, we could use the following
code\footnote{We wrote this code to compare to the previous block that
  returned an error. Even though the revised code works, it's clunky
  because we unpack the rolls and then rejoin them in random variable
  world and then unpack them again in simulation world. We could
  simplify a little by not unpacking and rejoining in random variable
  variable world, using \texttt{U\ =\ RV(P)};
  \texttt{u1\_and\_u2\ =\ U.sim(10)}. This still isn't the preferred way
  to sum the rolls, but we're just illustrating a few ways to work in
  both random variable world and simulation world.} which has a single
call to \texttt{sim} and runs without error.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{U1, U2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P)}

\NormalTok{u1\_and\_u2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (U1 }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ U2).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{u1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ u1\_and\_u2[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{u2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ u1\_and\_u2[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ u1 }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ u2}
\NormalTok{x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     4
1     8
2     8
3     7
4     6
5     3
6     8
7     4
8     2
9     5
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Brief summary of Symbulate
commands}\label{brief-summary-of-symbulate-commands}

We will see a variety of scenarious throughout the book, but many
simulations using Symbulate can be carried out with relatively few
commands. The following table comprises the requisite Symbulate commands
for a wide variety of situations.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Command & Function \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\texttt{BoxModel} & Define a box model \\
\texttt{ProbabilitySpace} & Define a custom probability space \\
\texttt{RV} & Define random variables, vectors, or processes \\
\texttt{RandomProcess} & Define a discrete or continuous time stochastic
process \\
\texttt{apply} & Apply transformations \\
\texttt{{[}{]}} (brackets) & Access a component of a random vector, or a
random process at a particular time \\
\texttt{*} (and \texttt{**}) & Define independent probability spaces or
distributions \\
\texttt{AssumeIndependent} & Assume random variables or processes are
independent \\
\texttt{\textbar{}} (vertical bar) & Condition on events \\
\texttt{\&} & Join multiple random variables into a random vector \\
\texttt{sim} & Simulate outcomes, events, and random variables, vectors,
and processes \\
\texttt{tabulate} & Tabulate simulated values \\
\texttt{plot} & Plot simulated values \\
\texttt{filter} (and relatives) & Create subsets of simulated values
(\texttt{filter\_eq}, \texttt{filter\_lt}, etc) \\
\texttt{count} (and relatives) & Count simulated values which satisfy
some critera (\texttt{count\_eq}, \texttt{count\_lt}, etc) \\
Statistical summaries & \texttt{mean}, \texttt{median}, \texttt{sd},
\texttt{var}, \texttt{quantile}, \texttt{corr}, \texttt{cov}, etc. \\
Common models & \texttt{Normal}, \texttt{BivariateNormal}, and many
others we will see \\
\end{longtable}

In addition to Symbulate commands, we can use basic Python commands to

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  define functions to define random variables
\item
  define for loops to investigate changing parameters
\item
  customize plots produced by the Symbulate \texttt{plot} command (add
  axis labels, legends, titles, etc)
\item
  summarize results of multiple simulations in tables and Matplotlib
  plots (e.g., for different values of problem parameters)
\end{itemize}

The next section and Section~\ref{sec-sim-matching-n} will provide some
examples of how we can use Symbulate together with Python (or R) code.

\subsection{Working with Symbulate output in Python and
R}\label{working-with-symbulate-output-in-python-and-r}

Symbulate has many built in commands that facilitate the summarization
of simulation output in basic plots, tables, and statistics. However, it
is also possible to convert Symbulate output into a \emph{data frame}
which can be manipulated using (non-Symbulate) Python or R code. This
section provides a brief introduction.

Let's start with some Symbulate code and output (from the dice rolling
simulation in Section~\ref{sec-technology-intro}).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{xy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{xy}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (4, 3)
1     (7, 4)
2     (4, 3)
3     (4, 3)
4     (7, 4)
5     (5, 3)
6     (7, 4)
7     (2, 1)
8     (8, 4)
....  ......
9999  (6, 4)
\end{verbatim}

\href{https://pandas.pydata.org/}{\texttt{pandas}}---commonly nicknamed
as \texttt{pd}---is a popular Python package for data science. We can
convert the output of a Symbulate \texttt{sim} to a pandas
\texttt{DataFrame}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(xy)}

\NormalTok{xy\_df}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
      0  1
0     4  3
1     7  4
2     4  3
3     4  3
4     7  4
...  .. ..
9995  4  2
9996  6  4
9997  5  3
9998  6  3
9999  6  4

[10000 rows x 2 columns]
\end{verbatim}

By default the column names are just their index (0, 1, 2,\ldots), but
they can be renamed.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ xy\_df.rename(columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{\{}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"x"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{\})}

\NormalTok{xy\_df}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
      x  y
0     4  3
1     7  4
2     4  3
3     4  3
4     7  4
...  .. ..
9995  4  2
9996  6  4
9997  5  3
9998  6  3
9999  6  4

[10000 rows x 2 columns]
\end{verbatim}

Now we can work with the simulation output as we would any pandas
\texttt{DataFrame}. Here are just a few examples

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy\_df[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{].value\_counts(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{).sort\_index()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
y
1    0.0673
2    0.1806
3    0.3092
4    0.4429
Name: proportion, dtype: float64
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy\_df[}\StringTok{"x"}\NormalTok{].value\_counts().sort\_index().plot.bar()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-211-3.png}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pd.crosstab(xy\_df[}\StringTok{"x"}\NormalTok{], xy\_df[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
y    1     2     3     4
x                       
2  673     0     0     0
3    0  1213     0     0
4    0   593  1200     0
5    0     0  1244  1269
6    0     0   648  1297
7    0     0     0  1227
8    0     0     0   636
\end{verbatim}

R is another popular software environment for statistical computing and
graphics. Symbulate is a Python package, but there are a number of ways
to interface between R and Python. Using an IDE such as Positron, you
can toggle between R and Python (as well as other formats). The
following provides examples of code cells you can include in a Quarto
document that you can edit in Positron and run both Python and R code.

Using Quarto, we can first run a Symbulate simulation and convert the
output to a pandas \texttt{DataFrame} (\texttt{xy\_df}) using a Python
code block.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{python\}}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{xy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{xy\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(xy)}

\NormalTok{xy\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ xy\_df.rename(columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{\{}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"x"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{: }\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{\})}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now we can use the R package
\href{https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/}{\texttt{reticulate}} and
access \texttt{xy\_df} within an R code block (as \texttt{py\$xy\_df}).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{r\}}

\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(reticulate)}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{r\}}
\NormalTok{py}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{xy\_df }\SpecialCharTok{|\textgreater{}} \FunctionTok{head}\NormalTok{()}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
  x y
1 4 3
2 4 3
3 5 4
4 8 4
5 6 3
6 6 4
\end{verbatim}

Now we have an R data frame that we can manipulate using commands from R
packages. For example, we can use the R package \texttt{ggplot2} to
create visualizations of Symbulate output.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{r\}}

\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggplot2)}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{r\}}
\NormalTok{xy\_df }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ py}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{xy\_df}

\NormalTok{N }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{nrow}\NormalTok{(xy\_df)}

\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(xy\_df,}
       \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(x), }\AttributeTok{y =} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(y))) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{stat\_bin\_2d}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{fill =} \FunctionTok{after\_stat}\NormalTok{(count }\SpecialCharTok{/}\NormalTok{ N))) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{labs}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =} \StringTok{"Sum of the two rolls"}\NormalTok{,}
       \AttributeTok{y =} \StringTok{"Larger of the two rolls"}\NormalTok{,}
       \AttributeTok{fill =} \StringTok{"Proportion of pairs"}\NormalTok{,}
       \AttributeTok{title =} \StringTok{"10000 pairs of rolls of a fair four{-}sided die"}\NormalTok{)}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-215-1.png}}

\section{Case Study: Matching Problem}\label{sec-sim-matching-n}

Dice rolling provides a simple scenario for us to introduce ideas, but
it's not very exciting. Now we'll apply ideas from this chapter to
investigate a more interesting problem: the matching problem. We'll also
see how we can combine Symbulate and Python code. Our analysis will
illustrate \emph{sensitity analysis}, where we see how probabilities,
distributions, and expected values change as we vary parameters or
assumptions.

Consider the matching problem for a general \(n\): objects labeled
\(1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\) are placed at random in spots labeled
\(1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\) with spot 1 the correct spot for object 1, etc.
Let the random variable \(X\) count the number of objects (out of \(n\))
that are put back in the correct spot; \(X\) is the number of
``matches''. Let \(\textrm{P}\) denote the probability measure
corresponding to the assumption that the objects are equally likely to
be placed in any spot, so that the \(n!\) possible placements are
equally.

We have previously considered the case \(n=4\)
(Example~\ref{exm-matching-outcome},
Example~\ref{exm-matching-indicator},
Exercise~\ref{exr-matching-rv-distribution}). By enumerating the
\(4! = 24\) possible outcomes (see Table~\ref{tbl-matching-outcome} and
Table~\ref{tbl-matching-indicator-tab}) we found the distribution of
\(X\) when \(n=4\), displayed in
Table~\ref{tbl-matching-rv-distribution} and
Figure~\ref{fig-matching-rv-distribution}. When \(n=4\) the probability
of at least one match is 0.625, and the expected value of \(X\) is 1.

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tbl-matching-rv-distribution}Distribution of \(X\), the
number of matches in the matching problem with \(n=4\) and uniformly
random placement of objects in spots.}

\centering{

\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{rr}
\toprule
x & P(X=x)\\
\midrule
0 & 0.3750\\
1 & 0.3333\\
2 & 0.2500\\
4 & 0.0417\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

}

\end{table}%

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/fig-matching-rv-distribution-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-matching-rv-distribution}Distribution of \(X\), the
number of matches in the matching problem with \(n=4\) and uniformly
random placement of objects in spots.}

\end{figure}%

When \(n=4\) we could enumerate the \(4!=24\) possible outcomes, but
such a strategy is not feasible for a general \(n\). For example, if
\(n=60\) then there are \(60! \approx 10^{82}\) possible outcomes, which
is about the total number of atoms in the observable universe. Therefore
we need other strategies to investigate the problem.

We'll use simulation to perform a \emph{sensitivity analysis} to
investigate how the distribution of \(X\), the probability of at least
one match, and the expected value of \(X\) depend on \(n\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Warning}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

This is not really a warning but before proceeding, stop to think: what
do you expect? How do you expect the probability of at least one match
to depend on \(n\)? Will the probability increase, decrease, or stay
about the same as \(n\) gets larger? What about the expected value of
the number of matches? It's always a good idea to think about a problem
and make some initial guesses before just jumping into calculations or
simulations.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-matching-sim-describe}{}\label{exm-matching-sim-describe}

For the matching problem for a given \(n\), describe in detail how you
would use simulation to approximate:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The distribution of \(X\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\)
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
We could use a box model.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The box has \(n\) tickets, labeled \(1, 2, \ldots, n\), one for each
  object.
\item
  An outcome is simulated by selecting \(n\) tickets from the box
  \emph{without} replacement and recording their order, e.g., (2, 1, 3,
  4) if \(n=4\).
\item
  Let \(x\) be the number of matches for the simulated outcome, e.g.,
  \(x=2\) for outcome (2, 1, 3, 4).
\item
  The above two steps consist of one repetition, yielding one realized
  value of the random variable \(X\).
\item
  Repeat these steps many times to obtain many simulated values of
  \(X\).
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Summarize the simulated values of \(X\) and their relative frequencies
  to approximate the distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Count the number of repetitions on which \(X\ge 1\) and divide by the
  total number of repetitions to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X\ge 1)\), the
  probability of at least one match.
\item
  We have seen that an expected value can be interpreted as a long run
  average value. To approximate \(\textrm{E}(X)\), compute the average
  of the many simulated \(X\) values---sum all simulated \(X\) values
  and divide by the number of simulated \(X\) values.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-matching-sim-describe}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

We'll start by coding a simulation for \(n=4\) so we can compare our
simulation results to the analytical results to check that our
simulation process is working correctly. Since Python uses zero-based
indexing, we label the objects \(0, 1, \ldots, n-1\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}

\NormalTok{labels }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n)) }\CommentTok{\# list of labels [0, ..., n{-}1]}
\NormalTok{labels}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[0, 1, 2, 3]
\end{verbatim}

Now we define the box model and simulate a few outcomes. Note that
\texttt{replace\ =\ False}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(labels, size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (0, 1, 2, 3)
1     (0, 2, 1, 3)
2     (2, 0, 3, 1)
3     (2, 0, 3, 1)
4     (1, 2, 3, 0)
\end{verbatim}

We simulate many outcomes to check that they are roughly equally likely.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P.sim(}\DecValTok{24000}\NormalTok{).tabulate()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Outcome      Frequency
(0, 1, 2, 3) 1023
(0, 1, 3, 2) 1017
(0, 2, 1, 3) 1027
(0, 2, 3, 1) 1007
(0, 3, 1, 2) 1007
(0, 3, 2, 1) 936
(1, 0, 2, 3) 981
(1, 0, 3, 2) 966
(1, 2, 0, 3) 954
(1, 2, 3, 0) 988
(1, 3, 0, 2) 1032
(1, 3, 2, 0) 993
(2, 0, 1, 3) 980
(2, 0, 3, 1) 1004
(2, 1, 0, 3) 984
(2, 1, 3, 0) 962
(2, 3, 0, 1) 1007
(2, 3, 1, 0) 1056
(3, 0, 1, 2) 1024
............ ....
(3, 2, 1, 0) 1008
       Total 24000
\end{verbatim}

Remember that a random variable \(X\) is a function whose inputs are the
sample space outcomes. In this example the function ``counts matches'',
so would like to define \(X\) as \texttt{X\ =\ RV(P,\ count\_matches)}.
Unfortunately, such a function isn't built in like \texttt{sum} or
\texttt{max}, but we can write a custom \texttt{count\_matches} Python
function. The \texttt{count\_matches} function below starts a counter at
0 and then goes spot-by-spot through each spot in the outcome and
increments the counter by 1 any time there is a match (along the lines
of the discussion in Section~\ref{sec-indicator-rv}). Don't worry too
much about the Python syntax yet. What's important is that we have
defined a \emph{function} that we can use to define a random variable.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_matches(outcome):}
\NormalTok{    count }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, n, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ outcome[i] }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ labels[i]:}
\NormalTok{            count }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ count}
  
\NormalTok{outcome }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) }\CommentTok{\# an example outcome, with 2 matches}
\NormalTok{count\_matches(outcome) }\CommentTok{\# the function evaluated for the example outcome}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
2
\end{verbatim}

Now we can use the function \texttt{count\_matches} to define a
Symbulate \texttt{RV} just like we have used \texttt{sum} or
\texttt{max}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_matches)}

\NormalTok{X((}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)) }\CommentTok{\# evaluate X for the sample outcome}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Warning: Calling an RV as a function simply applies the function that defines the RV to the input, regardless of whether that input is a possible outcome in the underlying probability space.
2
\end{verbatim}

We can simulate many values of \(X\) and use the simulated values to
approximate the distribution of \(X\), the probability of at least one
match, and the expected value of \(X\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
0     0.377
1     0.3274
2     0.2519
4     0.0437
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-222-1.png}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.count\_geq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.623
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
1.006
\end{verbatim}

The simulated distribution of \(X\) is close to the true distribution in
Table~\ref{tbl-matching-rv-distribution} when \(n=4\); the simulated
relative frequencies are within the margin of error (about 0.01-0.02 for
10000 simulated values) of the true probabilities. We also see that the
average of the simulated \(X\) values is around the theoretical expected
value of 1.

It appears that our simulation is working properly for \(n=4\). To
investigate a different value of \(n\), we simply need to revise the
line \texttt{n\ =\ 4}. Because we want to investigate many values of
\(n\), we wrap all the above code in a Python function
\texttt{matching\_sim} which takes \texttt{n} as an input\footnote{Because
  of the way we defined \texttt{count\_matches} we need to redefine it
  if we change \texttt{n} and \texttt{labels}, which is why
  \texttt{count\_matches} is defined inside \texttt{matching\_sim}.} and
outputs our objects of interest: a plot of the distribution of simulated
\(X\) values, the approximation of \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\), and the
approximation of \(\textrm{E}(X)\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ matching\_sim(n):}
  
\NormalTok{    labels }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n))}
    
    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_matches(omega):}
\NormalTok{        count }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, n, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ omega[i] }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ labels[i]:}
\NormalTok{                count }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ count}
    
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(labels, size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_matches)}
    
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}
    
\NormalTok{    plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{    x.plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}impulse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    plt.show()}
    
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ x.count\_geq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count(), x.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For example, for \(n=4\) we simply call

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{matching\_sim(}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(0.6244, 1.0065)
\end{verbatim}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-226-3.png}

Now we can easily investigate different values of \(n\). For example,
for \(n=10\) we see that the approximate probability of at least one
match is around 0.63 and the approximate expected value of the number of
matches is around 1.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{matching\_sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(0.6283, 0.9988)
\end{verbatim}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-227-5.png}

We can use a for loop to automate the process of changing the value of
\(n\), running the simulation, and recording the results. If \texttt{ns}
is the list of \(n\) values of interest we basically just need to run

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ n }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ ns:}
\NormalTok{    matching\_sim(n)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In Python we can also use list comprehension

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[matching\_sim(n) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ n }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ ns]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The table below summarizes the simulation results for
\(n=4, \ldots, 10\). The first line defines the values of \(n\), and the
second line implements the for loop. We have used the Python package
\href{https://pypi.org/project/tabulate/}{\texttt{tabulate}} to add a
little formatting to the table. (Don't confuse this with the Symbulate
\texttt{tabulate} method!) Note that we have temporarily redefined
\texttt{matching\_sim} to remove the lines that produced the plot, but
we have not displayed the revised code here. (We will bring the plot
back soon.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ tabulate }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ tabulate }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ns }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{11}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{results }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [matching\_sim(n) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ n }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ ns]}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(tabulate(\{}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}n\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: ns,}
                \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Approximate P(X \textgreater{}= 1), Approximate E(X)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: results\},}
\NormalTok{               headers }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}keys\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, floatfmt}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{".3f"}\NormalTok{))}

  n  Approximate P(X >= 1), Approximate E(X)
---  -----------------------------------------
  4  (0.618, 0.9873)

Stop and look at the table; what do you notice? How do the probability
of at least one match and the expected value of the number of matches
depend on \(n\)? They don't! Well, maybe they do, but they don't appear
to change very much with \(n\) after we take into account simulation
margin of error\footnote{The simulation margin of error for relative
  frequency of at least one match is about 0.01 based on 10000 simulated
  values. We haven't discussed simulation margins of error when
  aproximating expected values yet. In this case, the margin of error
  for a single average based on 10000 simulated values is about 0.02.}
of about 0.01-0.02. It appears that regardless of the value of \(n\),
the probability of at least one match is around 0.63 and the expected
value of the number of matches is around 1.

If we're interested in more values of \(n\), we just repeat the same
process with a longer list of \texttt{ns}. The code below uses the
Python package \href{https://matplotlib.org/}{\texttt{Matplotlib}} to
create a plot of the probability of at least one match and the expected
value of the number of matches versus \(n\). While there is some natural
simulation variability, we see that the probability of at least one
match (about 0.63) and the expected value of the number of matches
(about 1) essentially do not depend on \(n\)!

What about the distribution of \(X\)? This
\href{https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1wqc3ZJhLTKC-zP27WcnT-z-AIh0wBnoS?usp=sharing}{Colab
notebook} contains code for investigating how the distribution of \(X\)
depends on \(n\). The basic simulation code is identical to what we have
already seen. The notebook adds a few lines to create a Jupyter widget,
which produces an interactive plot (with some additional formatting) of
the distribution; you can change the slider to see how the distribution
of \(X\) changes with \(n\). Take a few minutes to play with the slider;
what do you see?

You should see that unless \(n\) is really small (like 5 or less) the
distribution of \(X\) is basically the same for any value of \(n\)! We
will see soon that the number of matches follows, approximately, a
``Poisson(1)'' distribution, regardless of the value of \(n\) (unless
\(n\) is really small). In particular, the probability of 0 matches is
approximately equal to 0.37, and also approximately equal to the
probability of exactly 1 match.
