The following Symbulate code conducts a simulation for
Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball}. The value of \(X\) depends on a
sequence of Bernoulli trials, but the number of trials is not know in
advance. We can simulate Bernoulli trials of unspecified length in
Symbulate using \texttt{Bernoulli(p)\ **\ inf}; each trial results in
either 1 (success) or 0 (failure). (The \texttt{inf} implies
``infinite'', but in reality Symbulate will keep simulating as many
Bernoulli trials as needed.) Given a sequence of Bernoulli trials (of
any length) we define a function \texttt{count\_until\_first\_success}
that outputs the number of trials until the first success and then use
it to define a \texttt{RV} \texttt{X}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_until\_first\_success(omega):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(omega):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ w }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# the +1 is for zero{-}based indexing}
        
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Bernoulli(}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ inf}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_until\_first\_success)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now we simulate many values of \(X\) and summarize the results; the
simulation results are consistent with the theoretical distribution
represented by Table~\ref{tbl-geometric-bball} and
Figure~\ref{fig-geometric-bball}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
1     0.3968
2     0.2454
3     0.1452
4     0.0876
5     0.053
6     0.0271
7     0.017
8     0.0111
9     0.0064
10    0.0042

12    0.0012

17    0.0002
Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.plot()}

\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{).plot() }\CommentTok{\# Overlay the theoretic pmf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
<symbulate.distributions.Geometric object at 0x0000020512963B60>
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png}

Many commonly encountered probability mass functions correspond to named
distributions. The distribution of \(X\) in
Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball} is called the ``Geometric(0.4)''
distribution. We'll discuss Geometric distributions in more detail soon.

The probability mass functions of many commonly encountered named
distributions are built in to Symbulate and can be called as
\texttt{Distribution(parameters).pmf(x)}. For example, we can use
Symbulate to compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 3) = 0.144\) in
Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{).pmf(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.144)
\end{verbatim}

\section{Simulating from a marginal
distribution}\label{simulating-from-a-marginal-distribution}

Recall from Section~\ref{sec-simulate-from-distribution} that there are
two basic methods for simulating a value \(x\) of a random variable
\(X\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Simulate from the probability space.} Simulate an outcome
  \(\omega\) from the underlying probability space and set
  \(x = X(\omega)\).
\item
  \textbf{Simulate from the distribution.} Simulate a value \(x\)
  directly from the distribution of \(X\).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-geometric-bball-sim}{}\label{exm-geometric-bball-sim}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture} and the discussion and
Symbulate code following it.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which method did we use to simulate values of \(X\)?
\item
  Describe how could we simulate values of \(X\) using the other method.
\item
  Write the Symbulate code to simulate values of \(X\) using the other
  method and summarize the simulated values. Is the simulation
  consistent with our early simulation?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  We used the ``simulate from the probability space method''. We
  simulated a sequence of five success/failure trials (outcome
  \(\omega\)) and counted the number of successes (\(X(\omega)\)).
\item
  The spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-capture-2} represents the
  distribution of \(X\). To simulate a value of \(X\) from the
  distribution, we just spin this spinner once.
\item
  See the Symbulate code below. We can ``simulate from the
  distribution'' in Symbulate by defining
  \texttt{X\ =\ RV(Binomial(5,\ 0.25))}; read this as ``\(X\) is a
  random variable with a Binomial(5, 0.25) distribution''. This code
  basically says that values of \(X\) will be simulated using the
  spinner in Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-capture-2}.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-geometric-bball-sim-sol}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{X.sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     1
1     2
2     2
3     1
4     3
5     1
6     1
7     0
8     2
9     1
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Value Relative Frequency
0     0.2449

Total 1.0
\end{verbatim}

The ``simulate from the distribution'' method corresponds to
constructing a spinner representing the marginal distribution of \(X\)
and spinning it once to generate \(x\). This method does require that
the distribution of \(X\) is known. However, as we will see in many
examples, \emph{it is common to specify the distribution of a random
variable directly without defining the underlying probability space}.

Many commonly encountered distributions have special names, and in
Symbulate we can define a random variable to have a specific named
distribution through code of the form
\texttt{RV(Distribution(parameters))}. For an unnamed discrete
distribution, specified as a table of possible values and probabilities,
\texttt{BoxModel} with the \texttt{probs} option can be used (when there
are finitely many possible values).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-geometric-bball-sim}{}\label{exm-geometric-bball-sim}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball}. Maya is a basketball player
who makes 40\% of her three point field goal attempts. Suppose that she
attempts three pointers until she makes one and then stops. Let \(X\) be
the total number of shots she attempts. Assume shot attempts are
independent.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Specify how you could simulate a value of \(X\) using the ``simulate
  from the probability space'' method.
\item
  Specify how you could simulate a value of \(X\) using the ``simulate
  from the distribution'' method.
\item
  Explain how you could use simulation to approximate the distribution
  of \(X\).
\item
  Write Symbulate code to approximate the distribution of \(X\) using
  the ``simulate from the distribution'' method.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Spin a spinner that lands on success with probability 0.4 (and failure
  otherwise) until it lands on success then stop; \(X\) is the number of
  spins. This is the method represented by the Symbulate code after
  Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball}.
\item
  Construct a spinner representing the probability mass function in part
  7 (see Figure~\ref{fig-geometric-bball}) then spin it once; the
  resulting value is \(X\).
\item
  Simulate many values of \(X\) (using either method) then summarize the
  simulated values: For each possible value, compute the simulated
  relative frequency, e.g.~to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X = 3)\) count
  the number of repetitions resulting in an \(X\) value of 3 and divide
  by the total number of repetitions.
\item
  See below. The simulation results are consistent with the
  Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball} and the simulation based on the
  ``simulate from the probability space'' method.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-geometric-bball-sim-sol}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\section{Binomial Distributions}\label{binomial-distributions}

A Binomial(\(n\), \(p\)) distribution has a probability mass function
that depends on \(n\) and \(p\) whose form---which we will see
later\footnote{If you can't wait, the Binomial(\(n\), \(p\)) pmf is \[
  p(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, x=0, 1, 2, \ldots, n
  \] where \(\binom{n}{x} = \frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}\). For example, if
  \(n=5\) and \(p = 0.25\),
  \(p(2) = \binom{5}{2}(0.25)^2(1-0.25)^{5-2} = 0.264\). We will derive
  this pmf later.}---is determined by the assumptions of
Definition~\ref{def-binomial-story}. The following code shows how we can
use Symbulate to compute probabilities involving a random variable \(X\)
with a Binomial(5, 0.25) distribution as in
Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, p }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).pmf(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.2373046874999998)
\end{verbatim}

We can plug in all possible values of \(X\) to compute the Binomial(5,
0.25) pmf.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, p }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).pmf([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([0.23730469, 0.39550781, 0.26367187, 0.08789062, 0.01464844,
       0.00097656])
\end{verbatim}

The following code achieves the same purpose, but uses list
comprehension and displays the results in a table.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xs }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{5} \OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{pmf\_x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [Binomial(n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, p }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).pmf(x) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ x }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ xs]}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(tabulate(\{}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}x\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: xs,}
                \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Binomial(5, 0.25) pmf(x)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{: pmf\_x\},}
\NormalTok{               headers }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}keys\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{, floatfmt}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{".3f"}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
  x    Binomial(5, 0.25) pmf(x)
---  --------------------------
  0                       0.237
  1                       0.396
  2                       0.264
  3                       0.088
  4                       0.015
  5                       0.001
\end{verbatim}

If we know a random variable has a Binomial distribution, then we can
use Symbulate as a probability calculator. Therefore, the key is to
identify the Binomial situation and the relevant parameters.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-symbulate-pmf}{}\label{exm-binomial-symbulate-pmf}

Use Symbulate to compute the following probabilities, then interpret the
values in context.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Shuffle a standard deck of 52 cards and deal 5 with replacement. What
  is the probability that there are no hearts among the cards dealt?
\item
  Shishito peppers are typically relatively mild, but about 10\% are
  spicy. If these peppers are sold in packs of 20, what is the
  probability that a pack contains at least one spicy pepper?
\item
  About 70\% of major league baseball pitchers are right-handed. If 13
  pitchers are selected at random, what is the probability that at most
  8 are right-handed?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The context is different, but probabilistically this situation is the
  same as Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture}. If \(X\) is the number of
  hearts among the 5 cards dealt, then \(X\) has a Binomial(5, 0.25)
  distribution, and \(\textrm{P}(X=0) = 0.237\). About 23.7\% of
  five-card-hands, dealt with replacement, will contain no hearts.
\item
  If \(X\) is the number of spicy peppers in a twenty-pepper-pack then
  \(X\) has a Binomial(20, 0.1) distribution. We want
  \(\textrm{P}(X\ge 1)\) which we can compute, using the complement
  rule, as \(1 - \textrm{P}(X = 0)\): either at least one pepper in the
  pack is spicy or none of them are. In Symbulate,
  \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(20,\ 0.1).pmf(0)} yields 0.878. About 88\% of
  20-pepper-packs of Shishito peppers contain at least one spicy pepper.
  In other words, a pack is about 7 times more likely than not to
  contain at least one spicy pepper.
\item
  If \(X\) is the number of the 13 pitchers that are right-handed, then
  \(X\) has a Binomial(13, 0.70) distribution. We want
  \(\textrm{P}(X \le 8)\), which we can compute as
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 0) + \textrm{P}(X = 1) + \cdots \textrm{P}(X = 8)\).
  Symbulate code (see below) yields 0.346. About 35\% of groups of 13
  pitchers will have at most 8 right-handed pitchers.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-binomial-symbulate-pmf}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

The pmf directly provides probabilities of ``equal to'' events, but we
can obtain probabilities of other events by summing appropriately, as in
the following Symbulate code.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xs }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{8} \OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{).pmf(xs).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.34568643929850007)
\end{verbatim}

The probability mass function (pmf) returns ``equal to'' probabilities:
\(\textrm{P}(X = x)\). The \textbf{cumulative distribution function
(cdf)} provides ``less than or equal to'' probabilities
\(\textrm{P}(X \le x)\). We can use the \texttt{cdf} method in Symbulate
to shortcut summing. (We will discuss cumulative distribution functions
in much more detail for continuous random variables.)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{).cdf(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.3456864392985002)
\end{verbatim}

Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-pmf-shade} displays the Binomial(13, 0.7) pmf
with \(p(x)\) for \(x\le 8\) highlighted.
\texttt{Binomial(13,\ 0.7).cdf(8)} computes the sum of the probabilities
represented by the spikes for \(x\le 8\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{).plot().shade(le }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
<symbulate.distributions.Binomial object at 0x0000020514D53040>
\end{verbatim}

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/fig-binomial-pmf-shade-5.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-binomial-pmf-shade}Binomial(13, 0.7) pmf, with
\(p(x)\) for \(x \leq 8\) highlighted}

\end{figure}%

Note that \texttt{cdf(x)} by definition returns \(\textrm{P}(X \le x)\).
We can obtain other probabilities by using the complement rule or
subtracting. For example, \texttt{1-Binomial(13,\ 0.7).cdf(8)} returns
\(1 - \textrm{P}(X\le 8)=\textrm{P}(X > 8) = \textrm{P}(X \ge 9)\).

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-power}{}\label{exm-binomial-power}

Roy, a baseball player, tells his coach: ``Throughout my career my
probability of getting a hit in an at bat has been 0.250. But ever since
baseball season ended, I've been practicing really hard and I have
definitely improved my hitting''. The coach needs some convincing and
decides to let Roy have 100 at bats to convince him. Let \(X\) be the
number of hits Roy gets in the 100 at bats.

You can assume Roy's probability of getting a hit on any single at bat,
\(p\) is the same for each at bat and that the at bats are independent
(and you can ignore baseball context like walks/etc. and assume that
there is no funny business in data collection).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the distribution of \(X\)? What is the distribution of \(X\)
  \emph{if Roy has not improved}?
\item
  Suppose the coach decides that if Roy gets at least 30 hits he'll be
  convinced. What is the probability that Roy convinces the coach that
  he has improved even if he has not really improved?
\item
  Suppose that Roy really has improved and his probability of getting a
  hit in an at bat is 0.300. What is the probability that Roy convinces
  the coach that he has improved?
\item
  Suppose the coach wants the probability in part 2 to be 0.01. What
  should his threshold for convincing---which was 30 in the part 2---be?
  Should the threshold be greater or less than 30?
\item
  Use Symbulate and trial and error to find a threshold which gets the
  probability in part 2 as close to 0.01 without going over.
\item
  The coach decides to use the threshold from the previous part. Suppose
  that Roy really has improved and his probability of getting a hit in
  an at bat is 0.300. What is the probability that Roy convinces the
  coach that he has improved? How does this compare to part 3?
\item
  Repeat parts 4 and 5 assuming Roy has 400 at bats. How do the values
  change?
\item
  Now Roy actually takes 100 at bats and gets hits in 38 at bats. What
  is the probability that Roy would get at least 38 hits if he really
  hadn't improved? Did he necessarily improve? Are you convinced that he
  improved? Explain.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  This the Binomial situation:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    each at bat is a trial that results in success (hit) or not
  \item
    the probability of success is assumed to be the same on each trial,
    \(p\)
  \item
    the trials are assumed to be independent
  \item
    there are a fixed number of trials, 100
  \item
    \(X\) counts the number of successes in 100 Bernoulli trials So
    \(X\) has a Binomial(100, \(p\)) distribution. If Roy has not
    improved \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.250) distribution.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Let \(\textrm{P}\) be the probability measure which reflects that
  \(Roy\) has not improved. We want
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 30)=1-\textrm{P}(X<30) = 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 29)\),
  where \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.250) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{P}\). In Symbulate:
  \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(100,\ 0.25).cdf(29)} which is 0.1495. See
  Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-power-1}
\item
  Let \(\textrm{Q}\) be the probability measure which reflects that
  \(Roy\) has improved to a 0.300 hitter. We want
  \(\textrm{Q}(X \ge 30)=1-\textrm{Q}(X<30) = 1 - \textrm{Q}(X \le 29)\),
  where \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.300) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{Q}\). In Symbulate:
  \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(100,\ 0.30).cdf(29)} which is 0.5377. See
  Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-power-2}
\item
  We need to decrease the probability so we want a greater (stricter)
  threshold than 30.
\item
  We want to find \(x\) such that
  \(0.01 \approx \textrm{P}(X \ge x)=1-\textrm{P}(X<x) = 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le x-1)\),
  where \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.250) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{P}\). Try \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(100,\ 0.25).cdf(x\ -\ 1)}
  for different values of \texttt{x} to find \(x=36\), which yields
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 36)= 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 35) = 0.009\). If the
  coach is only convinced if Roy gets hits in at least 36 at bats then
  the probability of being incorrectly convinced if Roy hasn't improved
  is 0.009.
\item
  We want
  \(\textrm{Q}(X \ge 36)=1-\textrm{Q}(X<36) = 1 - \textrm{Q}(X \le 35)\),
  where \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.300) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{Q}\). In Symbulate:
  \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(100,\ 0.30).cdf(35)} which is 0.1161. With the
  stricter threshold, Roy has a smaller probability of convincing the
  coach that he really has improved.
\item
  Now \(X\) has a Binomial(400, 0.25) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{P}\). Try \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(400,\ 0.25).cdf(x\ -\ 1)}
  for different values of \texttt{x} to find \(x=121\), which yields
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 121)= 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 120) = 0.01\). So if the
  coach is only convinced if Roy get at least 121 hits in 400 at bats
  then the probability of being incorrectly convinced if Roy hasn't
  improved is 0.01. The probability is the same in part 4, but in part 4
  Roy needed to demonstrate success in at least 36/100 = 36\% of at
  bats, but now the threshold is 121/400 = 30.25\% of at bats.

  Now \(X\) has a Binomial(400, 0.30) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{Q}\). We want
  \(\textrm{Q}(X \ge 121)= 1 - \textrm{Q}(X \le 120)\), where \(X\) has
  a Binomial(100, 0.300) distribution according to \(\textrm{Q}\). In
  Symbulate: \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(400,\ 0.30).cdf(120)} which is
  0.4754. By demonstrating good performance over more at bats, Roy has a
  greater probability of convincing the coach that he really has
  improved.
\item
  Let \(\textrm{P}\) be the probability measure which reflects that
  \(Roy\) has not improved. We want
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 38)=1-\textrm{P}(X<38) = 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 37)\),
  where \(X\) has a Binomial(100, 0.250) distribution according to
  \(\textrm{P}\). In Symbulate:
  \texttt{1\ -\ Binomial(100,\ 0.25).cdf(37)} which is 0.0027.

  There are two explanations for Roy's performance. Either Roy didn't
  really improve and he just got really lucky in these 100 at bats, or
  he actually did improve. Since it would be so unlikely (0.0027) for
  Roy to get hits in at least 38 out of 100 at bats if he really hadn't
  improved, the fact that he actually did this well gives us evidence
  that he really has improved. Did Roy necessarily improve? No. Could he
  have just gotten lucky? Sure. But since 38/100 would be so unlikely
  just by luck if he hadn't improved, the more plausible explanation is
  that he actually has improved. We would say that 38/100 offers pretty
  convincing evidence that he has improved.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-binomial-power}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Example~\ref{exm-binomial-power} featured some statistical applications
of Binomial distributions, in the context of a ``null hypothesis test''.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The ``null hypothesis'' is that Roy has not improved
\item
  A threshold like ``at least 30'' is a ``rejection region''
\item
  The probability of exceeding the threshold if the null hypothesis is
  true is the probability of ``Type I error'' (see
  Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-power-1})
\item
  The probability of exceeding the threshold if Roy really has improved
  is the ``power'', computed if \(p=0.300\), but this would generally be
  a function of \(p\) (see Figure~\ref{fig-binomial-power-2})
\item
  After we observe 38 hits in 100 at bats, the probability of observing
  a result at least that extreme if the null hypothesis is true is the
  ``p-value''. The smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence the
  observed data provides to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that
  Roy really has improved.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).plot().shade(ge }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.xlim(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{).plot().shade(ge }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.xlim(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{)}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}\OperatorTok{;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

}

\subcaption{\label{fig-binomial-power-1}If Roy has not improved and
\(p=0.25\)}

\end{minipage}%
\newline
\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/fig-binomial-power-8.png}

}

\subcaption{\label{fig-binomial-power-2}If Roy has improved and
\(p=0.30\)}

We will study further applications to statistics in more detail later.

In the next few examples we'll investigate expected value and variance
for Binomial distributions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-ev}{}\label{exm-binomial-ev}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture}, where \(X\) had a Binomial(5,
0.25) distribution.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Suggest a ``shortcut'' formula for \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
\item
  Use the table from the previous part to compute \(\textrm{E}(X)\). Did
  the shortcut formula work?
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X = \textrm{E}(X))\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X \le \textrm{E}(X))\). Is it 0.5?
\item
  Interpret \(\textrm{E}(X)\) in context.
\item
  Use simulation to approximate \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) and
  \(\textrm{SD}(X)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If 25\% are tagged we would expect \(5(0.25) = 1.25\) tagged
  butterflies in the sample of 5.
\item
  Indeed we do get 1.25 if we compute the expected value the ``long
  way'' based on the distribution table. \[
  (0)(0.2373) + (1)(0.3955) + (2)(0.2637) + (3)(0.0879) + (4)(0.0146) + (5)(0.0010) 
  \]
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X = \textrm{E}(X)) = \textrm{P}(X = 1.25)=0\); 1.25 is
  not a possible value of \(X\).
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \le \textrm{E}(X)) = \textrm{P}(X \le 1.25)=\textrm{P}(X = 0) + \textrm{P}(X =1) = 0.2373+0.3955 = 0.633\).
  This is not 0.5; the distribution of \(X\) is not symmetric so the
  mean is not necessarily ``in the middle''.
\item
  Over many samples of 5 butterflies we would expect to see 1.25 tagged
  butterlies per sample on average.
\item
  See simulation results below; \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) is approximately
  0.9375 (we'll see a shortcut formula for this soon) and
  \(\textrm{SD}(X)\) is approximately \(\sqrt{0.9375} =0.9682\).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-binomial-ev}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.mean(), x.var(), x.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(1.2498, 0.9439999600000001, 0.9715966035346151)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-var-n}{}\label{exm-binomial-var-n}

Figure~\ref{fig-binom-plots-n} displays Binomial distributions for a
given \(p\) (0.4) for a few different values of \(n\) (5, 10, 15, 20).
As \(n\) increases does the variance increase, decrease, or stay the
same?

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
For a Binomial(\(n\), \(p\)) distribution, variance increases as \(n\)
increases. Since the possible values of a random variable with a
Binomial distribution are \(0, 1, \ldots, n\), as \(n\) increases the
range of possible values of the variable increases.

However, in some sense it is unfair to compare values from Binomial
distributions with different values of \(n\). Ten successes has a very
different meaning if \(n\) is 10 or 20 or 100. Rather than focusing on
the absolute number of successes, in Binomial situations we are often
concerned with the \emph{proportion} of successes in the sample. We will
see later that as the sample size \(n\) increases, the variance of the
sample proportion decreases.

\label{sol-binomial-var-n}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-var-p}{}\label{exm-binomial-var-p}

Figure~\ref{fig-binom-plots-p} displays Binomial distributions for a
given \(n\) (10) for a few different values of \(n\) (0.1, 0.3, 0.5,
0.7, 0.9).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  How does the variance when \(p=0.1\) compare to when \(p=0.9\)? What
  about 0.3 and 0.7?
\item
  For what value of \(p\) is the variance the largest?
\item
  Among these values of \(p\), for what values of \(p\) is the variance
  the smallest?
\item
  What values of \(p\) (not just among those pictured) would lead to the
  smallest variance?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The variance when \(p=0.1\) is the same as when \(p=0.9\). The shapes
  are mirror images (reflected about 0.5) but the degree of dispersion
  about the mean is the same. Moving from \(p=0.1\) to \(p=0.9\) is just
  like interchanging the roles of success and failure. Likewise for 0.3
  and 0.7.
\item
  The distribution is most disperse, and the variance largest, when
  \(p=0.5\). When \(p=0.5\) we would expect the most ``alterations''
  between success and failure in the individual trials.
\item
  Variance decreases in a symmetric manner as \(p\) moves away from 0.5.
  That is, variance decreases as \(p\) gets closer to 0 or 1.
\item
  The extremes \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) both result in a variance of 0. When
  \(p=0\), every trials results in failure so the number of successes
  out of \(n\) trials is always 0 and so the variance is 0. Similarly,
  when \(p=1\) every trials results in success so the number of
  successes out of \(n\) trials is always \(n\), and so the variance is
  0.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-binomial-var-p}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

The following result formalizes the observations from the last few
exercises.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-binomial-ev-var}{}\label{lem-binomial-ev-var}

If \(X\) has a Binomial(\(n\), \(p\)) distribution then

\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}(X) & = np\\
\textrm{Var}(X) & = np(1-p)
\end{align*}

\end{lemma}

In Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture},
\(\textrm{Var}(X) = 5(0.25)(1-0.25) = 0.9375\), and
\(\textrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{0.9375} = 0.968\).

In Symbulate, the theoretical expected value and variance of a named
distribution can be computed as \texttt{Distribution(parameters).mean()}
and \texttt{Distribution(parameters).var()}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(1.25)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).var()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.9375)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-sum}{}\label{exm-binomial-sum}

Xavier bets on red on each of 3 spins of a roulette wheel. After the
third spin, Xavier leaves and Zander arrives and bets on black on the
next two spins. Let \(X\) be the number of bets that Xavier wins and let
\(Z\) be the number that Zander wins.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the distribution of \(X\) and the distribution of \(Z\).
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Z\) independent? Explain.
\item
  What does \(X+Z\) represent in this context? Identify the distribution
  of \(X+Z\) without doing any calculations.
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the distribution of \(X+Z\) and confirm
  your answer to the previous part.
\item
  Suppose that Yolanda bets on black on all 5 spins of the wheel. Does
  \(X + Y\) have a Binomial distribution? Explain.
\item
  Suppose instead that Zavier bet on the number 7 in his two bets. Does
  \(X + Z\) have a Binomial distribution in this case? Explain.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) has a Binomial(3, 18/38) distribution and \(Z\) has a
  Binomial(2, 18/38) distribution.
\item
  Yes, \(X\) only depends on the first three spins, and \(Z\) only
  depends on the last two, and the spins are (physically) independent,
  so \(X\) and \(Z\) are independent.
\item
  \(X+Z\) is the total number of bets won by either of these players.
  The five spins satisfy the Binomial situation. Each trial results in
  either ``win'' or not. The probability of a win on any bet is 18/38;
  it doesn't matter if they're betting on black or red because each has
  the same probability of winning. The spins are independent. Between
  the two players there is a fixed number of 5 bets and we are counting
  the number of wins. So \(X+Z\) has a Binomial(5, 18/38) distribution.
\item
  See the results below; the simulated values follow closely a
  Binomial(5, 13/38) distribution.
\item
  \(X + Y\) does not have a Binomial distribution, because the trials
  that determine \(X\) are not independent of those that determine
  \(Y\). The random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent.
\item
  \(X+Z\) would not have a Binomial distribution, because there is not
  the same probability of win (success) on all trials (18/38 for the
  first three but 1/38 for the last two).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-binomial-sum}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X, Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Binomial(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Z).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-31-11.png}

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-binomial-sum}{}\label{lem-binomial-sum}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(X\) has a Binomial(\(n_X\), \(p\))
distribution, and \(Y\) has a Binomial(\(n_Y\), \(p\)) distribution then
\(X+Y\) has a Binomial(\(n_X+n_Y\), \(p\))

\end{lemma}

A Binomial(1, \(p\)) distribution is also known as a
\textbf{Bernoulli(\(p\))} distribution, taking a value of 1 with
probability \(p\) and 0 with probability \(1-p\). Any \emph{indicator
random variable} has a Bernoulli distribution.

If \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) are independent each with a
Bernoulli(\(p\)) distribution, then \(X_1+\cdots+X_n\) has a
Binomial(\(n, p\)) distribution. So any random variable with a
Binomial(\(n\), \(p\)) distribution has the same distributional
properties as \(X_1+  X_2+  \cdots+  X_n\), where \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\)
are independent each with a Bernoulli(\(p\)) distribution. This provides
a very convenient representation in many problems.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-capture-phat}{}\label{exm-binomial-capture-phat}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture}. Define the random
variable \(\hat{p} = X/5\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What does \(\hat{p}\) represent in this context. What are its possible
  values?
\item
  Does \(\hat{p}\) have a Binomial distribution? Does the distribution
  of \(\hat{p}\) have the same basic \emph{shape} of a Binomial
  distribution?
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(\hat{p} = 0.2)\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(\hat{p})\). Why does this make sense?
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{SD}(\hat{p})\).
\item
  Suppose that 20 butterflies were selected for the second sample at
  random, with replacement. Compute \(\textrm{SD}(\hat{p})\); how does
  the value compare to the previous part?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-binomial-capture-phat}{}\label{exm-binomial-capture-phat}

~

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\hat{p}\) is the \emph{proportion} of butterflies in the second
  sample that are tagged. Possible values are 0, 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5, 1.
\item
  Technically \(\hat{p}\) does not have a Binomial distribution, since a
  Binomial distribution always corresponds to possible values 0, 1, 2,
  \(\ldots, n\). But the distribution of \(\hat{p}\) does follow the
  same shape as the Binomial(5, 0.25) distribution, just with a rescaled
  variable axis.
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(\hat{p} = 0.2) = \textrm{P}(X = 1)\), which is
  \texttt{Binomial(5,\ 0.25).pmf(1)}.
\item
  If 25\% of the butterflies in the population are tagged, we would
  expect 25\% of the butterflies in a random sample to be tagged. \[
  \textrm{E}(\hat{p}) = \textrm{E}(X/5) = \textrm{E}(X)/5 = 5(0.25)/5 = 0.25
  \]
\item
  \(\textrm{SD}(X/5) = \textrm{SD}(X)/5\), so \[
  \textrm{SD}(\hat{p}) = \textrm{SD}\left(\frac{X}{5}\right) = \frac{\textrm{SD}(X)}{5} = \frac{\sqrt{5(0.25)(1-0.25)}}{5} = \frac{\sqrt{0.25(1-0.25)}}{\sqrt{5}} = 0.31
  \]
\item
  The calculation is similar to the previous part. \[
  \textrm{SD}(\hat{p}) = \textrm{SD}\left(\frac{X}{20}\right) = \frac{\textrm{SD}(X)}{20} = \frac{\sqrt{20(0.25)(1-0.25)}}{20} = \frac{\sqrt{0.25(1-0.25)}}{\sqrt{20}} = 0.165
  \] The standard deviation of \(\hat{p}\) is smaller when \(n\) is
  larger. A sample of size 20 is 4 times larger than a sample of size 5,
  but the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{4}=2\) times smaller when
  \(n=20\) than when \(n=5\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_5 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{phat\_5 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X\_5 }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{phat\_5.mean(), phat\_5.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(0.25054, 0.19229588763153518)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_20 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{phat\_20 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X\_20 }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{phat\_20.mean(), phat\_20.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(0.24904, 0.09670872969902974)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{phat\_5.plot()}
\NormalTok{phat\_20.plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-32-13.png}

Binomial distributions model the absolute number of successes in a
sample of size \(n\). If \(X\) is the number of successes then the
\emph{sample proportion} is the random variable \[
\hat{p} = \frac{X}{n}
\] For a fixed value of \(p\), sample-to-sample variability of
\(\hat{p}\) \emph{decreases} as sample size \(n\) increases.
\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}\left(\hat{p}\right) & = p\\
\textrm{Var}\left(\hat{p}\right) & = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\\
\textrm{SD}\left(\hat{p}\right) & = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\\
\end{align*}

\section{Geometric and Negative Binomial
distributions}\label{geometric-and-negative-binomial-distributions}

Binomial distributions are models for the number of successes in a fixed
number of Bernoulli trials. But what if the number of trials is not
fixed? In particular, what if we keep performing trials until a certain
number of successes are obtained?

\subsection{Geometric distributions}\label{geometric-distributions}

Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball} provided one such example, where the
random variable had a Geometric distribution.

\begin{definition}[]\protect\hypertarget{def-geometric-story}{}\label{def-geometric-story}

Perform Bernoulli(\(p\)) trials until a success occurs and then stop.
Let \(X\) count the total number of trials, including the single
success. The distribution of \(X\) is defined to be the
\textbf{Geometric(\(p\)) distribution}.

\end{definition}

The Geometric(\(p\)) probability mass function follows from the fact
that if \(X\) has a Geometric distribution, then \(X = x\) if and only
if

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the first \(x-1\) trials are failures, and
\item
  the \(x\)th (last) trial results in success.
\end{itemize}

\begin{definition}[Geometric probability mass
function]\protect\hypertarget{def-geometric-pmf}{}\label{def-geometric-pmf}

A discrete random variable \(X\) has a Geometric(\(p\)) distribution if
and only if its probability mass function is \begin{align*}
p_{X}(x) & = p (1-p)^{x-1}, & x=1, 2, 3, \ldots
\end{align*}

\end{definition}

The next result follows from the fact that if \(X\) has a Geometric
distribution, then \(X > x\)---that is, more than \(x\) trials are
needed to achieve the first success---if and only if the first \(x\)
trials result in failure.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-geometric-cdf}{}\label{lem-geometric-cdf}

If \(X\) has a Geometric(\(p\)) distribution then

\[
\textrm{P}(X > x) = (1-p)^{x}, \qquad  x=1, 2, 3, \ldots
\]

\end{lemma}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-geometric-bball-ev-var}{}\label{exm-geometric-bball-ev-var}

Continuing Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball}, where \(X\) has a
Geometric(\(p\)) distribution with \(p=0.4\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What seems like a reasonable shortcut formula for \(\textrm{E}(X)\) in
  terms of \(p\)? Hint: it might help to consider the case \(p=0.1\)
  first, then apply similar logic to \(p=0.4\) and general \(p\).
\item
  Use Table~\ref{tbl-geometric-bball} to compute \(\textrm{E}(X)\). Did
  the shortcut work?
\item
  Interpret \(\textrm{E}(X)\) in context.
\item
  Use simulation to approximate \(\textrm{E}(X)\) and
  \(\textrm{Var}(X)\).
\item
  Would \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) be bigger or smaller if \(p=0.9\)? If
  \(p=0.1\)?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Suppose that she only makes 10\% of her attempts, so \(p=0.1\). That
  is, she makes 1 in every 10 attempts on average, so it seems
  reasonable that we would expect her to attempt 10 three pointers on
  average before she makes one. Therefore, \(1/0.1= 10\) seems like a
  reasonable formula for \(\textrm{E}(X)\) when \(p=0.1\). In general,
  \(1/p\) seems like a reasonable shortcut for \(\textrm{E}(X)\) if
  \(X\) has a Geometric(\(p\)) distribution.
\item
  The shortcut gives \(\textrm{E}(X) = 1/0.4 = 2.5\), which is
  consistent with the ``long way'' \[
  \scriptsize{
  (1)(0.4) + (2)(0.24) + (3)(0.144)+(4)(0.0864) + (5)(0.0518) + (6)(0.0311) + (7)(0.0186) + (8)(0.0112) + (9)(0.0067) + \cdots
  }
  \] Technically, the sum keeps going but since the probabilities get so
  small, the contribution of the additional terms is negligible.
\item
  Imagine she does this at every practice session. Over many practice
  sessions, it takes her 2.5 three point attempts, until she makes one,
  per practice on average.
\item
  See simulation results below. We're using the ``simulate from the
  distribution method''.
\item
  If the probability of success is \(p=0.9\) we would not expect to wait
  very long until the first success, so it would be unlikely for her to
  need more than a few attempts. If the probability of success is
  \(p=0.1\) then she could make her first attempt and be done quickly,
  or it could take her a long time. So the variance is greater when
  \(p=0.1\) and less when \(p=0.9\). The probabilities in the
  Geometric(\(p\)) pmf decrease to 0 more quickly as \(x\) increases
  when \(p\) is close to 1 then when \(p\) is close to 0, so the
  distribution becomes ``spread out'' as \(p\) decreases from 1.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-geometric-bball-ev-var}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.mean(), x.var(), x.sd()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(2.4651, 3.6607819900000003, 1.9133170124158725)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-34-15.png}

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-geometric-ev-var}{}\label{lem-geometric-ev-var}

If \(X\) has a Geometric(\(p\)) distribution then

\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}(X) & = \frac{1}{p}\\
\textrm{Var}(X) & = \frac{1-p}{p^2}
\end{align*}

\end{lemma}

In Example~\ref{exm-geometric-bball-ev-var},
\(\textrm{Var}(X) = (1-0.4)/0.4^2 = 3.75\), which is consistent with the
simulation results.

If \(p=1\) then every trial results in success so \(X=1\) always and
therefore the variance is 0. If \(p\) is close to 1, we expect to see
success in the first few trials, so the variance is relatively small. If
\(p\) is close to 0, success could occur on the first trial but we would
expect to have to wait a larger number of trials until the first success
occurs, resulting in a larger variance. As \(p\) gets closer to 0, the
expression \((1-p)/p^2\) gets larger and larger.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-lookaway-geometric}{}\label{exm-lookaway-geometric}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-lookaway-ltp}.

You and your friend are playing the
\href{https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/what-are-your-chances-of-winning-the-u-s-open/}{``lookaway
challenge''}. The game consists of possibly multiple rounds. In the
first round, you point in one of four directions: up, down, left or
right. At the exact same time, your friend also looks in one of those
four directions. If your friend looks in the same direction you're
pointing, you win! Otherwise, you switch roles and the game continues to
the next round---now your friend points in a direction and you try to
look away. As long as no one wins, you keep switching off who points and
who looks. The game ends, and the current ``pointer'' wins, whenever the
``looker'' looks in the same direction as the pointer.

Suppose that each player is equally likely to point/look in each of the
four directions, independently from round to round.

Let \(X\) be the number of rounds played in a game.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain why \(X\) has a Geometric distribution, and specify the value
  of \(p\).
\item
  Express the event ``the player who starts as the pointer wins the
  game'' as an event involving \(X\).
\item
  Explain how you could use simulation to approximate the probability
  that the player who starts as the pointer wins the game and the
  expected number of rounds the game lasts.
\item
  Use the Geometric pmf (use software) to compute the probability that
  the player who starts as the pointer wins the game. Compare to the
  result of Example~\ref{exm-lookaway-ltp}.
\item
  Compute and interpret \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \(X\) has a Geometric distribution with parameter \(p=0.25\).

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Each round is a trial,
  \item
    the round either results in success (current pointer wins the round
    and game ends) or failure (current pointer does not win the round
    and the game continues),
  \item
    the rounds are assumed to be independent
  \item
    the probability that the current point wins any particular round is
    0.25
  \item
    and \(X\) counts the number of rounds until the first success
  \end{itemize}
\item
  The player who starts as the pointer can only win the game in odd
  number rounds---when they're the pointer---so the event of interest is
  the event that \(X\) is odd, \(\{X \in \{1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots\}\}\).
\item
  See the code below. We could just simulate \(X\) from the
  Geometric(\(p\)) distribution, but we'll use the ``simulate from the
  probability space'' method just to compare.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    To simulate one round, simulate a (pointer, looker) pair of values
    (up, down, left, right) (or just 1, 2, 3, 4) independently, with
    equal probability.
  \item
    If the pair of values match then the game ends in that round,
    otherwise the game continues
  \item
    Repeat rounds as above, independently, until the game ends (the pair
    is a match) and then stop. Let \(X\) be the number of rounds.
  \item
    Repeat the above to simulate many values of \(X\).
  \item
    Average the simulated values of \(X\) to approximate
    \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
  \item
    Count the number of simulated values of \(X\) that are odd and
    divide by the total number of simulated values to approximate the
    probability that the player who starts as the pointer wins the game.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  We need to sum the Geometric(0.25) pmf over \(x=1,3,5,\ldots\). See
  code below. The probability is 4/7=0.571, the same as in
  Example~\ref{exm-lookaway-ltp}
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = 1/0.25 = 4\). Over many games of the lookaway
  challenge, the game lasts 4 rounds on average.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-lookaway-geometric}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# given a sequence of (point, look) pairs}
\CommentTok{\# determine the round in which the first match occurs}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_rounds(sequence):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ r, pair }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(sequence):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ pair[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ pair[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ r }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# +1 for 0 indexing}

\CommentTok{\# simulate (point, look) pairs independently and equally likely}
\CommentTok{\# ** inf is to continue indefinitely}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ inf}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_rounds)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     7
1     1
2     1
3     5
4     14
5     1
6     3
7     1
8     2
....  .
9999  2
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{x.plot() }\CommentTok{\# simulated distribution}
\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;} \CommentTok{\# overlay theoretical pmf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The following approximate probability that the player who starts as the
pointer wins the game (which occurs if the game ends in an odd number of
rounds).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ is\_odd(u):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ (u }\OperatorTok{\%} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# odd if the remainder when dividing by 2 is 1}

\NormalTok{x.count(is\_odd) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.5772
\end{verbatim}

We can find the theoretical probability that \(X\) is odd by summing the
Geometric(0.25) pmf over \(x = 1, 3, 5, \ldots\). Technically, the sum
keeps going but the probabilities get extremely small as \(x\)
increases, so we just cut it off after some large value (99 below).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# range(1, 100, 2) is odd numbers from 1 to 99}
\NormalTok{Geometric(}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{).pmf(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.5714285714283882)
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Negative Binomial
distributions}\label{negative-binomial-distributions}

Now we'll investigate a generalization of the Geometric situation where
we perform Bernoulli trials until a certain number (not necessarily one)
of successes are obtained.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-nb-bball}{}\label{exm-nb-bball}

Maya is a basketball player who makes 86\% of her free throw attempts.
Suppose that she attempts free throws until she makes 5 and then stops.
Let \(X\) be the total number of free throws she attempts. Assume shot
attempts are independent.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Does \(X\) have a Binomial distribution? A Geometric distribution? Why
  or why not?
\item
  What are the possible values of \(X\)? Is \(X\) discrete or
  continuous?
\item
  Describe how you could use a tactile simulation to simulate a single
  value of \(X\).
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate
  \(\textrm{P}(X=5)\).
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate the
  distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Write and run Symbulate code to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X=5)\) and
  the distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Compute the theoretical value of \(\textrm{P}(X = 5)\). Compare to
  your simulated value. Is the theoretical value within the margin of
  error of the simulated value?
\item
  Interpret in context \(\textrm{P}(X = 5)\) as a long run relative
  frequency.
\item
  The distribution of \(X\) is called the ``NegativeBinomial(5, 0.86)''
  distribution. Use Symbulate to compute \(\textrm{P}(X = x\) for all
  possible values \(x\), then construct a table, plot, and spinner
  representing the approximate distribution of \(X\). (You can cut it
  off after the probabilities get very small.) Are the simulation
  results consistent with the theoretical distribution?
\item
  What seems like a reasonable shortcut formula for \(\textrm{E}(X)\)?
\item
  Use the theoretical pmf to compute \(\textrm{E}(X)\). Did the shortcut
  formula work.
\item
  Interpret \(\textrm{E}(X)\) for this example.
\item
  Would the variance be larger or smaller if attempted free throws until
  she made 10 instead of 5?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) does not have a Binomial distribution since the number of
  \emph{trials} is not fixed. The number of \emph{successes} is fixed to
  be 5, but the number of trials is random. \(X\) also does not have a
  Geometric distribution because \(X\) counts the number of trials
  needed for 5 successes, not just one.
\item
  \(X\) can take values 5, 6, 7, \(\ldots\). Even though it is unlikely
  that \(X\) is very large, there is no fixed upper bound. Even though
  \(X\) can take infinitely values, \(X\) is a discrete random variables
  because it takes \emph{countably} many possible values.
\item
  Construct a spinner that lands on success with probability 0.86. Spin
  the spinner until it lands on 5 successes and stop and count the total
  number of spins; this is one simulated value of \(X\).
\item
  Simulate many values of \(X\) as in the previous part. Count the
  number of simulated values equal to 5 and divide by the total number
  of simulated values to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X=5)\).
\item
  Simulate many values of \(X\) and summarize the simulated values to
  find the simulated relative frequency for each possible value.
\item
  See code below.
\item
  In order for \(X\) to be 5, Maya must make her first 5 attempts. Since
  the attempts are independent \(\textrm{P}(X=5)=(0.86)^5=0.47\), which
  is consistent with the simulation results.\\
\item
  If Maya does this every practice, then in about 47\% of practices she
  will make her first five free throw attempts.
\item
  See the Symbulate code below and Table~\ref{tbl-nb-ball} and
  Table~\ref{tbl-nb-ball}. The simulation results are consistent with
  the theoretical distribution.
\item
  On average it takes \(1/0.86 = 1.163\) attempts to make a free throw,
  so it seems reasonable that it would take on average
  \(5(1/0.86)=5.81\) attempts to make 5 free throws.
\item
  The shortcut gives \(\textrm{E}(X) = 5(1/0.86)=5.81\), which is
  consistent with the ``long way'' \[
  \scriptsize{
  (5)(0.4705) + (6)(0.3293) + (7)(0.1383)+(8)(0.0452) + (9)(0.0127) + (10)(0.0032) + (11)(0.0007) + \cdots
  }
  \] Technically, the sum keeps going but since the probabilities get so
  small, the contribution of the additional terms is negligible.
\item
  If Maya does this at every practice, it takes her on average 5.8
  attempts to make 5 free throws.
\item
  The variance would be larger with 10 attempts. With every additional
  required success we ``accumulate variability'' in the total number of
  attempts needed to achieve that many successes.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-nb-bball}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_until\_rth\_success(omega):}
\NormalTok{    trials\_so\_far }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(omega):}
\NormalTok{        trials\_so\_far.append(w)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(trials\_so\_far) }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ r:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# +1 for zero{-}based indexing}

\CommentTok{\# simulate an indefinite (** inf) sequence of Bernoulli trials       }
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Bernoulli(}\FloatTok{0.86}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ inf}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_until\_rth\_success)}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x.plot()}

\CommentTok{\# overlay theretical distribution}
\NormalTok{NegativeBinomial(r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, p }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.86}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
