\begin{definition}[]\protect\hypertarget{def-negative-binomial-story}{}\label{def-negative-binomial-story}

Perform Bernoulli(\(p\)) trials until a fixed number, \(r\), of
successes and then stop. Let \(X\) count the total number of trials,
including the \(r\) successes. The distribution of \(X\) is defined to
be the \textbf{Negative Binomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution}.

\end{definition}

A Negative Binomial distribution is specified by two parameters:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(r\) (an integer): the fixed number of successes
\item
  \(p\) (in \([0, 1]\)): the fixed marginal probability of success on
  each Bernoulli trial, or the population proportion of success
\end{itemize}

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-nb-ev-var}{}\label{lem-nb-ev-var}

If \(X\) has a NegativeBinomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution
\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}(X) & = \frac{r}{p}\\
\textrm{Var}(X) & = \frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}
\end{align*}

\end{lemma}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-nb-geom}{}\label{exm-nb-geom}

What is another name for a NegativeBinomial(1, \(p\)) distribution?

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
A NegativeBinomial(1, \(p\)) distribution is a Geometric(\(p\))
distribution.

\label{sol-nb-geom}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-negative-binomial-sum}{}\label{exm-negative-binomial-sum}

Xavier bets on red on roulette until he wins 3 bets and then he leaves.
After Xavier leaves, Zander arrives and bets on black until he wins 2
bets and then he leaves. Let \(X\) be the number of bets that Xavier
makes and let \(Z\) be the number of bets that Zander makes.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Identify the distribution of \(X\) and the distribution of \(Z\).
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Z\) independent? Explain.
\item
  What does \(X+Z\) represent in this context? Identify the distribution
  of \(X+Z\) without doing any calculations.
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the distribution of \(X+Z\) and confirm
  your answer to the previous part.
\item
  Suppose that Yolanda starts making bets on the same game as Xavier,
  and she bets on black until she wins 5 bets. Does \(X + Y\) have a
  Negative Binomial distribution? Explain.
\item
  Suppose instead that Zavier bets on the number 7 until he wins 5 bets.
  Does \(X + Z\) have a Negative Binomial distribution in this case?
  Explain.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) has a NegativeBinomial(3, 18/38) distribution and \(Z\) has a
  NegativeBinomial(2, 18/38) distribution.
\item
  Yes, Xavier and Zander bet on different sets of games and the spins
  are (physically) independent, so \(X\) and \(Z\) are independent.
\item
  \(X+Z\) is the total number of games played until a total of 5 games
  are won. This satisfies the Negative Binomial situation. Each trial
  results in either ``win'' or not. The probability of a win on any bet
  is 18/38; it doesn't matter if they're betting on black or red because
  each has the same probability of winning. The spins are independent.
  Between the two players there is a fixed number of 5 wins and we are
  counting the total number of bets (trials). So \(X+Z\) has a
  NegativeBinomial(5, 18/38) distribution.
\item
  See the results below; the simulated values follow closely a
  NegativeBinomial(5, 18/38) distribution.
\item
  \(X + Y\) does not have a Negative Binomial distribution, because the
  trials that determine \(X\) are not independent of those that
  determine \(Y\). The random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are not
  independent.
\item
  \(X+Z\) would not have a Negative Binomial distribution, because there
  is not the same probability of win (success) on all trials (18/38 for
  Xavier's bets but 1/38 for Zander's).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-negative-binomial-sum}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X, Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(NegativeBinomial(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ NegativeBinomial(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Z).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{NegativeBinomial(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{18} \OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{38}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-48-1.png}

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-negative-binomial-sum}{}\label{lem-negative-binomial-sum}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(X\) has a
NegativeBinomial(\(r_X\), \(p\)) distribution, and \(Y\) has a
NegativeBinomial(\(r_Y\), \(p\)) distribution then \(X+Y\) has a
NegativeBinomial(\(r_X+r_Y\), \(p\))

\end{lemma}

If \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_r\) are independent each with a
Geometric(\(p\)) distribution, then \(X_1+\cdots+X_r\) has a
NegativeBinomial(\(r, p\)) distribution. So any random variable with a
NegativeBinomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution has the same distributional
properties as \(X_1+  X_2+  \cdots+  X_r\), where \(X_1, \ldots, X_r\)
are independent each with a Geometric(\(p\)) distribution. This provides
a very convenient representation in many problems.

\subsection{Pascal distributions}\label{pascal-distributions}

In a Negative Binomial situation, the total number of successes is fixed
(\(r\)), i.e., not random. What is random is the number of failures, and
hence the total number of trials.

Our definition of a Negative Binomial distribution (and hence a
Geometric distribution) provides a model for a random variable which
counts the number of Bernoulli(\(p\)) \emph{trials} required until \(r\)
successes occur, \emph{including} the \(r\) trials on which success
occurs, so the possible values are \(r, r+1, r+2,\ldots\)

There is an alternative definition of a Negative Binomial distribution
(and hence a Geometric distribution) which provides a model for a random
variable which counts the number of \emph{failures} in Bernoulli(\(p\))
trials required until \(r\) successes occur, \emph{excluding} the \(r\)
trials on which success occurs, so the possible values are
\(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) We will refer to this alternative definition as a
``Pascal distribution''.

\begin{definition}[]\protect\hypertarget{def-pascal-story}{}\label{def-pascal-story}

Perform Bernoulli(\(p\)) trials until a fixed number, \(r\), of
successes and then stop. Let \(X\) count the total number of failures
(excluding the \(r\) successes). The distribution of \(X\) is defined to
be the \textbf{Pascal(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution}.

\end{definition}

There is not a standard definition of Negative Binomial, and some
software programs use ``Negative Binomial'' to refer to what we're
calling ``Pascal''. It's a good idea to always check the documentation
of a software package to see what definition is used.

In Symbulate, a Pascal(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution follows this alternate
definition. In Symbulate,

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The possible values of a NegativeBinomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution
  are \(r, r+1, r+2,\ldots\)
\item
  The possible values of a Pascal(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution are
  \(0, 1, 2,\ldots\)
\end{itemize}

If \(X\) has a NegativeBinomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution then
\((X-r)\) has a Pascal(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution. Similarly, if \(Y\)
has a Pascal(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution then \((Y+r)\) has a
NegativeBinomial(\(r\), \(p\)) distribution.

\section{Poisson distributions}\label{poisson-distributions}

Binomial and Negative Binomial distributions are commonly used for
modeling discrete random variables. However, Binomial and Negative
Binomial models are not appropriate in many situations that involve
counting ``successes''.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-poisson-hr-intro}{}\label{exm-poisson-hr-intro}

Let \(X\) be the number of home runs hit (in total by both teams) in a
randomly selected Major League Baseball game.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In what ways is this situation like the Binomial situation? (What is a
  trial? What is ``success''?)
\item
  In what ways is this NOT like the Binomial situation?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Each pitch is a trial, and on each trial either a home run is hit
  (``success'') or not. The random variable \(X\) counts the number of
  home runs (successes) over all the trials
\item
  Even though \(X\) is counting successes, this is not the Binomial
  situation.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    The number of trials is not fixed. The total number of pitches
    varies from game to game. (The average is around 300 pitches per
    game).
  \item
    The probability of success is not the same on each trial. Different
    batters have different probabilities of hitting home runs. Also,
    different pitch counts or game situations lead to different
    probabilities of home runs.
  \item
    The trials might not be independent. Make sure you distinguish
    independence from the previous assumption of unequal probabilities
    of success; you need to consider conditional probabilities to assess
    independence. Maybe if a pitcher gives up a home run on one pitch,
    then the pitcher is ``rattled'' so the probability that he also
    gives up a home run on the next pitch increases, or the pitcher gets
    pulled for a new pitcher which changes the probability of a home run
    on the next pitch.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-poisson-hr-intro}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-poisson-accidents-intro}{}\label{exm-poisson-accidents-intro}

Let \(X\) be the number of vehicle crashes involving fatalities that
occur in San Luis Obispo County in a randomly selected week.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In what ways is this like the Binomial situation? (What is a trial?
  What is ``success''?)
\item
  In what ways is this NOT like the Binomial situation?
\item
  Which of the following do you think it would be easier to estimate by
  collecting and analyzing relevant data?

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    The total number of vehicles on the road in the county in a week,
    and the probability that each vehicle is involved in a fatal crash.
  \item
    The average number of fatal vehicle crashes per week in the county.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Each vehicle on the road in the week is a trial, and each vehicle
  either is either involved in a fatal crash (``success'') or not. The
  random variable \(X\) counts the number of vehicles involved in fatal
  crashes (successes). (Remember ``success'' is just a generic label for
  what you're interested in counting; ``success'' is not necessarily
  good.)
\item
  Even though \(X\) is counting successes, this is not the Binomial
  situation.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    The number of trials is not fixed. The total number of vehicles on
    the road varies from week to week.
  \item
    The probability of success is not the same on each trial. Different
    drivers have different probabilities of being involved in fatal
    crashes; some drivers are safer than others. Also, different
    conditions increase the probability of a crash, like driving at
    night.
  \item
    The trials are plausibly not independent. Make sure you distinguish
    independence from the previous assumption of unequal probabilities
    of success; you need to consider conditional probabilities to assess
    independence. If a vehicle is in a crash, then the probability of
    being involved in a crash increases for the vehicles that are
    driving near it.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  It would be extremely difficult to estimate the probability that each
  individual vehicle is involved in a fatal crash. You might be able to
  measure the total number of vehicles in a week at a certain location
  (e.g., with cables across the road), but doing so for the entire
  county would be extremely difficult, and it vary from week to week. It
  would be much easier to find data on total number of fatal vehicle
  crashes in a week, e.g., from police reports, and use it to estimate
  the average number of fatal vehicle crashes per week in the county.
  That is, you could count the number of ``successes'' without knowing
  how many ``trials'' there were or the probability of ``success'' on
  individual trials.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-poisson-accidents-intro}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Binomial and Negative Binomial models have several restrictive
assumptions that might not be satisfied in practice:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  The number of trials must be fixed (not random) and known (for
  Negative Binomial, the number of successes must be fixed)
\item
  The probability of success must be the same for each trial (fixed, not
  random) and known.
\item
  The trials must be independent.
\end{itemize}

Even when the trials are independent with the same probability of
success, fitting a Binomial model to data requires estimation of both
\(n\) and \(p\) individually. When the only data available are counts of
successes but not trials (e.g., number of fatal vehicle crashes in a
week but not number of vehicles) it might not be possible to estimate
both \(n\) and \(p\).

``Poisson models'' are more flexible models for counts which do not
require all the conditions of the Binomial situation. \emph{Poisson
distributions} are often used to model the distribution of random
variables that count the number of ``relatively rare'' events that occur
over a certain interval of time or in a certain region (e.g., number of
car insurance policies that have claims in a day, number of bank loans
that go into default, number of mutations in a DNA sequence, number of
earthquakes that occurs in SoCal in an hour, etc.)

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-matching-poisson}{}\label{exm-matching-poisson}

Recall our discussion of the matching problem in
Section~\ref{sec-sim-matching-n}. We observed that, unless \(n\) is
really small,

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the long run average number of matches does is (approximately) 1
\item
  the distribution of the number of matches (\(X\)) is approximately the
  ``Poisson(1)'' distribution.
\end{itemize}

The Poisson(1) pmf is represented by
Table~\ref{tbl-matching-poisson-distribution} and
Figure~\ref{fig-matching-poisson-distribution}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Interpret \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\) as a long run relative frequency.
\item
  Describe in words the Poisson(1) distribution. What are some relevant
  features? Which values are most likely? How much more likely are they
  than the next most likely value? And so on.
\item
  Would it be appropriate to assume that \(X\) has a Binomial
  distribution? Explain.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In about 37\% of repetitions of the matching problem, there will be no
  matches. For example, in about 37\% of Secret Santa drawings, no one
  will draw their own name.
\item
  We could interpret the distribution in terms of relative frequencies
  as in the previous part: 18.4\% of repetitions of the matching problem
  result in exactly 2 matches, etc. We can also interpret the
  distribution in terms of relative degrees of likelihood.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    0 and 1 are equally likely, and then the pmf is decreasing as a
    function of \(x\)
  \item
    2 is 1/2 as likely as 1
  \item
    3 is 1/3 as likely as 2,
  \item
    4 is 1/4 as likely as 3
  \item
    5 is 1/5 as likely as 4, and so on
  \end{itemize}
\item
  In some ways the matching problem does resemble the Binomial
  situation:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Each object is a trial and success occurs if it is put in the
    correct spot.
  \item
    There are \(n\) trials, fixed.
  \item
    Unconditionally, each object is equally likely to be placed in any
    of the \(n\) spots, so the \emph{marginal} probability of success is
    the same on each trial, \(1/n\).
  \item
    \(X\) counts the number of successes in \(n\) trials.
  \end{itemize}

  However, the trials are not independent. For example, if object 1 is
  placed correctly in spot 1, the \emph{conditional} probability that
  object 2 is placed in spot 2 is \(1/(n-1)\); if objects 1 through
  \(n-1\) are placed in their correct spots, then the \emph{conditional}
  probability that object \(n\) is placed in the correct spot is 1.
  Since the trials are not independent, \(X\) does not have a Binomial
  distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-matching-poisson}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

A Poisson distribution has a single parameter, denoted \(\mu\), which
must be a positive number, \(\mu > 0\). One way to interpret \(\mu\) is
as the expected value, that is, long run average value. In the matching
problem 1 is the parameter of the Poisson distribution because 1 is the
long run average number of matches. Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-pmfs}
displays Poisson distributions for a few values of \(\mu\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.6}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{3.4}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}\OperatorTok{;}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ mu }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ mus:}
\NormalTok{  Poisson(mu).plot()}\OperatorTok{;}
  
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/fig-poisson-pmfs-3.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-poisson-pmfs}Probability mass functions of Poisson
distributions; \(\mu\) values, from left to right, 0.7, 1.6, 2.5, 3.4.}

\end{figure}%

Example~\ref{exm-matching-poisson} and Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-pmfs}
illustrate the ``Poisson pattern''. As a function of
\(x=0, 1, 2, \ldots\), a Poisson(\(\mu\)) pmf increases for \(x<\mu\)
and then decreases\footnote{If \(\mu\) is a whole number, then the
  Poisson pmf assigns the same probability to the values \(\mu\) and
  \(\mu-1\). If \(\mu<1\) then \(x=0\) has the highest probability and
  the pmf decreases from there.} for \(x>\mu\), following a particular
\emph{Poisson pattern}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  1 is \(\mu\) times as likely as 0
\item
  2 is \(\mu/2\) times as likely as 1
\item
  3 is \(\mu/3\) times as likely as 2
\item
  4 is \(\mu/4\) times as likely as 3
\item
  and so on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{definition}[]\protect\hypertarget{def-poisson-pattern}{}\label{def-poisson-pattern}

A random variable \(X\) has a \textbf{Poisson(\(\mu\)) distribution} if
the possible values are \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) and the pmf follows the

\[
\text{Poisson(}\mu\text{) pattern:}\quad x \text{ is } \frac{\mu}{x} \text{ as likely as } x-1 \quad \text{ (for } x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)
\]

\end{definition}

The Poisson pattern is sufficient to define the shape of a
Poisson(\(\mu\)) pmf \(p(x), x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\). The final step is to
normalize the probabilities defined by the Poisson pattern so that they
sum to 1.

For example, for the Poisson(1) distribution in
Example~\ref{exm-matching-poisson} suppose that 0 accounts for 10000
``units'' of probability; remember, this is just an arbitrary baseline.
Then the Poisson pattern implies that

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  0 accounts for \(10000\) units (just an assumed baseline)
\item
  1 accounts for \(10000\times 1/1 = 10000\) units
\item
  2 accounts for \(10000\times 1/2 = 5000\) units
\item
  3 accounts for \(5000\times 1/3 = 1666.67\) units
\item
  4 accounts for \(1666.67\times 1/4 = 416.67\) units
\item
  5 accounts for \(416.67\times 1/5 = 83.33\) units
\item
  6 accounts for \(83.33\times 1/6 = 13.89\) units
\item
  7 accounts for \(13.89\times 1/7 = 1.98\) units
\end{itemize}

And so on. Technically, a Poisson(1) distribution assigns positive
probability to all whole numbers, but the values \(0,\ldots,7\) comprise
nearly 100\% of the probability. The values \(0,\ldots,7\) account for a
total of 27182.82 ``units'', so we divide the units corresponding to
each of \(0,\ldots,7\) by 27182.82 to obtain probabilities which sum to
1, resulting in the values in
Table~\ref{tbl-matching-poisson-distribution} (e.g., the value 3
corresponds to probability \(1666.67 / 27182.82 = 0.0613\)). Note that,
after normalizing, the value 0 corresponds to probability
\(e^{-1} = 0.3679\).

If \(X\) has a Poisson(\(\mu\)) distribution, normalization implies
that\footnote{We will see the math behind this later.} the probability
that \(X\) equals 0 is \(e^{-\mu}\). This fact provides a baseline for
computing other probabilities via the Poisson pattern without dealing
with arbitrary ``units''\footnote{We can build a Poisson(\(\mu\)) pmf
  \(p(x)\) from the Poisson pattern, \(p(x)=p(x-1)(\mu/x)\), and
  normalizing, which yields \(p(0) = e^{-\mu}\): \begin{align*}
  p(1) & = p(0)(\mu/1) = e^{-\mu}\mu,\\
  p(2) & = p(1)(\mu/2) = e^{-\mu}\mu^2/2,\\
  p(3) & = p(2)(\mu/3) = e^{-\mu}\mu^3/3!,\\
  p(4) & = p(3)(\mu/4) = e^{-\mu}\mu^4/4!,
  \end{align*} and in general \[
  p(x) = e^{-\mu}\mu^x/x!, \qquad x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
  \]}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-homerun-poisson}{}\label{exm-homerun-poisson}

Let \(X\) be the number of home runs hit (in total by both teams) in a
randomly selected Major League Baseball game. Assume that \(X\) has a
Poisson(2.4) distribution.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In what sense are home runs ``relatively rare''?
\item
  What are the possible values of \(X\)?
\item
  Interpret the parameter 2.4 in context.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 2.4)\) without using software.
\item
  Identify the most likely value of \(X\) without doing any
  computations.
\item
  Use Symbulate to compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\) and interpret the value
  in context.
\item
  Starting with \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\) from the previous part, use the
  ``Poisson pattern'' to find, by hand without Symbulate,
  \(\textrm{P}(X = x)\) for \(x = 1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots\). Then use
  Symbulate to check your values, and display them in a table and plot.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X \le 13)\) and interpret the value in context.
  (\href{https://www.mlb.com/news/d-backs-and-phillies-set-mlb-home-run-record}{The
  most home runs ever hit in a baseball game is 13}.)
\item
  Construct a spinner to simulate values of \(X\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Var}(X)\).
\item
  Use Symbulate to simulate many values of \(X\) and compare the
  simulated distribution to the theoretical Poisson distribution and its
  expected value and variance.
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  In a typical baseball game there are around 300 pitches but only a
  handful of home runs. So home runs (successes) are rare relative to
  the number of pitches (trials).
\item
  Since \(X\) has a Poisson distribution, its possible values are
  \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) Even though it is rare for a game to have more
  than a few home runs (see below), technically there is no fixed upper
  bound for the number of home runs that can happen in a game.
\item
  2.4 is the long run average value of \(X\): Over many baseball games
  there are a total of 2.4 home runs per game on average.
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 2.4) = 0\) since 2.4 is not a possible value of
  \(X\). The long run average is 2.4, but the number of home runs in any
  game must be a whole number.
\item
  As a function of \(x\) a Poisson pmf increases up to \(\mu\) and then
  decreases, so with \(\mu = 2.4\) the value \(x=2\) will have the
  highest probability.
\item
  We can use \texttt{Poisson(2.4).pmf(0)} to obtain
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 0) = 0.091\). (We could also use the Poisson
  normalizing constant: \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)=e^{-2.4} = 0.091\).) Over
  many baseball games, about 9.1\% of games have 0 home runs, so about
  89.9\% of games have at least one home run. In other words, a baseball
  game is about 10 times more likely to have at least one home run than
  to have 0 home runs.
\item
  Starting with \(\textrm{P}(X = 0) = 0.091\):

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 1) = \textrm{P}(X = 0) \times 2.4 / 1 = 0.091 \times 2.4 / 1 = 0.218\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 2) = \textrm{P}(X = 1) \times 2.4 / 2 = 0.218 \times 2.4 / 2 = 0.261\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 3) = \textrm{P}(X = 2) \times 2.4 / 3 = 0.261 \times 2.4 / 3 = 0.209\)
  \item
    \(\textrm{P}(X = 4) = \textrm{P}(X = 3) \times 2.4 / 4 = 0.209 \times 2.4 / 4 = 0.125\)
  \item
    and so on; see Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-homerun-1} and the right
    column of Table~\ref{tbl-poisson-hr}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Just sum the values of the pmf corresponding to the values
  \(x = 0, 1, \ldots, 13\): \(\textrm{P}(X \le 13) = 0.9999997\). There
  isn't any shorter way to do it. In the long run, almost all MLB games
  have at most 13 home runs. Even though the Poisson(2.4) pmf assigns
  nonzero probability to all whole numbers 0, 1, 2, \(\ldots\), the
  probability that \(X\) takes a value greater than 13 is extremely
  small.
\item
  See Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-homerun-2}. To simplify the display we
  have lumped values \(6, 7, \ldots\) into one ``6+'' category.
\item
  Compute the probability-weighted average to find
  \(\textrm{E}(X)=2.4\). \[
  \scriptsize{
  (0)(0.0907)+(1)(0.2177)+(2)(0.2613)+(3)(0.2090)+(4)(0.1254)+(5)(0.0602)+(6)(0.0241)+(7)(0.0083)+(8)(0.0025)+(9)(0.0007)+\cdots
  }
  \] Technically the sum would keep going but since the probabilities
  get so small the contribution of the remaining terms is negligible.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(X^2)=8.16\). \[
  \scriptsize{
  (0^2)(0.0907)+(1^2)(0.2177)+(2^2)(0.2613)+(3^2)(0.2090)+(4^2)(0.1254)+(5^2)(0.0602)+(6^2)(0.0241)+(7^2)(0.0083)+(8^2)(0.0025)+(9^2)(0.0007)+\cdots
  }
  \] Technically the sum would keep going but since the probabilities
  get so small the contribution of the remaining terms is negligible.
  Then
  \(\textrm{Var}(X) = \textrm{E}(X^2)- (\textrm{E}(X))^2 = 8.16 - 2.4^2 = 2.4\)
\item
  See the simulation results below, which match up closely with the
  theoretical distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-homerun-poisson}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

}

Since \texttt{Poisson} is a named distribution family in Symbulate, we
can use \texttt{pmf} to compute probabilities such as
\(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\), \(\textrm{P}(X = x)\) for
\(x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\), and \(\textrm{P}(X \le 13)\).

A Poisson distribution is a discrete distribution which assign nonzero
probability to countably infinitely many values: \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\).
While there is no fixed upper bound, for many Poisson distributions most
of the probability is concentrated over a relatively small range of
possible values.

Poisson distributions are often reasonable models for random variables
which count successes in situations where successes are rare relative to
the number of trials. In Example~\ref{exm-poisson-accidents-intro},
there are many vehicles on the road but very few of them are involved in
fatal crashes. Therefore, if \(X\) is the number of vehicles crashes
involving fatalities that occur in San Luis Obispo County in a randomly
selected week, we might assume that \(X\) follows a Poisson
distribution. We could estimate the parameter by collecting data on the
number of fatal vehicle crashes in a sample of weeks and computing the
average number of fatal crashes per week.
Table~\ref{tbl-poisson-crashes} summarizes such data\footnote{Source:
  the
  \href{https://www.chp.ca.gov/programs-services/services-information/switrs-internet-statewide-integrated-traffic-records-system}{California
  Highway Patrol Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System
  (CHP-SWITRS)} public dataset available through the Berkeley
  \href{https://tims.berkeley.edu/}{Transportation Incident Mapping
  System (TIMS)}.} for 2011 through 2020 from San Luis Obispo County.
There were 277 fatal vehicle crashes in 519 weeks, an average of 0.53
fatal vehicle crashes per week. The observed relative frequencies in
Table~\ref{tbl-poisson-crashes} are pretty close to the theoretical
Poisson(0.53) probabilities; see also Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-crashes}.

We have seen two data sets that provide some motivation for the Poisson
pattern, and there are many other examples. Why is the Poisson pattern
so ubiquitous? Later we will explore more deeply the theory and
properties of Poisson distributions. For now just remember that Poisson
distributions are one of the most commonly used probability models for
discrete random variables, especially when counting ``relatively rare''
events.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-poisson-var}{}\label{exm-poisson-var}

Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-pmfs} displays Poisson(\(\mu\)) pmfs for a few
values of \(\mu\). As \(\mu\) increases, does the variance increases,
decrease, or stay the same?

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
As \(\mu\) increases, the variance increases. For Poisson(\(\mu\)) pmf
\(p(x)\)

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(p(x)\) increases for \(x<\mu\):
  \(\frac{p(x)}{p(x-1)} = \frac{\mu}{x}>1\) if \(x<\mu\). The larger
  \(\mu\) is, the longer and slower the probabilities increase for
  \(x<\mu\).
\item
  \(p(x)\) decreases for \(x>\mu\):
  \(\frac{p(x)}{p(x-1)} = \frac{\mu}{x}<1\) if \(x>\mu\). The larger
  \(\mu\) is, the longer and slower the probabilities decrease for
  \(x>\mu\).
\end{itemize}

\label{sol-poisson-var}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

It wasn't a coincidence in Example~\ref{exm-homerun-poisson} that both
\(\textrm{E}(X)\) and \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) were equal to 2.4.

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-poisson-ev-var}{}\label{lem-poisson-ev-var}

If \(X\) has a Poisson(\(\mu\)) distribution then

\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}(X) & = \mu\\
\textrm{Var}(X) & = \mu
\end{align*}

\end{lemma}

For a Poisson distribution, both the mean and variance are equal to
\(\mu\), but remember that the mean is measured in the count units
(e.g., home runs) but the variance is measured in squared units (e.g.,
\(\text{(home runs)}^2\)).

\subsection{Poisson aggregration}\label{poisson-aggregration}

Table~\ref{tbl-poisson-crashes} showed that the number of fatal crashes
in each \emph{week} in SLO County followed, approximately, the Poisson
pattern. What if instead we had looked at crashes in each \emph{month}
or each \emph{year}?

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-poisson-aggregation}{}\label{exm-poisson-aggregation}

Suppose that the number of fatal crashes in SLO County in a week
follows, approximately, a Poisson(0.53) distribution, independently from
week to week. Let \(X\) be the number of fatal crashes in a period of 4
consecutive weeks (close enough to a ``month'').

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  How could you use a spinner to simulate a value of \(X\)?
\item
  What is \(\textrm{E}(X)\)? You should be able to compute it without
  knowing the distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the distribution of \(X\). Does the
  approximate distribution follow (approximately) the Poisson pattern?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Construct a spinner corresponding to Poisson(0.53) distribution; see
  Table~\ref{tbl-poisson-crashes}. Spin the spinner 4 times and sum the
  values; this is one value of \(X\).
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = 4(0.53)=2.12\). If there are 0.53 accidents per week
  on average, there are 2.12 accidents per 4-week period on average.
\item
  See simulation results below. The simulated distribution of \(X\) does
  roughly follow the Poisson pattern with \(\mu = 2.12\).
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-poisson-aggregation}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

Example~\ref{exm-poisson-aggregation} is an example of ``Poisson
aggregation''.

\section{Poisson aggregation}\label{poisson-aggregation}

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(X\) has a Poisson(\(\mu_X\))
distribution, and \(Y\) has a Poisson(\(\mu_Y\)) distribution, then
\(X+Y\) has a Poisson(\(\mu_X+\mu_Y\)) distribution.

If \(X\) has mean \(\mu_X\) and \(Y\) has mean \(\mu_Y\) then linearity
of expected value implies that \(X+Y\) has mean \(\mu_X + \mu_Y\). What
Poisson aggregation says is that if component counts are independent and
each follows a Poisson pattern, then the total count also follows a
Poisson pattern.

\subsection{Poisson paradigm}\label{poisson-paradigm}

This section will provide some background on why the Poisson pattern is
so ubiquitous.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

Suppose that the number of typographical errors on a randomly selected
page of a textbook has a Poisson distribution with parameter
\(\mu = 0.3\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Find the probability that a randomly selected page has no
  typographical errors.
\item
  Find the probability that a randomly selected page has exactly one
  typographical error.
\item
  Find the probability that a randomly selected page has exactly two
  typographical errors.
\item
  Find the probability that a randomly selected page has at least three
  typographical errors.
\item
  Provide a long run interpretation of the parameter \(\mu=0.3\).
\item
  Suppose that each page in the book contains exactly 2000 characters
  and that the probability that any single character is a typo is
  0.00015, independently of all other characters. Let \(X\) be the
  number of characters on a randomly selected page that are typos.
  Identify the distribution of \(X\) and its expected value and
  variance, and compare to a Poisson(0.3) distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
Let \(X\) be the number of typos. Since \(\mu=0.3<1\), the Poisson
pattern implies that the probability mass function will be largest when
\(x=0\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \texttt{Poisson(0.3).pmf(0)} show that\footnotemark{}
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 0) = 0.741\). About 74.1\% of pages have 0 typos.
\item
  By the Poisson pattern,
  \(\textrm{P}(X =1) = (0.3/1)\textrm{P}(X = 0) = (0.3)(0.741) = 0.222\).
  About 22.2\% of pages have exactly 1 typo.
\item
  By the Poisson pattern,
  \(\textrm{P}(X =2) = (0.3/2)\textrm{P}(X = 1) = (0.3/2)(0.222) = 0.033\).
  About 3.3\% of pages have exactly 2 typos.
\item
  Since \(\textrm{P}(X \ge  3) = 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 2)\) we can try
  \texttt{1\ -\ Poisson(0.3).cdf(2)} or use the results of the previous
  parts \[
  \textrm{P}(X \ge  3) = 1 - \textrm{P}(X \le 2) = 1 - (0.741 + 0.222 + 0.033) = 0.0036
  \] About 0.36\% of pages have at least 3 typos.
\item
  There are 0.3 typos per page on average.
\item
  In this case \(X\) has a Binomial(2000, 0.00015) distribution with
  mean \(2000(0.00015) = 0.3\) and variance
  \(2000(0.00015)(1-0.00015) = 0.299955 \approx 0.3 = 2000(0.00015)\).
  See below for a simulation; the Binomial(2000, 0.00015) is very
  similar to the Poisson(0.3) distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-poisson-typos}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\footnotetext{You could also compute \(e^{-0.3} = 0.741\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}

\CommentTok{\# simulate from Binomial(2000, 0.0015)}
\NormalTok{RV(Binomial(}\DecValTok{2000}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00015}\NormalTok{)).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}impulse\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# compare to Poisson(0.3) pmf}
\NormalTok{Poisson(}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
<symbulate.distributions.Poisson object at 0x0000020514C1F590>
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-66-3.png}

\textbf{?@exm-poisson-typos} is an example of the ``Poisson
approximation to the Binomial''.

\begin{lemma}[Poisson approximation to
Binomial]\protect\hypertarget{lem-poisson-approximation-to-binomial}{}\label{lem-poisson-approximation-to-binomial}

If \(X\) counts the number of successes in a Binomial situation where
the number of trials \(n\) is large and the probability of success on
any trial \(p\) is small, then \(X\) has an approximate Poisson
distribution with parameter \(np\).

\end{lemma}

Poisson approximation of Binomial is one way that Poisson distributions
arise, but it is far from the only way. Much of the usefulness of
Poisson models is that they do not require the strict assumptions of the
Binomial situation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-birthday-poisson}{}\label{exm-birthday-poisson}

Recall the birthday problem from Example Example~\ref{exm-birthday}: in
a group of \(n\) people what is the probability that at least two have
the same birthday? (Ignore multiple births and February 29 and assume
that the other 365 days are all equally likely.) We will investigate
this problem using Poisson approximation. Imagine that we have a trial
for each possible \emph{pair} of people in the group, and let
``success'' indicate that the pair shares a birthday.

In each of the following parts, consider both \(n=30\) and general
\(n\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  How many trials are there?
\item
  Do the trials have the same probability of success? If so, what is it?
\item
  Are any \emph{two} trials independent? To answer this questions,
  suppose that three people in the group are Ki-taek, Chung-sook, and
  Ki-jung and consider any \emph{two} of the trials that involve these
  three people.
\item
  Are any \emph{three} trials independent? Consider the three trials
  that involve Ki-taek, Chung-sook, and Ki-jung.
\item
  Let \(X\) be the number of \emph{pairs} that share a birthday. Does
  \(X\) have a Binomial distribution?
\item
  In what way are the trials ``not too dependent''?
\item
  Compute and interpret \(\textrm{E}(X)\).
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the distribution of \(X\) when \(n=30\).
  Does it follow the Poisson pattern?
\item
  Repeat the previous part for a few different values of \(n\).
\item
  Approximate the probability that at least two people share the same
  birthday. Compare to the theoretical values from Example
  Example~\ref{exm-birthday}.
\item
  Using the approximation from the previous part, how large does \(n\)
  need to be for the approximate probability to be at least 0.5?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Each pair is a trial so there are \(\binom{n}{2}\) trials. If \(n=30\)
  there are \(\binom{30}{2}=435\) pairs.
\item
  The probability of success on any trial is 1/365. Whatever the
  birthday of one of the people in the pair, the probability that the
  other has the same birthday is 1/365. Another way to see this: For any
  two people, there are \(365\times 365\) possible pairs of birthdays
  ((Jan 1, Jan 1), (Jan 1, Jan 2), etc.), of which there are 365
  possibilities in which the two share a birthday ((Jan 1, Jan 1), (Jan
  2, Jan 2), etc.), so the probability is \(\frac{365}{365\times 365}\).
\item
  Yes, any \emph{two} trials are independent. Let \(A\) be the event
  that Ki-taek and Chung-sook share a birthday, and let \(B\) be the
  event that Ki-taek and Ki-jung share a birthday. Then
  \(\textrm{P}(A)=1/365\) and \(\textrm{P}(B)=1/365\). The event
  \(A\cap B\) is the event that all three share a birthday.
  \(\textrm{P}(A\cap B) =(1/365)^2\), since whatever the birthday of one
  of the people, the probability that the other two people both have
  that birthday is \((1/365)^2\). Another way: There are \(365^3\)
  possible triples of birthdays for the three people ((Jan 1 for
  Ki-taek, Jan 1 for Ki-jung, Jan 2 for Chung-sook), etc) of which there
  are 365 possibilities in which all three share a birthday (e.g., (Jan
  1, Jan 1, Jan 1), etc). Therefore \[
  \textrm{P}(A\cap B) = \frac{365}{365^3} =    \left(\frac{1}{365}\right)\left(\frac{1}{365}\right) = \textrm{P}(A)\textrm{P}(B),
  \] so \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
\item
  No, not every set of three trials is independent. Let \(A\) be the
  event that Ki-taek and Chung-sook share a birthday, let \(B\) be the
  event that Ki-taek and Ki-jung share a birthday, and let \(C\) be the
  event that Chung-sook and Ki-jung share a birthday. Then
  \(\textrm{P}(A)=\textrm{P}(B)=\textrm{P}(C)=1/365\). The event
  \(A \cap B\cap C\) is the event that all three people share the same
  birthday, which has probability \(\frac{1}{365^2}\) as in the previous
  part. Therefore, \[
    \textrm{P}(A\cap B\cap B) = \frac{365}{365^3} \neq \left(\frac{1}{365}\right)\left(\frac{1}{365}\right)\left(\frac{1}{365}\right) = \textrm{P}(A)\textrm{P}(B)\textrm{P}(C)
  \] So these three trials are not independent. Alternatively, if \(A\)
  and \(B\) are both true, then \(C\) must also be true so
  \(\textrm{P}(C|A\cap B)=1 \neq 1/365 =\textrm{P}(C)\). However, there
  are many sets of three trials that are independent. In particular, any
  three trials involving six distinct people are independent.
\item
  Since the trials are not independent, \(X\) does not have a Binomial
  distribution.
\item
  Any two trials are independent. Many sets of three trials are
  independent. Many sets of four trials are independent (e.g., any set
  involving 8 distinct people), etc. So generally, information on
  multiple events is required to change the conditional probabilities of
  other events. In this way, the trials are ``not too dependent''.
\item
  There are \(\binom{n}{2}\) trials and the probability of success on
  each trial is 1/365, so \[
  \textrm{E}(X) = \binom{n}{2}\left(\frac{1}{365}\right)  
  \] For \(n=30\):
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = \binom{30}{2}\left(\frac{1}{365}\right) = 435/365 = 1.19\).
  Over many groups of 30 people, we expect 1.19 pairs of people to share
  a birthday per group on average.

  Remember, the ``number of trials \(\times\) probability of success''
  formula works regardless of whether the trials are independent (as
  long as the probability of success is the same for all trials).
\item
  See the simulation results for \(n=30\) below. The simulated
  distribution follows approximately the Poisson pattern with
  \(\mu = 1.19\).
\item
  You can do a sensivity analysis to see that the distribution of \(X\)
  follows approximately the Poisson pattern, with
  \(\mu = \binom{n}{2}/365\) (which depends on \(n\).) We only display
  the results for \(n=50\) in which case
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = \binom{50}{2}/365 = 3.36\).
\item
  The probability that at least two people share the same birthday is
  \(1-\textrm{P}(X=0)\). When \(n=30\), \(X\) has an approximate
  Poisson(1.19) distribution, so \(1-Poisson(1.19).pmf(0)\) yields
  0.696, which is pretty close to the theoretical value of 0.706 from
  Example~\ref{exm-birthday}. We could also compute
  \(1 - \textrm{P}(X=0) \approx 1 - e^{-1.19}\).

  For a general \(n\) we approximate \(1-\textrm{P}(X=0)\) as
  \texttt{1\ -\ Poisson(-math.comb(n,\ 2)\ /\ 365).pmf(0)} (or
  \(1 - \textrm{P}(X=0) \approx 1 - e^{-\binom{n}{2}/365}\)).
  Figure~\ref{fig-birthday-poisson} plots the theoretical probability
  and the approximate probability for different values of \(n\); the
  approximation seems to work pretty well.
\item
  We can try different values of \texttt{n} in
  \texttt{1\ -\ Poisson(-math.comb(n,\ 2)\ /\ 365).pmf(0)} to find that
  the smallest value of \(n\) for which the approximate probability
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\) is at least 0.5 is \(n=23\), in which case
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = \binom{23}{2}/365 = 253/365 = 0.693\) and the
  approximate \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\) is \(1-e^{-0.693}=0.500\). The
  theoretical probability for \(n=23\) is 0.507.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-birthday-poisson}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ itertools}

\CommentTok{\# count\_matching\_pairs takes as an input a list of birthdays}
\CommentTok{\# returns as output the number of pairs that share a birthday}
\CommentTok{\# Note the 2 in itertools.combinations is for pairs}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_matching\_pairs(outcome):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{([}\DecValTok{1} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ itertools.combinations(outcome, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\ControlFlowTok{if} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(i)) }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
    
\CommentTok{\# 2 pairs have a match in the following: (0, 1), (2, 3)}
\NormalTok{count\_matching\_pairs((}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
2
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# 6 pairs have a match in the following:}
\CommentTok{\# (0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}
\NormalTok{count\_matching\_pairs((}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
6
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{365}\NormalTok{)), size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_matching\_pairs)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}


\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ math}

\CommentTok{\# theoretical E(X)}
\NormalTok{mu }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ math.comb(n, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{365}
\NormalTok{mu}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
1.1917808219178083
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# simulation{-}based approximation of E(X)}
\NormalTok{x.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
1.1945
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# simulation{-}based approximation of P(X \textgreater{}= 1)}
\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ x.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{10000}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

0.7034
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}

\CommentTok{\# plot the simulate values}
\NormalTok{x.plot()}

\CommentTok{\# overlay Poisson patterm}
\NormalTok{Poisson(mu).plot()}

\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{50}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{365}\NormalTok{)), size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{simulation-marginal-discrete_files/figure-pdf/fig-birthday-poisson-9.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-birthday-poisson}Probability of at least one
birthday match as a function of the number of people in the room, along
with the Poisson approximation. When there are at least 23 people, the
probability of at least one birthday match is at least 0.5.}

\end{figure}%

We already computed the probability that at least two people share a
birthday, so the Poisson approximation in
Example~\ref{exm-birthday-poisson} isn't that exciting. But what about
the probability that at least \emph{three} people share a birthday? This
is much harder to solve analytically, but we can apply Poisson
approximation in much the same was as we did in
Example~\ref{exm-birthday-poisson}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-poisson-birthday-three}{}\label{exm-poisson-birthday-three}

Under the assumptions of the birthday problem, consider the probability
that at least \emph{three} people in a group of \(n\) people share a
birthday. How large does \(n\) need to be for the probability to be
greater than 0.5? We'll use Poisson approximation to address these
questions.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is an appropriate random variable \(X\)? Hint: consider what we
  did in Example~\ref{exm-birthday-poisson}.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{E}(X)\) for both \(n=30\) and general \(n\).
\item
  Why might it be reasonable to assume \(X\) has a Poisson distribution?
\item
  Assume that \(X\) has a Poisson distribution and approximate the
  probability that at least three people share a birthday when \(n=30\).
\item
  Try different values of \(n\) and find the \(n\) for which the
  probability is at least \(n\).
\item
  Use simulation to approximate the distribution of \(X\) for a few
  values of \(n\), including the value you found in the previous part.
  Does the distribution of \(X\) follow (approximately) the Poisson
  pattern?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  We can consider any three people as a trial. Let \(X\) be the number
  of trio in which all three people share a birthday.
\item
  There are \(\binom{n}{3}\) trios of people; e.g., there are
  \(\binom{30}{3} = 4060\) trios when \(n=30\). We showed in
  Example~\ref{exm-birthday-poisson} that the probability that any three
  people share a birthday is \(\frac{1}{365^2}\). Therefore,
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = \binom{n}{3}\left(\frac{1}{365^2}\right)\). When
  \(n=30\), \(\textrm{E}(X) = (4060)/365^2 = 0.03\). Over many groups of
  30 people, we would only expect 0.03 trios to share a birthday per
  group on average.
\item
  We are counting successes when the number of trials is large and the
  probability of success on any trial is small, so it might be
  reasonable to assume \(X\) has an approximate Poisson distribution.
\item
  The probability that at least three people share the same birthday is
  \(1-\textrm{P}(X=0)\). When \(n=30\), \(X\) has an approximate
  Poisson(0.03) distribution, so \(1-Poisson(0.03).pmf(0)\) yields 0.03;
  in only 3\% of groups of 30 people do at least three people share a
  birthday. We could also compute
  \(1 - \textrm{P}(X=0) \approx 1 - e^{-0.03}\).

  For a general \(n\) we approximate \(1-\textrm{P}(X=0)\) as
  \texttt{1\ -\ Poisson(-math.comb(n,\ 3)\ /\ 365**2).pmf(0)} (or
  \(1 - \textrm{P}(X=0) \approx 1 - e^{-\binom{n}{3}/365^2}\)).
\item
  We can try different values of \texttt{n} in
  \texttt{1\ -\ Poisson(-math.comb(n,\ 2)\ /\ 365).pmf(0)} to find that
  the smallest value of \(n\) for which the approximate probability
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\) is at least 0.5 is \(n=84\), in which case,
  \(\binom{84}{3} = 95284\),
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = \binom{84}{3}/365^2 = 0.715\) and the approximate
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 1)\) is \(1-e^{-0.715}=0.511\).
\item
  Therefore, the probability that at least three people share a birthday
  is \[
  1 - \textrm{P}(X=0) \approx   1-\exp\left(-\binom{n}{3}\left(\frac{1}{365^2}\right)\right)
  \] The smallest \(n\) for which this probability is greater than 0.5
  is \(n=84\). For \(n\ge 124\), the probability is at least 0.9.
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-poisson-birthday-three}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ itertools}

\CommentTok{\# count\_matching\_pairs takes as an input a list of birthdays}
\CommentTok{\# returns as output the number of trios that share a birthday}
\CommentTok{\# Note the 3 in itertools.combinations is for trios}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_matching\_trios(outcome):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{([}\DecValTok{1} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ itertools.combinations(outcome, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) }\ControlFlowTok{if} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(i)) }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
    
\CommentTok{\# 0 trios have a match in the following}
\NormalTok{count\_matching\_trios((}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# 4 trios have a match in the following:}
\CommentTok{\# (0, 1, 2), (0, 1, 3), (0, 2, 3), (1, 2, 3)}
\NormalTok{count\_matching\_trios((}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
4
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{84}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{365}\NormalTok{)), size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n, replace }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_matching\_trios)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

Example~\ref{exm-birthday-poisson} and
\textbf{?@exm-birthday-poisson-three} illustrate that a Poisson
approximation for the number of successes can be applied when the number
of trials is large and the probability of success is small even when the
trials are not independent. In fact, a Poisson approximation often
applies even when the probability of success isn't the same for every
trial, as is the case for Example~\ref{exm-poisson-hr-intro} (see
Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-hr}) and
Example~\ref{exm-poisson-accidents-intro} (see
Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-crashes}).

\begin{lemma}[Poisson
paradigm]\protect\hypertarget{lem-poisson-paradigm}{}\label{lem-poisson-paradigm}

Let \(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n\) be a collection of \(n\) events. Suppose
event \(i\) occurs with marginal probability \(p_i=\textrm{P}(A_i)\).
Let
\(N = \textrm{I}_{A_i} + \textrm{I}_{A_2} + \cdots + \textrm{I}_{A_n}\)
be the random variable which counts the number of the events in the
collection which occur. Suppose

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(n\) is ``large'',
\item
  \(p_1, \ldots, p_n\) are ``comparably small'', and
\item
  the events \(A_1, \ldots, A_n\) are ``not too dependent'',
\end{itemize}

Then \(N\) has an approximate Poisson distribution with parameter
\(\textrm{E}(N) = p_1 + \cdots + p_n\).

\end{lemma}

We are leaving the terms ``large'', ``comparably small'', and ``not too
dependent'' undefined. There are many different versions of Poisson
approximations which make these ideas more precise. We only remark that
Poisson approximation holds in a wide variety of situations.

The individual event probabilities \(p_i\) can be different, but they
must be ``comparably small''. If one \(p_i\) is much greater than the
others, then the count random variable \(N\) is dominated by whether
event \(A_i\) occurs or not. Also, as long as \(\textrm{E}(N)\) is
available, it is not necessary to know the individual \(p_i\).

As long as the \(p_i\) are comparably small, we only need to know the
sum \(p_1 +\cdots +p_n\) and not the individual \(p_i\)'s' to apply the
Poisson approximation. We can estimate
\(\textrm{E}(N) = p_1+\cdots+p_n\) directly by collecting data on
observed counts (like in Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-hr} and
Figure~\ref{fig-poisson-crashes}) without having to estimate individual
\(p_i\)'s.'

Even though \(n\) is a constant in the above statement of the Poisson
paradigm, there are other versions in which the number of events is
random and unknown.

Some advantages for using a Poisson model rather than a Binomial (or
Negative Binomial) model

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  In a Poisson model, the number of trials doesn't need to be specified;
  it can be unknown or random (e.g.~the number of automobiles on a
  highway varies from day to day). The number of trials just has to be
  ``large'' (though what constitutes large depends on the situation;
  \(n\) didn't have to be very large in the matching problem for the
  Poisson approximation to kick in.)

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    In a Binomial model, the number of trials must be fixed and known
    (or fixed and known successed for Negative Binomial).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  In a Poisson model, the probability of success does not need to be the
  same for all trials, and the probability of success for individual
  trials does not need to be known or estimated. The only requirement is
  that the probability of success is ``comparably small'' for all
  trials.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    In a Binomial (or Negative Binomial) model, the probability of
    success must be the same for all trials and must be fixed and known.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Fitting a Poisson model to data only requires data on total counts, so
  that the average number of successes can be estimated.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Fitting a Binomial model to data requires results from individual
    trials so that the probability of success can be estimated. (For
    example, you would need to know both the total number of automobiles
    on the road and the number that got into accidents.)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  In a Poisson model, the trials are not required to be strictly
  independent as long as the trials are ``not too dependent''.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    In a Binomial (or Negative Binomial) model, the trials must be
    independent.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Exercises}\label{exercises-28}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-crashes-poisson}{}\label{exr-crashes-poisson}

Let \(X\) be the number of vehicles crashes involving fatalities that
occur in San Luis Obispo County in a randomly selected week. Assume that
\(X\) follows a Poisson(0.53) distribution.

\end{exercise}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What are the possible values of \(X\)?
\item
  Interpret the parameter 0.53 in context.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 0.53)\) without using software.
\item
  Identify the most likely value of \(X\) without doing any
  computations.
\item
  Use Symbulate to compute \(\textrm{P}(X \le 6)\) and interpret the
  value in context.
\item
  Use the ``Poisson pattern'' and normalization to find, by hand,
  \(\textrm{P}(X = x)\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\). Hint: assume
  that 0 represents 100000 ``units'', use the Poisson pattern to find
  the ``units'' corresponding to each of \(1, \ldots, 6\), then divide
  by the total number of ``units''. (Technically, the values
  \(7, 8, 9, \ldots\) have non-zero probability, but the previous part
  shows that the values \(0, \ldots, 6\) account for almost 100\% of the
  probability.) Then use Symbulate to check your values, and display
  them in a table and plot.
\item
  Interpret \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\) in context.
\item
  Construct a spinner to simulate values of \(X\).
\item
  Use Symbulate to simulate many values of \(X\) and compare the
  simulated distribution to the theoretical Poisson distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Hypergeometric
distributions}\label{hypergeometric-distributions}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, leftrule=.75mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacityback=0, colback=white, left=2mm, toprule=.15mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, bottomrule=.15mm]

\begin{example}[]\protect\hypertarget{exm-hyper-capture}{}\label{exm-hyper-capture}

Recall Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture}. Now we'll assume the sampling
is conducted \emph{without replacement}.

You first capture a sample of \(N_1\) butterflies, selected randomly
without replacement, and tag them and release them. At a later date, you
then capture a second sample of \(n\) butterflies, selected randomly
\textbf{\emph{without} replacement}. Let \(X\) be the number of
butterflies in the second sample that have tags (because they were also
caught in the first sample). (Assume that the tagging has no effect on
behavior, so that selection in the first sample is independent of
selection in the second sample.)

In practice, \(N\) is unknown. But let's start with a simpler, but
unrealistic, example where there are \(N=52\) butterflies, \(N_1 = 13\)
are tagged in the first sample, and \(n=5\) is the size of the second
sample.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What are the possible values of \(X\)?
\item
  Does \(X\) has a Binomial distribution? Hint: be careful about why.
\item
  Describe how you could use a tactile simulation to simulate a single
  value of \(X\).
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate
  \(\textrm{P}(X=0)\).
\item
  Describe in words how you could use simulation to approximate the
  distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Write and run Symbulate code to approximate \(\textrm{P}(X=0)\) and
  the distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Construct a table, plot, and spinner representing the approximate
  distribution of \(X\).
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\). Compare to your simulated value.
\item
  Interpret in context \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\).
\item
  Suggest a shortcut formula for \(\textrm{E}(X)\). Does it seem
  consistent with the simulation results?
\item
  Would \(\textrm{Var}(X)\) be greater than, less than, or equal to the
  variance from Example~\ref{exm-binomial-capture} (where the sampling
  was with replacement)?
\end{enumerate}

\end{example}

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, rightrule=.15mm, opacitybacktitle=0.6, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, left=2mm, titlerule=0mm, breakable, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, toptitle=1mm, leftrule=.75mm, title={Solution (click to expand)}, opacityback=0, colback=white, toprule=.15mm, coltitle=black, bottomtitle=1mm]

\begin{refsolution}
\leavevmode

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) can take values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
\item
  No.~ \(X\) satifies all the conditions of the Binomial situation
  except for one: When sampling without replacement the individual
  selections are not independent. For example, the conditional
  probability that the second butterfly is tagged given that the first
  is tagged is 12/51, but the conditional probability that the second
  butterfly is tagged given that the first is not tagged is 13/51. (The
  unconditional probability of success is still 13/52 on each trial.)
\item
  We could use a deck of 52 cards, with 13 labeled ``tagged'' (say the
  clubs) and the others not. Shuffle the deck and draw 5 cards
  \emph{without} replacement, and let \(X\) be the number of cards out
  of the 5 drawn that say ``tagged''.
\item
  Repeat the steps in part 2 many times to simulate many values of
  \(X\), say 10000. Count the number of repetitions that result in
  \(X=0\) and divide by the total number of repetitions (10000); this
  relative frequency approximates \(\textrm{P}(X = 0)\).
\item
  Simulate many values of \(X\) (say 10000) and find the simulated
  relative frequency of each possible value: \(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\).
\item
  See Symbulate code below.
\item
  Compare to Table~\ref{tbl-hyper-capture} and
  Figure~\ref{fig-hyper-capture}. These represent the theoretical
  distribution of \(X\), but your simulation-based approximation should
  be similar (see our Symbulate output below).
\item
  We can use the multiplication rule (just not for independent events).
  The probability that the first butterfly selected is not tagged is
  39/52. Given that the first is not tagged, the conditional probability
  that the second butterfly selected is not tagged is \(38/51\). Given
  that the first two butterflies selected are not tagged, the
  conditional probability that the third butterfly selected is not
  tagged is \(37/50\). And so on. The probability that none of the
  butterflies selected are tagged is \[
  \textrm{P}(X = 0) = \left(\frac{39}{52}\right)\left(\frac{38}{51}\right)\left(\frac{37}{50}\right)\left(\frac{36}{49}\right)\left(\frac{35}{48}\right) = 0.2215
  \]
\item
  In this scenario, 22.2\% of possible \emph{samples} of 5 butterflies
  contain 0 tagged butterflies.
\item
  Since the proportion of butterflies in the population that are tagged
  is 13/52, we expect the proportion in the sample that are tagged to
  also be 13/52; in other words we expect \((13/52)(5) = 1.25\)
  butterflies in the sample to be tagged.
\item
  The variance be greater if the sampling was with replacement. Sampling
  without replacement, each selection conditionally restricts the number
  of possibilities, allowing for less variability in the number of
  successes in the sample. For example, sampling with replacement yields
  a slightly larger probability for \(\{X=5\}\) than sampling without
  replacement does. (As a more extreme example, suppose instead that the
  sample size was \(n=20\). Then, the largest possible value of \(X\) is
  13 when sampling without replacement but 20 when sampling with
  replacement.)
\end{enumerate}

\label{sol-hyper-capture}

\end{refsolution}

\end{tcolorbox}

The following Symbulate code implements the simulation in
Example~\ref{exm-hyper-capture}. We define a box model with 13 tickets
labeled 1 (``tagged'') and 39 labeled 0 (``not tagged''), and select 5
\emph{without} replacement.

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}\OperatorTok{;}
\NormalTok{x.plot()}\OperatorTok{;} \CommentTok{\# plot the simulated values}
\NormalTok{Hypergeometric(N1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, N0 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{39}\NormalTok{, n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{).plot()}\OperatorTok{;} \CommentTok{\# overlay theoretical pmf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The random variable \(X\) in Example~\ref{exm-hyper-capture} has a
Hypergeometric distribution with parameters \(n=5\), \(N_1=13\), and
\(N_0=39\).

\begin{definition}[]\protect\hypertarget{def-hypergeometric-story}{}\label{def-hypergeometric-story}

Imagine a box containing \(N=N_1+N_0\) tickets, \(N_1\) of which are
labeled 1 (``success'') and \(N_0\) of which are labeled 0
(``failure''). Randomly select \(n\) tickets from the box \emph{without
replacement} and let \(X\) be the number of tickets in the sample that
are labeled 1 (success). The distribution of \(X\) is defined to be the
\textbf{Hypergeometric(\(n\), \(N_1\), \(N_0\))} distribution.

\end{definition}

A Hypergeometric distribution is specified by three parameters:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(n\) (an integer): the sample size
\item
  \(N_1\): the number of successes in the population
\item
  \(N_0\): the number of failures in the population (so that the
  population size is \(N_1+N_0\))
\end{itemize}

We can use Symbulate to compute the pmf for
Example~\ref{exm-hyper-capture}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hypergeometric(n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, N1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, N0 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{).pmf(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
np.float64(0.14804310833806014)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hypergeometric(n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, N1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{, N0 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{).pmf([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{])}

The population size is \(N=N_1+N_0\) and the sample size is \(n\). The
population proportion of success is \(p=N_1/N\). The random variable
\(X\) counts the number of successes in the sample, and so \(X/n\) is
the sample proportion of success. However, since the selections are made
without replacement, the draws are not independent, and it is not enough
to just specify \(p\) to determine the distribution of \(X\) (or
\(X/n\)).

The largest possible value of \(X\) is \(\min(n, N_1)\), since there
can't be more successes in the sample than in the population. The
smallest possible value of \(X\) is \(\max(0, n-N_0)\) since there can't
be more failures in the sample than in the population (that is,
\(n-X\le N_0\)). Often \(N_0\) and \(N_1\) are large relative to \(n\)
in which case \(X\) takes values \(0, 1,\ldots, n\).

\begin{lemma}[]\protect\hypertarget{lem-hyper-ev-var}{}\label{lem-hyper-ev-var}

If \(X\) has a Hypergeometric(\(n\), \(N_1\), \(N_0\)) distribution,
with \(p=\frac{N_1}{N_1+N_0}\) distribution then

\begin{align*}
\textrm{E}(X) & = np\\
\textrm{Var}(X) & = np(1-p)\frac{N-n}{N-1}
\end{align*}

\end{lemma}

The quantity \(\frac{N-n}{N-1}<1\) which appears in the variance formula
is called the \emph{finite population correction}.\\
We will investigate this factor in more detail later.

require the weakest assumptions.
