\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-collector3-a}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-probspace-collector3-a}

The latest series of collectible Lego Minifigures contains 3 different
Minifigure prizes (labeled 1, 2, 3). Each package contains a single
unknown prize. Suppose we only buy 3 packages and we consider as our
sample space outcome the results of just these 3 packages (prize in
package 1, prize in package 2, prize in package 3). For example, 323 (or
(3, 2, 3)) represents prize 3 in the first package, prize 2 in the
second package, prize 3 in the third package. Suppose that each package
is equally likely to contain any of the 3 prizes, regardless of the
contents of other packages, so that there are 27 equally likely
outcomes, and let \(\textrm{P}\) be the corresponding probability
measure.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(A_1\) be the event that prize 1 is obtained---that is, \emph{at
  least one} of the packages contains prize 1---and define \(A_2, A_3\)
  similarly for prize 2, 3.
\item
  Let \(B_1\) be the event that \emph{only} prize 1 is obtained---that
  is, \emph{all three} packages contain prize 1---and define
  \(B_2, B_3\) similarly for prize 2, 3.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(A_1)\)
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(B_1)\)
\item
  Interpret the values from parts 1 and 2 as long run relative
  frequencies.
\item
  Interpret the values from parts 1 and 2 as relative likelihoods.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3)\)
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3)\)
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(B_1 \cap B_2 \cap B_3)\)
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{P}(B_1 \cup B_2 \cup B_3)\)
\item
  \(A_1^c = \{222, 223, 232, 322, 233, 323, 332, 333\}\) is the event
  that none of the boxes contain prize 1, so \(A_1\) consists of the
  \(27-8 = 19\) other outcomes. Since the outcomes are equally likely,
  \(\text{P}(A_1) = 18/27=0.667\).
\item
  There is only one outcome that satisfies \(B_1\) so
  \(\text{P}(B_1) = 1/27 = 0.037\).
\item
  Over many sets of 3 boxes, about 66.7\% of sets of 3 boxes will
  contain at least one prize 1, and about 3.7\% of sets of 3 boxes will
  contain only prize 1.
\item
  It is 18 times more likely to obtain at least one prize 1 than it is
  to obtain only prize 1. Also, it is 2 times more likely to obtain at
  least one prize 1 than to not obtain it (18/9), and it is 26 times
  less likely to obtain only prize 1 than it is to obtain any other
  collection of prizes.
\item
  \(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3 = \{123, 132, 213, 231, 312, 321\}\) is the
  event that at least one of each prize is obtained (that is, a complete
  set of prizes) so \(\textrm{P}(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3) = 6/27 = 0.222\)
\item
  \(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 = \Omega\), the set of all possible outcomes;
  you have to get at least 1 of one of the prizes so
  \(\textrm{P}(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3) = 1\)
\item
  \(B_1 \cap B_2 \cap B_3=\emptyset\); you can't get only prize 1 and
  only prize 2, so \(\textrm{P}(B_1 \cap B_2 \cap B_3) = 0\)
\item
  \(B_1 \cup B_2 \cup B_3 = \{111, 222, 333\}\) is the event you only
  obtain one of the prizes (in every box), so
  \(\textrm{P}(B_1 \cup B_2 \cup B_3) = 3/27 = 0.111\)
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-dartboard-b}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-probspace-dartboard-b}

Since the dart lands uniformly at random anywhere on the dartboard,
probabilities are computed as the ratio between the area corresponding
to the event of interest divided by the area of the total dartboard
(\(12^2\pi\))

See Figure~\ref{fig-event-dartboard}. Find the area of the shaded pieces
by subtracting areas of circles.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\text{P}(X \le 1) = \frac{1^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = 1/144 = 0.00694\)
\item
  \(\text{P}(1 < X < 2) = \frac{2^2\pi - 1^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = 3/144 = 0.021\)
\item
  \(\text{P}(X > 11) = 1 - \frac{11^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = 1 - (11/12)^2 = 0.160\)
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-dartboard-c}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-probspace-dartboard-c}

Since the dart lands uniformly at random anywhere on the dartboard,
probabilities are computed as the ratio between the area corresponding
to the event of interest divided by the area of the total dartboard
(\(12^2\pi\))

Find the area of the events of interest by finding areas of
corresponding circles and subtracting as needed.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \le 0.1) = \frac{0.1^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = (0.1/12)^2 = 0.0000694\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \le 0.01) = \frac{0.01^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = (0.01/12)^2 = 0.000000694\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 0) = 0\), the single point has no area
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 11.9) = 1 - \frac{11.9^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = 1 - (11.9/12)^2 = 0.0166\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X \ge 11.99) = 1 - \frac{11.99^2\pi}{12^2\pi} = 1 - (11.99/12)^2 = 0.00166\)
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 12) = 0\), the circle representing the outside edge
  has no area
\item
  Well, both of these events---the dart lands exactly in the center and
  the darts lands exactly on the edge---have 0 probability. However for
  practical purposes we would never be interested in probabilities like
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 0.000000000\ldots)\) or
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 12.000000000\ldots)\) with infinite precision.
\item
  However we define ``close to''---within 1 inch or within 0.1 inch or
  within 0.01 inch, etc---the dart is more likely to land close to the
  edge than close to the center.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-distribution-intro-collector3}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-distribution-intro-collector3}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Construct a two-way table representing the \emph{joint distribution}
  of \(X\) and \(Y\).
\item
  Sketch a plot representing the joint distribution of \(X\) and \(Y\).
\item
  Identify the \emph{marginal} distribution of \(X\), and sketch a plot
  of it.
\item
  Identify the \emph{marginal} distribution of \(Y\), and sketch a plot
  of it.
\item
  Compute and interpret \(\text{E}(X)\).
\item
  Compute and interpret \(\text{E}(Y)\).
\item
  One dimension will have possible values of \(x\), the other possible
  values of \(y\). The interior cells should contain the probability of
  each \((x, y)\) pair.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  & \(y\) & & & & \\
  \(x\) & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & Total \\
  1 & 2/27 & 0 & 0 & 1/27 & 3/27 \\
  2 & 6/27 & 6/27 & 6/27 & 0 & 18/27 \\
  3 & 0 & 6/27 & 0 & 0 & 6/27 \\
  Total & 8/27 & 12/27 & 6/27 & 1/27 & 1 \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  Make a tile plot with color or shading representing probability; see
  Figure~\ref{fig-distribution-intro-collector3}
\item
  The possible values of \(X\) are in the leftmost column (1, 2, 3) and
  the probabilities are in the Total column. See
  Figure~\ref{fig-distribution-intro-collector3-X}.
\item
  The possible values of \(Y\) are in the top row (0, 1, 2, 3) and the
  probabilities are in the Total row. See
  Figure~\ref{fig-distribution-intro-collector3-Y}.
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(X) = 1\times (3/27) + 2 \times (18/27) + 3 \times (6/ 27) = 2.11\).
  Over many sets of 3 boxes, we expect 2.11 distinct prizes on average.
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(Y) = 0\times (8/27) + 1\times (12/27) + 2 \times (6/27) + 3 \times (1/ 27) = 1\).
  Over many sets of 3 boxes, we expect 1 box containing prize 1 on
  average.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-distribution-conditional-collector3}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-distribution-conditional-collector3}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Each row of the table below represents a different conditional
  distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\). For example, the row for \(x=1\)
  represents the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=1\): Given
  \(X=1\), \(Y\) is 0 with probability 2/3 and 3 with probability 1/3.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  & \(y\) & & & & \\
  & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & Total \\
  \(x\) & & & & & \\
  1 & 2/3 & 0 & 0 & 1/3 & 1 \\
  2 & 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 & 0 & 1 \\
  3 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  Take expected values according to each conditional distribution. In
  general, \(\text{E}(Y|X=x)\) depends on \(x\), but in this case
  \(\text{E}(Y|X=x) = 1\) for all values of \(x\).; regardless of how
  many distinct prizez people obtain in their, the average number of
  prize 1s obtains is 1.

  \begin{align*}
  x & \quad \text{E}(Y|X=x)\\
  1 & \quad 0(2/3) + 3(1/3) = 1\\
  2 & \quad 0(1/3) + 1(1/3) + 2(1/3) = 1\\
  3 & \quad 1(1) = 1
  \end{align*}
\item
  Each column of the table below represents a different conditional
  distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y\). For example, the column for
  \(y=1\) represents the conditional distribution of \(X\) given
  \(Y=1\): Given \(Y=1\), \(X\) is 1 with probability 1/4 and 2 with
  probability 3/4.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  & \(y\) & & & \\
  & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\
  \(x\) & & & & \\
  1 & 1/4 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
  2 & 3/4 & 1/2 & 1 & 0 \\
  3 & 0 & 1/2 & 0 & 0 \\
  Total & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  Take expected values according to each conditional distribution. For
  example, \(\text{E}(X|Y = 0) = 1.75\); among the people who never get
  prize 1 in their 3 boxes, the average number of distinct prizes they
  obtain is 1.75.

  \begin{align*}
  y & \quad \text{E}(X|Y=y)\\
  0 & \quad 1(1/4) + 2(3/4) = 1.75\\
  1 & \quad 2(1/2) + 3(1/2) = 2.5\\
  2 & \quad 2(1) = 2\\
  3 & \quad 1(1) = 1
  \end{align*}
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-ltp-multiple-choice}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-ltp-multiple-choice}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Suppose there are 1000 questions on the test. (That's a long test! But
  remember, 1000 is just a convenient round number.) We can classify
  each question by its type (know, eliminate, guess) and whether we
  answer it correctly or not. The probability that we answer a question
  correctly is 1 given that we know it, 0.5 given that we can eliminate
  two choices, or 0.25 given that we guess randomly.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrrrr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  & Know & Eliminate & Guess & Total \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  Correct & 700 & 100 & 25 & 825 \\
  Incorrect & 0 & 100 & 75 & 175 \\
  Total & 700 & 200 & 100 & 1000 \\
  \end{longtable}

  The probability that we answer a randomly selected question correctly
  is 825/1000 = 0.825.
\item
  The overall probability of answering a question correctly is closer to
  1 than 0.5 or 0.25. To construct the table and obtain the value 0.825,
  we basically did the following calculation

  \[
   0.825 = (1)(0.7) + (0.5)(0.2) + (0.25)(0.1)
   \]

  We see that the overall probability, 0.825, is a weighted average of
  the case-by-case probabilities 1, 0.5, and 0.25, where 1 gets the most
  weight in the average because there is a higher percentage of
  questions that we know.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-ltp-rats}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-ltp-rats}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Most people produce a sequence that has 30 G's and 10 R's, or close to
  those proportions, because they are trying to generate a sequence for
  which each outcome has a 75\% chance for G and a 25\% chance for R.
  That is, they use a strategy in which they predict G with probability
  0.75, and R with probability 0.25.
\item
  There are two cases: the true flash is either green (with probability
  0.75) or red (with probability 0.25). Given that the flash is green,
  your probability of correctly predicting it is 0.75 (because your
  probability of guessing ``G'' is 0.75). Given that the flash is red,
  your probability of correctly predicting it is 0.25 (because your
  probability of guessing ``R'' is 0.25). Use the law of total
  probability to find the probability that your prediction is correct:
  \((0.75)(0.75) + (0.25)(0.25) = 0.625\).
\item
  Just pick G every time! Picking green every time has a 0.75
  probability of correctly predicting any flash. When events are
  \emph{independent}, trying to guess the pattern doesn't help.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-bayes-elisa}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-bayes-elisa}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  We don't know what you guessed, but from experience many people guess
  80-100\%. Afterall, the test is correct for most of people who carry
  HIV, and also correct for most people who don't carry HIV, so it seems
  like the test is correct most of the time. But this argument ignores
  one important piece of information that has a huge impact on the
  results: most people do not carry HIV.
\item
  Let \(H\) denote the event that the person carries HIV (hypothesis),
  and let \(E\) denote the event that the test is positive (evidence).
  Therefore, \(H^c\) is the event that the person does not carry HIV,
  another hypothesis. We are given
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  prior probability: \(P(H) = 0.005\)
\item
  likelihood of testing positive, if the person carries HIV:
  \(P(E|H) = 0.977\)
\item
  \(P(E^c|H^c) = 0.926\)
\item
  likelihood of testing positive, if the person does not carry HIV:
  \(P(E|H^c) = 1-P(E^c|H^c) = 1-0.926 = 0.074\)
\item
  We want to find the posterior probability \(P(H|E)\).
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Assuming 1000000 Americans

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}
    >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2899}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2319}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3478}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1304}}@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
  \end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
  Tests positive
  \end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
  Does not test positive
  \end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
  Total
  \end{minipage} \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  Carries HIV & 4885 & 115 & 5000 \\
  Does not carry HIV & 73630 & 921370 & 995000 \\
  Total & 78515 & 921485 & 1000000 \\
  \end{longtable}

  Among the 78515 who test positive, 4885 carry HIV, so the probability
  that an American who tests positive actually carries HIV is 4885/78515
  = 0.062.
\item
  See Table~\ref{tbl-bayes-elisa}.
\item
  The result says that only 6.2\% \emph{of Americans who test positive}
  actually carry HIV. It is true that the test is correct for most
  Americans with HIV (4885 out of 5000) and incorrect only for a small
  proportion of Americans who do not carry HIV (73630 out of 995000).
  But since so few Americans carry HIV, the sheer \emph{number} of false
  positives (73630) swamps the \emph{number} of true positives (4885).
\item
  Prior to observing the test result, the prior probability that an
  American carries HIV is \(P(H) = 0.005\). The posterior probability
  that an American carries HIV given a positive test result is
  \(P(H|E)=0.062\). \[
    \frac{P(H|E)}{P(H)} = \frac{0.062}{0.005} =  12.44
  \] An American who tests positive is about 12.4 times more likely to
  carry HIV than an American whom the test result is not known.\\
  So while 0.067 is still small in absolute terms, the posterior
  probability is much larger relative to the prior probability.
\item
  In this risk group
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a person is 19 times more likely to not have HIV than to have it
  (\(0.95/0.05 = 19\)).
\item
  A positive test is 13.2 times \emph{less} likely when the person does
  not have HIV than when they have it (\(0.074/0.977 = 1/13.2\)).
\item
  The product of these ratios is \(19(1/13.2) = 1.44\).
\end{itemize}

Since posterior is proportional to the product of prior and likelihood,
a person in this risk group who tests positive is 1.44 times more likely
to not have HIV than to have HIV.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The posterior probabilities of not having HIV and having HIV are in a
  1.44 to 1 ratio, the so the posterior probability of not having HIV is
  \(1.44/(1+1.44) = 0.59\) and the posterior probability of having HIV
  is 0.41.
\item
  Yes, the posterior probability is influenced by the prior probability.
  Even though the prior probability of 5\% is still relatively small in
  absolute terms, the posterior probability given a positive test is not
  close to 50/50.
\end{enumerate}

Exercise~\ref{exr-bayes-elisa}}

\tabularnewline

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead

\endlastfoot
Carries HIV & 0.005 & 0.977 & 0.0049 & 0.0622 \\
Does not carry HIV & 0.995 & 0.074 & 0.0736 & 0.9378 \\
sum & 1.000 & NA & 0.0785 & 1.0000 \\

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-bayes-best-player}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-bayes-best-player}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Hypotheses are which player is best (A, B, C). Evidence is that A
  beats B. The likelihood is the probability that A beats B given each
  of the best players.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If A is best, probability A beats B is 2/3.
\item
  If B is best, probability A beats B is 1/3.
\item
  If C is best, probability A beats B is 1/2.
\end{itemize}

Compute the posterior probabilities as in the following Bayes table.

\begin{table}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{l|r|r|r|r}
\hline
best\_player & prior & likelihood\_A\_beats\_B & product & posterior\\
\hline
A & 0.50 & 0.6667 & 0.3333 & 0.6349\\
\hline
B & 0.35 & 0.3333 & 0.1167 & 0.2222\\
\hline
C & 0.15 & 0.5000 & 0.0750 & 0.1429\\
\hline
Total & 1.00 & 1.5000 & 0.5250 & 1.0000\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  A's probability of being the best increased, which makes sense because
  A won the match. B's probability of being the best decreased
  considerably, which makes sense because B lost the match. C's
  probability of being the best decreased slightly, despite C not being
  involved in the match. (We have now observed some actual evidence in
  A's favor while we don't have any observations about C yet, and this
  information asymmetry results in a decrease in C's posterior
  probability.)
\item
  Hypotheses are which player is best (A, B, C). Evidence is that B
  beats A. The likelihood is the probability that B beats A given each
  of the best players.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If A is best, probability B beats A is 1/3.
\item
  If B is best, probability B beats A is 2/3.
\item
  If C is best, probability B beats A is 1/2.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{l|r|r|r|r}
\hline
best\_player & prior & likelihood\_B\_beats\_A & product & posterior\\
\hline
A & 0.50 & 0.3333 & 0.1667 & 0.3509\\
\hline
B & 0.35 & 0.6667 & 0.2333 & 0.4912\\
\hline
C & 0.15 & 0.5000 & 0.0750 & 0.1579\\
\hline
Total & 1.00 & 1.5000 & 0.4750 & 1.0000\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  A's probability of being the best decreased, which makes sense because
  A lost the match. B's probability of being the best increased, which
  makes sense because B won the match. C's probability of being the best
  changed slightly, despite C not being involved in the match.
\item
  The prior is the posterior from the first part. Evidence is that A
  beats C. The likelihood is the probability that A beats C given each
  of the best players.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If A is best, probability A beats C is 2/3.
\item
  If B is best, probability A beats C is 1/2.
\item
  If C is best, probability A beats C is 1/3.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}
\centering

\hline
best\_player & prior & likelihood\_A\_beats\_C & product & posterior\\
\hline
A & 0.6349 & 0.6667 & 0.4233 & 0.7273\\
\hline
B & 0.2222 & 0.5000 & 0.1111 & 0.1909\\
\hline
C & 0.1429 & 0.3333 & 0.0476 & 0.0818\\
\hline

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  By winning both matches, A's probability of being the best has
  increased considerably. By losing their only matches, B's and C's
  probabilities of being the best have decreased considerably.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-bayes-best-player-predict}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-bayes-best-player-predict}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  You'd pick A and your subjective probability of being correct is 0.5.
\item
  Use the law of total probability, conditioning on who is the best
  player (A, B, C) \begin{align*}
  \text{P}(\text{A beats B}) & = \text{P}(\text{A beats B}|A)\text{P}(A) + \text{P}(\text{A beats B}|B)\text{P}(B) + \text{P}(\text{A beats B}|C)\text{P}(C)\\
  & = (2/3)(0.5) + (1/3)(0.35) + (1/2)(0.15) = 0.525
  \end{align*}
\item
  Given that A beats B, we would predict A to be the best player, and we
  would have probability 0.6349 of being correct.
\item
  Given that B beats A, we would predict B to be the best player, and we
  would have probability 0.4912 of being correct.
\item
  Use the law of total probability, conditioning on the result of the
  first match (A beats B or B beats A). \begin{align*}
  \text{P}(\text{correct}) & = \text{P}(\text{correct} | \text{A beats B})\text{P}(\text{A beats B}) + \text{P}(\text{correct} | \text{B beats A})  \text{P}(\text{B beats A})\\
  & = (0.6349)(0.5250) + (0.4912)(0.4750) = 0.5666
  \end{align*} The information gained from observing the first match
  increases our probability of being correct from 0.5 to 0.5666.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-independent-geometric}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-independent-geometric}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) can take values 1, 2, 3, \(\ldots\). Even though it is unlikely
  that \(X\) is very large, there is no fixed upper bound. Even though
  \(X\) can take infinitely many values, \(X\) is a discrete random
  variables because it takes \emph{countably} many possible values.
\item
  \(X= 1\) only if she makes her first attempt, so
  \(\text{P}(X = 1) = 0.4\). If Maya does this every practice, then in
  about 40\% of practices she will make her first three pointer on her
  first attempt.
\item
  \(X= 2\) only if she misses her first attempt and makes her second
  attempt, so since the attempts are independent
  \(\text{P}(X = 2) = (0.6)(0.4)=0.24\). If Maya does this every
  practice, then in about 24\% of practices she will make her first
  three pointer on her second attempt.
\item
  In order for \(X\) to be 3, Maya must miss her first two attempts and
  make her third. Since the attempts are independent
  \(\text{P}(X=3)=(1-0.4)^2(0.4)=0.144\). If Maya does this every
  practice, then in about 14.4\% of practices she will make her first
  three pointer on her third attempt.
\item
  The key is to realize that Maya requires more than 3 attempts to
  obtain her first success if and only if the first 5 attempts are
  failures. Therefore, \[
  P(X > 3) = (1-0.4)^3  = 0.216
  \]
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-branching-extinction}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-branching-extinction}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Let \(D\) be the probability that the original microorganism dies
  after the first minute; \(\textrm{P}(D) = 1/4\). Condition on the
  first ``step'' and use the law of total probability \[
  p = \textrm{P}(E) = \textrm{P}(E|D)\textrm{P}(D) + \textrm{P}(E|D^c)\textrm{P}(D^c) = (1)(1/4) + \textrm{P}(E|D^c)(3/4)
  \] \(\textrm{P}(E|D) = 1\) since if the first microorganism dies the
  population goes extinct immediately.

  The key is to find an expression for \(\textrm{P}(E|D^c)\) in terms of
  \(p\). If the first microorganism does not die (\(D^c\)) there are 2
  microorganisms at the start of the second minute; let's call them
  Marge and Homer. In order for the population to go extinct, we need
  Marge and all her descendants to go extinct, and the same for Homer.
  But Marge is just a single microorganism, so the probability that her
  line eventually goes extinct is \(p\); similarly the probability that
  Homer's line goes extinct is \(p\). Since all microorganisms behave
  independently, the probability that both Marge and Homer's lines
  eventually go extinct is \((p)(p)=p^2\). That is,
  \(\textrm{P}(E | D^c) = p^2\).

  Plugging into the equation above yields \[
  p = (1)(1/4) + p^2(3/4)
  \]

  Solve (quadratic formula) this equation to get\footnote{Technically,
    there are two solutions, 1 and \(1/3\). There are some technical
    justifications that can be made to show that the extinction
    probability is the smaller of the two solutions, but this is beyond
    our scope.} \(p= 1/3\). The probability that the population
  eventually goes extinct is 1/3. This microorganism population is 2
  times more likely to survive forever than to go extinct!
\item
  The process is the same as the above, with 3/4 replaced by \(s\) \[
  p = (1)(1-s) + p^2s
  \] Solving gives two solutions, 1 and \(1/s - 1\). However, if
  \(s<1/2\) then \(1/s - 1 > 1\), which is not a valid probability.
  Therefore the probability of eventual extinction is 1 if
  \(s \le 1/2\), and \(1/s - 1<1\) if \(s > 1/2\).
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-best-of-five}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-best-of-five}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  It is helpful to construct a two-way table to answer the following
  questions.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}
    >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1944}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1944}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1944}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2222}}
    >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1944}}@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  & \emph{x} & & & \\
  & 3 & 4 & 5 & Total \\
  A wins & 0.553 = 0.166 & 3(0.553)(0.45) = 0.225 &
  6(0.553)(0.45)2 = 0.202 & 0.593 \\
  A does not win & 0.453 = 0.091 & 3(0.453)(0.55) = 0.150 &
  6(0.453)(0.55)2 = 0.165 & 0.407 \\
  Total & 0.258 & 0.375 & 0.368 & 1 \\
  \end{longtable}

  There is only one outcome for which A wins in 3 games: AAA. There are
  three outcomes in which A wins in 4 games: AABA, ABAA, BAAA. (Not AAAB
  because then the series would be over in 3 games.) Since the games are
  independent, an outcome like AABA has probability \((0.55^3)(0.45)\),
  so the probability that A wins in 4 games is \(3(0.55^3)(0.45)\).
  There are six outcomes in which A wins in 5 games: AABBA, ABABA,
  BAABA, ABBAA, BABAA, BBAAA. (Not outcomes like AAABB or AABAB because
  then the series would be over in 3 or 4 games.) Since the games are
  independent, an outcome like AABBA has probability
  \((0.55^3)(0.45)^2\), so the probability that A wins in 5 games is
  \(6(0.55^3)(0.45)\). You can fill in the rest of the table similarly.

  The probability that team A wins the series in 3 games is
  \(\text{P}(X=3, A) = 0.55^3=0.166\).
\item
  Either the stronger team wins 3 in a row or loses 3 in a row. The
  probability is \(0.55^3+(1-0.55)^3=0.2575\).
\item
  The probability that team A wins the series is the sum of first row:
  \(\text{P}(A) = 0.593\).
\item
  No.~\(\text{P}(X=3, A) = 0.55^3=0.166 \neq 0.152 = (0.2575)(0.593) = \text{P}(X=3)\text{P}(A)\).
  Alternatively,
  \(\text{P}(X = 3 | A) = 0.166/0.593 = 0.2799 \neq 0.2575 = \text{P}(X = 3)\).
  Given that \(A\) wins the series the series it more likely to end in 3
  games than when B wins the series.
\item
  Total row above. \(X\) can take values 3, 4, or 5. Consider first the
  ways in which the stronger team wins in 4 games: AABA, ABAA, BAAA.
  (For example AABA, means the stronger team wins game 1, 2, and 4, and
  the weaker team wins game 3). Each of these outcomes has probability
  \(0.55^3(0.45)\) so the probability that team A wins in 4 games in
  \(3(0.55)^3(0.45)\). Similarly, the probability that team B wins in 4
  games is \(3(0.45)^3(0.55)\). So \[
  \text{P}(X = 4) = 3(0.55)^3(0.45) + 3(0.45)^3(0.55) = 0.3750
  \] You could find \(\text{P}(X=5)\) in a similar way, or just use the
  fact that the probabilities have to add up to 1. The distribution of
  \(X\) is given by the following table. \begin{align*}
   x & \qquad & & \qquad \text{P}(X = x)\\
   3 & \qquad & & \qquad 0.2575\\
   4 & \qquad & & \qquad 0.3750\\
   5 & \qquad & & \qquad 0.3675\\
  \end{align*}
\end{enumerate}

The posterior is the same. It doesn't matter if the posterior is updated

Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-birthday}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-tactile-birthday}

Label 365 cards with the numbers 1 through 365. Shuffle the cards and

numbers, then \(B\) does not occur; otherwise \(B\) occurs.

Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-geometric}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-tactile-geometric}

Create a spinner with two sectors, one sector labeled ``make'' which
accounts for 40\% of the area, and the other 60\% labeled ``miss''.
Spinner the spinner until it lands on ``make'' and then stop; let \(X\)
be the total number of spins.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-tactile-collector}

Create a spinner with three equal sectors, labeled 1, 2, 3. Spin the
spinner 3 times. Let \(X\) be the number of distinct numbers the spinner
lands on; for example if the spinner lands on 3 then 1 then 3, then
\(X\) is 2. Let \(Y\) be the number of spins that land on 1.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-dartboard}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-tactile-dartboard}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A Uniform(0, 12) spinner is basically a clock. It goes from 0 to 12 in
  equally spaced increments. See Figure~\ref{fig-spinner-uniform-0-12}.
\item
  To simulate \(X\), flip the coin to determine if the point is in the
  ``east'' or ``west'' and then spin the Uniform(0, 12) spinner to
  determine how far from the center in the east or west direction. Let
  the result of the spin be \(U_1\). If the coin lands on heads (east)
  set \(X=U_1\); if the coin lands on tails (west) set \(X=-U_1\). To
  simulate \(Y\), spin the spinner again to get \(U_2\), and flip the
  coin again. If the result of the flip is heads (north) then set
  \(Y = U_2\); if the result of the flip is tails (south) then set
  \(Y=-U_2\). Compute the distance from \((X, Y)\) to (0, 0) as
  \(R=\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}\). If \(R>12\) the dart would land off the board,
  so just discard the repetition and try again.
\item
  Exercise~\ref{exr-probspace-dartboard-b} shows that \(R\) is not
  uniformly distributed between 0 and 12. In particular, \(R\) is more
  likely to be between 11 and 12 than it is to be between 0 and 1.
  Therefore a Uniform(0, 12) spinner would not be appropriate.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/fig-spinner-uniform-0-12-1.png}}

}

\caption{\label{fig-spinner-uniform-0-12}A continuous \emph{Uniform(0,
12)} spinner. Only selected rounded values are displayed, but in the
idealized model the spinner is infinitely precise so that any real
number between 0 and 12 is a possible outcome.}

\end{figure}%

Exercise~\ref{exr-tactile-dartboard-b}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-tactile-dartboard-b}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-computer-simulation-geometric}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-computer-simulation-geometric}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_success }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.4}

\CommentTok{\# define a function that takes as an input a sequence of 0s and 1s (omega)}
\CommentTok{\# and returns when the first 1 occurs}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_until\_first\_success(omega):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(omega):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ w }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# the +1 is for zero{-}based indexing}

\CommentTok{\# Either of the following probability spaces works        }
\CommentTok{\# P = Bernoulli(p\_success) ** inf}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [p\_success, }\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ p\_success], size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ inf)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_until\_first\_success)}

\NormalTok{(RV(P) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ X).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     ((0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, ...), 4)
1     ((0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, ...), 14)
2     ((1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, ...), 1)
3     ((1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, ...), 1)
4     ((1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, ...), 1)
5     ((1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, ...), 1)
6     ((1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, ...), 1)
7     ((0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, ...), 2)

\end{verbatim}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-computer-simulation-dartboard}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-computer-simulation-dartboard}

In the code below

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{Uniform(0,\ 12)\ **\ 2} corresponds to the two spins
\item
  \texttt{BoxModel({[}-1,\ 1{]},\ size\ =\ 2)} corresponds to the two
  coin flips
\item
  \texttt{Uniform(0,\ 12)\ **\ 2\ *\ BoxModel({[}-1,\ 1{]},\ size\ =\ 2)}
  simulates a pair which we unpack and define as \texttt{RV}s
  \texttt{U,\ F}, but \texttt{U} is itself a pair and so is \texttt{F}.
\item
  \texttt{U{[}0{]}} is the first spin and \texttt{F{[}0{]}} is the first
  flip.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U, F }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ F[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ F[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sqrt(X }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{(U }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ F }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ R).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-approximate-probability-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-approximate-probability-collector}

\textbf{Part 1}

See previous solutions which discuss how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs.

Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs, say 10000.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{P}(X = 2)\): Divide the number of repetitions
  with \(X = 2\) by the total number of repetitions
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{P}(Y = 1)\): Divide the number of repetitions
  with \(Y = 1\) by the total number of repetitions
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{P}(X = 2, Y = 1)\): Divide the number of
  repetitions with \(X = 2\) and \(Y=1\) by the total number of
  repetitions
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part 2}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_distinct(u):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(u))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_distinct)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_eq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.6619
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y.count\_eq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.4512
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{((x }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ x.count()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.2213
\end{verbatim}

\textbf{Part 3}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.tabulate(normalize }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-approximate-probability-geometric}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-approximate-probability-geometric}

\textbf{Part 1}

See previous solutions for description of how to simulate values of
\(X\).

Simulate many values of \(X\) and summarize the simulate values and
their relative frequencies to approximate the distribution of \(X\).

To approximate \(\textrm{P}(X  > 3)\): divide the number of repetitions
with \(X>3\) by the total number of repetitions.

\textbf{Part 2}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_success }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.4}

\CommentTok{\# define a function that takes as an input a sequence of 0s and 1s (omega)}
\CommentTok{\# and returns when the first 1 occurs}
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_until\_first\_success(omega):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(omega):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ w }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1} \CommentTok{\# the +1 is for zero{-}based indexing}

\CommentTok{\# Either of the following probability spaces works        }
\CommentTok{\# P = Bernoulli(p\_success) ** inf}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [p\_success, }\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ p\_success], size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ inf)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_until\_first\_success)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

1     2
2     1
3     2
4     8
5     4
6     5
7     1
8     1
....  .
9999  3
\end{verbatim}

\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to

\textbf{Part 1}

See previous solutions for how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs.

Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs, say 10000. To approximate:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X < 3.5)\): divide number of repetitions with \(X<3.5\)
  by the total number of repetitions
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(Y > 2.7)\): divide number of repetitions with \(Y>2.7\)
  by the total number of repetitions
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X < 3.5, Y > 2.7)\): divide number of repetitions with
  \(X<3.5\) and \(Y>2.7\) by the total number of repetitions
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part 2}

We usually summarize simulated values of continuous random variables
with histogram.

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-approximate-moe-birthday}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-approximate-moe-birthday}

Simulate 10000 repetitions and find the relative frequency of
repetitions on which at least 2 people share a birthday. The margin of
error is \(1/\sqrt{10000} = 0.01\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{30}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel(}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{365}\NormalTok{)), size }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ n)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_distinct(u):}
  \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(u))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_distinct)}

\NormalTok{B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ n)}

\NormalTok{p\_hat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ B.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).count\_eq(}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/} \DecValTok{10000}

\NormalTok{p\_hat}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
0.7058
\end{verbatim}

We estimate (with 95\% confidence) that the probability that at least
two people in a group of 30 share the same birthday is 0.706 with a
margin of error of 0.01. In other words, we estimate (with 95\%
confidence) that the probability that at least two people in a group of
30 share the same birthday is between 0.7 and 0.72.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-approximate-moe-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-approximate-moe-collector}

The margin of error for any single probability would be
\(1/\sqrt{10000} = 0.01\), but since we are estimating many
probabilities simultaneously we would use a margin of error of
\(2\times 0.01\). For example, if the simulated relative frequency of
\(X = 2\) is 0.662, then we approximate \(\textrm{P}(X = 2)\) to be
0.662 with a margin of error of 0.02; in other words, we estimate that
\(\textrm{P}(X = 2)\) is between 0.642 and 0.682.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-ev-class-size}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-ev-class-size}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) takes the value 210 with probability 1/5 and 35 with probability
  4/5.
\item
  \(\text{E}(X) = 210(1/5) + 35(4/5)=70\) is the average number of
  students per class from the instructors' perspective. If we randomly
  select an instructor, record the number of students in the
  instructor's class, and repeat, the long run average number of
  students will be 70.
\item
  \(\text{P}(X = \text{E}(X)) = \text{P}(X = 70) = 0\). No instructor
  has a class whose size is equal to the average class size (from the
  instructor's perspective).
\item
  \(Y\) takes the value 210 with probability 210/350 and 35 with
  probability 140/350.
\item
  \(\text{E}(Y) = 210(210/350) + 35(140/350)=140\) is the average number
  of students per class from the students' perspective. If we randomly
  select a student, record the number of students in the selected
  student's class, and repeat, the long run average number of students
  will be 140.
\item
  \(\text{P}(Y = \text{E}(Y)) = \text{P}(Y = 140) = 0\). No student is
  in a class whose size is equal to the average class size (from the
  students' perspective).
\item
  Colleges usually report average class size from the instructor/class
  perspective, which in this case would be 70 students. From the
  students' perspective, the average class size is not even close to 70!
  In fact, it's twice that size. Some students (140 of them, which is
  40\% of the total of 350 students) have the benefit of a small class
  size of 35. But most students (210 of them, which is 60\% of the
  students) are stuck in a large class of 210 students. In other words,
  most students would be pretty seriously misled if they chose this
  college based on the advertised average class size of 35 students per
  class. From the students' perspective, it seems that 140 is the more
  relevant average to report. However, neither average really adequately
  represents what is happening here: there is wide variability in class
  sizes between large and small.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-ev-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-ev-collector}

See previous for solutions for how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs

\textbf{Part 1}

Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs, say 10000

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{E}(X)\): average the simulated \(X\) values
  (sum the 10000 simulated \(X\) values and divide by 10000)
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{E}(Y)\): average the simulated \(Y\) values
  (sum the 10000 simulated \(Y\) values and divide by 10000)
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{E}(X^2)\): average the simulated \(X^2\)
  values (square each simulated \(X\) value then sum the 10000 \(X^2\)
  values and divide by 10000)
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{E}(XY)\): average the simulated \(XY\) values
  (for each \((X, Y)\) pair compute the product \(XY\) then sum the
  10000 \(XY\) values and divide by 10000)
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Part 2}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_distinct(u):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(u))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_distinct)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_eq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{x\_and\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ x\_and\_y[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
2.1084
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
1.0109
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}

\end{verbatim}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-64-3.png}

\textbf{Part 2}

\(X\) will have larger standard deviation than \(Y\). The values of
\(X\) range from 2 to 8 while the values of \(Y\) only range from 1 to
4. Also, the values of \(Y\) tend to be closer to their mean (around
3.0) than the values of \(X\) are to their mean (around 5).

The values of \(X\) can be anywhere from 0 to 3 units away from the mean
of 5, but more values are closer than farther; we might estimate the SD
to be less than 1.5. (Remember, the squaring then averaging then taking
the square root makes it hard to guess the actual number)

We would estimate the SD of \(Y\) to be less that of \(X\), and maybe a
little less than 1, since a large percentage of values are between 2 and
4 (hence less than 1 unit away from the mean).

\textbf{Part 3}

To approximate \(\textrm{Var}(X)\):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulate many \(X\) values and compute the average of the simulated
  values
\item
  Square each simulated \(X\) value and compute the average of the
  squared values
\item
  Subrtract the square of the average from part a) from the average of
  the squares in part b).
\end{enumerate}

Take the square of the variance to approximate the standard deviation.

Similarly for \(Y\).

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-covariance-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-covariance-collector}

\begin{exercise}[]\protect\hypertarget{exr-simulation-covariance-collector}{}\label{exr-simulation-covariance-collector}

~

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain how you could, in principle, conduct a simulation by hand and
  use the results to approximate \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Write Symbulate code to conduct a simulation and approximate the
  covariance and correlation.
\item
  Compute \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\) and \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y)\).
\item
  Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent? Explain your reasoning.
\end{enumerate}

\end{exercise}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  See previous solutions for how to simulate \((X, Y)\) pairs.

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Simulate many \((X, Y)\) pairs
  \item
    Compute the average of the simulated \(X\) values (i.e., sum the
    simulated values of \(X\) and divide by the number of simulated
    values) to approximate \(\textrm{E}(X)\)
  \item
    Compute the average of the simulated \(Y\) values (i.e., sum the
    simulated values of \(Y\) and divide by the number of simulated
    values) to approximate \(\textrm{E}(Y)\)
  \item
    Find the product \(XY\) for each pair, and compute the average value
    of the products (i.e., sum the simulated values of \(XY\) and divide
    by the number of simulated pairs) to approximate \(\textrm{E}(XY)\)
  \item
    Subract the approximations
    \(\textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y)\) to approximate
    \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y)\)
  \end{itemize}
\item
  See code below
\item
  In Exercise~\ref{exr-distribution-intro-collector3} we found the joint
  distribution of \(X\) and \(Y\) in a previous problem, and also
  computed \(\textrm{E}(X) = 57/27 = 2.111\) and \(\textrm{E}(Y)=1\). In
  computing \(\textrm{E}(XY)\) many of the terms are 0, either because
  one of \(Y\) is 0 or because the probability of the pair is 0 \[
  \textrm{E}(XY) = (1)(3)(1/27) + (2)(1)(6/27) + (2)(2)(6/27) + (3)(1)(6/27) + 0 = 57/27 = 2.111
  \] So
  \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \textrm{E}(XY) - \textrm{E}(X)\textrm{E}(Y) = 57/27 - (57/27)(1) = 0\).
  Therefore \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y) = 0\) and \(X\) and \(Y\) are
  uncorrelated.
\item
  Even though the covariance is 0, \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent.
  For example \(\textrm{P}(X = 1) = 3/27\) but
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 1|Y=1) = 0\). Knowing the value of \(Y\) changes the
  distribution of \(X\), and vice versa.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-covariance-1}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-covariance-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \(X\) takes values 0, 1, 2, 3. One outcome corresponds to each of
  \(X=0\) (LLL) and \(X=3\) (WWW), and 3 outcomes correpond to each of
  \(X=1\) (WLL, LWL, LLW) and \(X=2\) (WWL, WLW, LWW), but the outcomes
  are not equally likely.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}llr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \(x\) & Outcomes & \(\textrm{P}(X = X)\) \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  0 & LLL & \((1)(18/38)^0(20/38)^3=0.146\) \\
  1 & WLL, LWL, LLW & \((3)(18/38)^1(20/38)^2=0.394\) \\
  2 & WWL, WLW, LWW & \((3)(18/38)^2(20/38)^1=0.354\) \\
  3 & WWW & \((1)(18/38)^3(20/38)^0=0.106\) \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  \(\text{E}(X)=0(0.146)+1(0.394)+2(0.354)+3(0.106)= 1.42\).
\item
  \(\text{E}(X^2)=0^2(0.146)+1^2(0.394)+2^2(0.354)+3^2(0.106)= 2.76\),
  so \(\textrm{Var}(X)=0.75\).
\item
  In the first 3 bets Yolanda wins the same number of games as Xavier,
  and Yolanda only plays two more games. So \(Y\) can't be more than
  \(X+2\), and \(Y\) can't be less than \(X\).
\item
  To have \(X = 2\) and \(Y=3\) we need to have exactly two wins in the
  first 3 bets (where both play) and exactly 1 win in the last 2 bets
  (Yolanda only). \[
  \text{P}(X = 2, Y = 3) = \left((3)(18/38)^2(20/38)^1\right)\left((2)(18/38)^1(20/38)^1\right) = 0.177
  \]
\item
  \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent. For example,
  \(\textrm{P}(X = 1, Y = 0)=0\) which is not
  \(\textrm{P}(X=1)\textrm{P}(Y=0)\).
\item
  \(\textrm{P}(X + Y = 4) = 0.0883+0.0981 = 0.1864\).
\item
  Sum the appropriate values from the joint distribution table.

  \begin{longtable}[]{@{}lr@{}}
  \toprule\noalign{}
  \(z\) & \(\textrm{P}(X+Y = z)\) \\
  \midrule\noalign{}
  \endhead
  \bottomrule\noalign{}
  \endlastfoot
  0 & 0.0404 \\
  1 & 0.0727 \\
  2 & 0.1417 \\
  3 & 0.1963 \\
  4 & 0.1864 \\
  5 & 0.1766 \\
  6 & 0.1089 \\
  7 & 0.0530 \\
  8 & 0.0238 \\
  \end{longtable}
\item
  Use the table from the previous part to compute
  \(\text{E}(X+Y) = 3.79\).
\item
  \(\textrm{E}(XY) = 4.11\) so
  \(\textrm{Cov}(X, Y) =  4.11 - (1.42)(2.37) = 0.75\). There is a
  positive association; if \(X\) is large that means Xavier won a lot of
  games so Yolanda tends to win more games too.
\item
  \(\textrm{Corr}(X, Y) = 0.75/\sqrt{(0.75)(1.25)} = 0.77\).
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-condition-collector}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-condition-collector}

Approximate the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=1\):

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Simulate \((X, Y)\) pair
\item
  If \(X\neq1\) discard the repetition, otherwise keep
\item
  Repeat until 10000 repetitions with \(X=1\) are obtained
\item
  Summarize the simulated values of \(Y\) from these repetitions to
  approximate the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X = 1\)
\item
  To approximate \(\textrm{P}(Y = 0 | X=1)\) count the number of
  repetitions with \(Y=0\) and divide by 10000 (remember, all of the
  repetitions have \(X = 1\))
\end{itemize}

Approximate the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=0\)
similarly, with a different simulation of 10000 \((X, Y)\) pairs that
satisfy \(Y=0\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_distinct(u):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(u))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_distinct)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, count\_eq(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y\_given\_Xeq1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ( Y }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-condition-dartboard}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-condition-dartboard}

In the code below

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{Uniform(0,\ 12)\ **\ 2} corresponds to the two spins
\item
  \texttt{BoxModel({[}-1,\ 1{]},\ size\ =\ 2)} corresponds to the two
  coin flips
\item
  \texttt{Uniform(0,\ 12)\ **\ 2\ *\ BoxModel({[}-1,\ 1{]},\ size\ =\ 2)}
  simulates a pair which we unpack and define as \texttt{RV}s
  \texttt{U,\ F}, but \texttt{U} is itself a pair and so is \texttt{F}.
\item
  \texttt{U{[}0{]}} is the first spin and \texttt{F{[}0{]}} is the first
  flip.
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U, F }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Uniform(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ BoxModel([}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ F[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ F[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sqrt(X }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{( (U }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ F }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ R) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (R }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-simulation-condition-continuous-dice}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-simulation-condition-continuous-dice}

We condition on \(X\) being ``close to'' 3.5, say within 0.1 of 3.5

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Uniform(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(P, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{( (X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y) }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{3.5}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Index Result
0     (3.5325513941092206, 2.300787321400952)
1     (3.501091953328525, 2.1404935681543145)
2     (3.428616885448106, 1.72311079700803)
3     (3.4630746774270067, 2.222879027364401)
4     (3.475965128641322, 2.2726327240412076)
5     (3.46858144815081, 2.2912508431156158)
6     (3.530115511492812, 1.8730792019211373)
7     (3.5662504933472, 1.9821617615954978)
8     (3.4727845306207574, 2.4452059965472883)
9     (3.416446987819203, 2.054345113575841)
\end{verbatim}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y\_given\_Xeq3p5 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ( Y }\OperatorTok{|}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{3.5}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\textless{}} \FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{) ).sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{y\_given\_Xeq3p5.plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-86-13.png}

The true conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=3.5\) is
Uniform(1.75, 2.5). We see that the approximate distribution is a little
rough at the boundaries (near 1.75 and 2.5), because of the ``close to
3.5'' approximation. But we would not be able to simulate the
conditional distribution given \(X=3.5\) without more sophisticated
methods.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-sensitivity-dartboard-bvn}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-sensitivity-dartboard-bvn}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sigma }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{X, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Normal(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, sigma) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sqrt(X }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ Y).sim(}\DecValTok{1000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-87-15.png}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{R.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{).plot()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-88-17.png}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ dartboard\_sim(sigma):}
\NormalTok{  X, Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ RV(Normal(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, sigma) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
  
\NormalTok{  R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sqrt(X }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
  
\NormalTok{  r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ R.sim(}\DecValTok{10000}\NormalTok{)}
  
  \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ r.count\_lt(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ r.count(), r.count\_gt(}\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ r.count(), r.mean()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sigmas }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{5.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{results }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([dartboard\_sim(sigma) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ sigma }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sigmas])}

\NormalTok{plt.figure()}
\NormalTok{plt.plot(sigmas, results[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}sigma\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Approximate P(X  \textless{} 1)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\includegraphics[width=5.5in,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{language-simulation-exercises_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-90-19.png}

\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}sigma\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}Approximate P(X  \textgreater{} 12)\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{)}

\chapter{Chapter 7 Exercise
Solutions}\label{chapter-7-exercise-solutions}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Solution to
Exercise~\ref{exr-card-counting}}{Solution to Exercise~}}\label{solution-to-exr-card-counting}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Partition into aces and others. Over many 5 card hands, about 3.99\%
  contain exactly 2 aces. \[
  \frac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}} 
  \]
\item
  Partition into hearts and others. Over many 5 card hands, about
  27.43\% contain exactly 2 hearts. \[
  \frac{\binom{13}{2}\binom{39}{3}}{\binom{52}{5}} 
  \]
\item
  Partition into ace of hearts, the 3 other aces, the 12 other hearts,
  and the 36 other cards. Over many 5 card hands, about 0.87\% contain
  the ace of hearts, exactly one more ace, and exactly one more heart.
  \[
  \frac{\binom{1}{1}\binom{3}{1}\binom{12}{1}\binom{36}{2}}{\binom{52}{5}} 
  \]
\item
  You need to choose 2 cards from 1 face, and one from the others. There
  are 4 possibilities for the face value that gets 2 cards. Over many 5
  card hands, about 26.37\% contains at least one card from each of the
  four suits. \[
  4\frac{\binom{13}{2}\binom{13}{1}\binom{13}{1}\binom{13}{1}}{\binom{52}{5}} 
  \]
\item
  There are 13 choices for the face value of the four-of-a-kind, and 48
  choices for the other card. Over many 5 card hands, about 0.02\%
  contain a four-of-a-kind. \[
  \frac{(13)(48)}{\binom{52}{5}} 
  \]
\item
  You deal more than 4 cards only if the first 4 cards are not hearts:
  0.30382 \[
  \left(\frac{39}{52}\right)\left(\frac{38}{51}\right)\left(\frac{37}{50}\right)\left(\frac{36}{49}\right)
  \]
\end{enumerate}
